title: How BRIEFR is built, and why — the long version
text: Preface How BRIEFR is built, and why — the long version This is not a quick reference. It's written to be read start to finish, the way you'd work through a textbook chapter by chapter: a concept, then real code, then the reasoning behind it, then questions to check you actually absorbed it — not just recognized it. How to study this, not just read it BRIEFR's own internal docs/LEARNING_PATH.md has the right method, and this book follows it at full depth across the whole codebase instead of four modules: you don't learn a system by reading about it, you learn it by tracing it and re-explaining it in your own words. Read one chapter fully — the concept, the code, the reasoning. Open the real file in the repo and find the exact function discussed. Read it in context, not just the excerpt here. Close the chapter and explain it out loud, unaided, as if to an interviewer who will ask a follow-up. Answer every self-check question at the end without looking back. If you can't, that's the signal to re-read — not a failure, that's what the question is for. Move on only when you could defend a design decision, not just describe it. Part 0 covers concepts you'll need before anything else makes sense — read it first even if some of it is familiar, because a few terms (watermark, hub suppression, operational priority) are BRIEFR-specific and get redefined here. Before that, the System Design page gives you the whole shape of the system in four pictures — worth a first look now, and worth returning to after every Part as a reality check.

title: Concepts primer
text: Part 0 · Foundations Concepts primer You have a security background, so some of this will be review — skim those and slow down for the ones marked BRIEFR-specific. Every concept here gets reused, unexplained, in every chapter that follows.

title: The engineering patterns you'll see everywhere
text: Part 0 · Mechanics The engineering patterns you'll see everywhere Fourteen recurring ideas. None are BRIEFR inventions — they're standard patterns — but you'll meet every one of them again by name in the chapters ahead, so it's worth having a crisp definition of each before that happens. A word on why this book leads with mechanics rather than jumping straight to main.py : almost every "why did they build it this way" answer in the chapters ahead turns out to be one of these fourteen patterns applied to a specific problem. Once you recognize the pattern, the specific application stops looking arbitrary. Client–server & REST The browser (client) never touches the database directly. It sends HTTP requests to the FastAPI backend (server), which is the only thing with database credentials. "REST" here just means: resources are nouns in the URL ( /api/cves/{id} ), and the HTTP verb (GET/POST/DELETE) says what you're doing to that noun. Why it matters here: every security boundary in BRIEFR sits at this line. The frontend enforces nothing — it just doesn't render buttons a user can't use. Real authorization always happens in dependencies.py , server-side. Session cookie vs. JWT A session cookie is an opaque ID; the server looks it up in a table to find out who you are. A JWT (JSON Web Token) is self-describing — it carries the claims ( user_id , role ) inside itself, cryptographically signed, so the server can verify it without a database lookup. Why it matters here: BRIEFR uses both , deliberately, for different halves of the same login: a short-lived JWT access token for speed, and an opaque, database-backed refresh token for revocability. Chapter 11 is entirely about why one alone wasn't enough. Password hashing (bcrypt) You never store a password — you store bcrypt(password, salt) , a one-way function. bcrypt is deliberately slow (tunable via a "rounds" cost factor) so that even if the hash table leaks, brute-forcing it is expensive per guess. Why it matters here: BRIEFR uses bcrypt directly rather than a wrapper library — see Chapter 11 for exactly why, and for the "dummy hash" trick that closes a timing side-channel. Connection pooling Opening a new database connection is expensive (TCP handshake, auth, session setup). A pool keeps a set of connections open and hands them out to requests as needed, instead of opening/closing one per request. Why it matters here: Postgres uses a real pool (asyncpg) that can be exhausted under load, raising a specific PoolExhaustedError . SQLite, BRIEFR's dev/test fallback, has no pool at all — a fact with real consequences, in Chapter 9. Token bucket rate limiting Imagine a bucket that refills with tokens at a fixed rate and holds a maximum capacity. Every request costs one token; no tokens, no request (or it waits/gets rejected). This smooths bursts while still allowing occasional spikes, unlike a rigid "N requests per fixed minute" counter. Why it matters here: BRIEFR runs token buckets in both directions — throttling inbound clients (Chapter 12) and pacing its own outbound calls to NVD/GitHub/OTX so it never gets banned (Chapter 16). Circuit breaker Borrowed from electrical engineering: after too many consecutive failures calling a dependency, "open the circuit" — stop even trying, fail fast, for a cooldown window. This protects both your own system (no thread pool exhaustion waiting on a dead dependency) and the dependency (no hammering a service that's already down). Why it matters here: every external feed (NVD, OTX, GitHub, KEV) goes through a shared circuit breaker in resilient_client.py — Chapter 16 walks through the actual state machine. SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery) An attack where a server is tricked into making an HTTP request on the attacker's behalf — often to internal-only services (metadata endpoints, internal admin panels) the attacker couldn't reach directly. Classic vector: any feature where the server fetches a URL supplied by a user. Why it matters here: operator-supplied webhook destination URLs are exactly this shape of risk. Chapter 27 covers BRIEFR's mitigation (resolve → validate → pin) in full, with the real code. Idempotency & watermarks An operation is idempotent if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once — critical for anything that might crash mid-run and get retried. A "watermark" is a saved checkpoint (a timestamp, an ID, a commit SHA) marking how far a sync has progressed, so a resumed run starts from there rather than from the beginning — or worse, from nowhere. Why it matters here: this is the single most repeated idea in the ingest layer (Chapter 14) — every feed answers "what's my watermark, and what happens if I crash right after reading it but before saving it?" differently, and those differences are revealing. Async/await & the event loop Python's async def functions don't run in parallel threads — they cooperatively yield control at each await point, letting one thread juggle thousands of in-flight I/O operations (HTTP calls, DB queries) without blocking. It's concurrency, not parallelism. Why it matters here: nearly every backend function in this book is async def . It's also why a single asyncpg connection can't run two queries "at once" even from concurrent-looking code — a real bug class referenced in Chapter 21. ORM vs. raw SQL An ORM (SQLAlchemy, Django's ORM) maps database rows to objects and can generate SQL for you, abstracting the dialect differences between databases. Raw SQL means you write the query text yourself. Why it matters here: BRIEFR deliberately has no ORM. Every query is hand-written SQL, in two dialect-specific versions where needed (Chapter 9) — a real cost (more code, more discipline) paid for query-level control and zero abstraction-leak surprises. CVSS — Common Vulnerability Scoring System A 0–10 severity score computed from a vulnerability's technical characteristics (attack vector, complexity, privileges required, impact). It answers "how bad is this if exploited" — it says nothing about whether anyone is actually exploiting it, or whether it affects you. Why it matters here: CVSS is one of six inputs to BRIEFR's Risk Score, weighted at only 0.10 — deliberately low, because it's the least differentiating signal (Chapter 18 explains why). EPSS — Exploit Prediction Scoring System A FIRST.org model producing a 0–1 probability that a given CVE will be exploited in the wild in the next 30 days, based on observed scanning/exploitation telemetry across the internet. Unlike CVSS, it's a live, moving prediction, not a static technical rating. Why it matters here: EPSS is weighted 0.15 in the Risk Score, and its day-over-day delta (not just its level) independently feeds the Momentum component and the morning brief's "EPSS movers" section. KEV — Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (CISA) CISA's curated catalog of CVEs confirmed to have been actively exploited in real attacks — not predicted, confirmed . US federal agencies are required to patch KEV entries by a published due date. Why it matters here: KEV membership is weighted 0.25 in the Risk Score (second only to asset relevance) and independently floors the newer Threat Score at 80 regardless of anything else — Chapter 18 explains why a confirmed-exploited CVE is treated almost as a special case rather than just another weighted input. CPE — Common Platform Enumeration A structured naming scheme for software/hardware ( cpe:2.3:a:vendor:product:version:... ) that NVD attaches to CVEs to say precisely which versions are affected — the machine-readable version of "affects Apache 2.4.0 through 2.4.53". Why it matters here: matching your declared asset stack against CPE version ranges is the mechanical core of the 0.35-weighted asset component — Chapter 19 is the whole story of how that matching actually works, including what happens when a CVE has no CPE data at all. MITRE ATT&CK A knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques observed in real intrusions, organized into a matrix (Initial Access, Execution, Persistence, ...) with each technique given an ID like T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application). Why it matters here: ATT&CK technique IDs are the routing key for BRIEFR's detection-engineering templates (Chapter 21) and its threat-scenario narratives (Chapter 23) — a CVE maps to a technique, and the technique maps to everything downstream. Sigma rules A vendor-neutral, YAML-based format for writing detection logic once and translating it into any SIEM's native query language (Splunk SPL, Elastic KQL, Microsoft Sentinel KQL, and others) via a converter. Why it matters here: BRIEFR both fetches community Sigma rules and generates its own from templates (Chapter 21), then translates them into concrete SIEM queries for whichever platform an analyst actually runs.

title: The shape of the whole system, before the parts
text: Part 0B · System architecture The shape of the whole system, before the parts Three chapters answering the questions a "how is this actually put together" review always asks first: is it a monolith or microservices, and why; what hardware footprint the design choices actually target; and — the one that ties every later chapter together — what talks to what, and just as importantly, what was deliberately kept from talking to what.

title: Monolith by design — and why not microservices
text: Part 0B · Chapter A1 Monolith by design — and why not microservices One process, one database, one deploy artifact. The absence of microservices here isn't a gap to fill later — it's a fit to the actual problem. ROADMAP.md deploy/briefr-backend.service What "microservices" would even mean here A microservices architecture splits a system into independently deployable services, each usually owning its own database, talking to each other over the network (HTTP or a message queue), so that different teams can develop, deploy, and scale each piece separately. BRIEFR is the opposite of that on every axis: one FastAPI process ( main.py ) serves every route, one Postgres (or SQLite) database holds every table, one systemd unit ( deploy/briefr-backend.service ) is the entire deployable artifact, and the scheduler that runs feeds, scoring, and correlation lives inside that same process , not as a separate worker service. Even Procrastinate (Chapter 17) — which sounds like it might be a separate job-queue service — is a library running an in-process worker inside the same Python process, coordinating purely through shared Postgres tables, not through a network call to some other running service. Why a monolith fits this specific problem, not just "monoliths are simpler in general" The generic case for microservices is real but conditional: it pays off when different parts of a system need independent scaling (one component gets 100x the traffic of another), independent deployment cadence (different teams shipping on different schedules without blocking each other), or genuine fault isolation (one component crashing shouldn't take down an unrelated one). None of those conditions hold for BRIEFR as it's actually used. It's explicitly a single-operator tool today (ROADMAP.md's non-goals table states plainly: "Multi-tenant SaaS in V1.x" is out of scope, with schema seams left for a possible future, not built now) — there's no independent traffic pattern to scale one piece against another, because there's fundamentally one analyst's browser making requests. There's no multi-team deploy-cadence problem to solve, because one person (or a small team) maintains the whole thing. And fault isolation between, say, the correlation engine and the CVE list view is achieved more simply — and more cheaply — by the request-path discipline you've now seen enforced everywhere in this book (heavy work happens in the scheduler, never blocking a request) than by splitting them into separate network-connected services. What microservices would have actually cost here is concrete, not abstract: every cross-component call that's currently a Python function call within one process would become a network request, needing its own error handling, retries, timeouts, and versioning story — exactly the kind of complexity Chapter 16's circuit breakers and Chapter 15's locking already have to solve for BRIEFR's genuinely external dependencies (NVD, OTX, GitHub). Multiplying that same complexity across internal components that don't need it would be pure overhead, paid for a scaling and fault-isolation benefit the system doesn't currently need. The one thing that looks like a second service — and how it's actually kept separate correctly ROADMAP.md's non-goals table names the one place BRIEFR's own team considered something closer to a real second service: an optional telemetry/log-analytics sidecar referred to internally as "Jupiter" (built on ClickStack), explicitly kept optional and outside core — the table states the core app is deliberately not becoming "log firehose ingestion" and that this capability, if wanted, is "an optional Jupiter sidecar," not a rebuild of the core system's architecture. The same table rules out forking or rebuilding a tool like Kibana/HyperDX for that purpose ("use stock ClickStack for telemetry UI if needed") — the instinct to reach for off-the-shelf infrastructure rather than building and maintaining a bespoke second service is the same monolith-favoring instinct applied one level up: even the one legitimate case for "another service" gets handled by adopting an existing tool as an optional add-on, not by growing BRIEFR's own architecture into a distributed system. Also explicitly ruled out, and worth knowing precisely why: ROADMAP.md's non-goals also name "commercial SIEM replacement" and "generic LLM chat SOC" — both real products other tools already build well. BRIEFR positions itself narrowly as an intel, detection-content, and investigation pane, not a log-ingestion platform or a chatbot wrapper — a scope decision that, not coincidentally, is also what keeps the monolith viable: a SIEM's log-firehose ingestion volume is exactly the kind of workload that would eventually force a distributed architecture, and BRIEFR has deliberately scoped that requirement out rather than build toward it. Self-check Name the three usual justifications for microservices (independent scaling, independent deploy cadence, fault isolation) and explain, for each one, why it doesn't currently apply to BRIEFR. Why is the "Jupiter" telemetry sidecar not a counter-example to "BRIEFR is a monolith" — what specifically keeps it from being a second core service? If BRIEFR did become a genuine multi-tenant SaaS product, which of today's monolith assumptions would be the first to break, and why?

title: The resource-consciousness thread — designed for modest hardware
text: Part 0B · Chapter A2 The resource-consciousness thread — designed for modest hardware A recurring, mostly-unstated design bias runs through nearly every chapter in this book: keep the footprint small enough to run comfortably on a low-end VPS. This chapter names it explicitly and is honest about where it isn't yet backed by a documented number. ml/embeddings.py rate_limit.py docs/audit/PHASE_06_performance.md Naming the thread — a design bias visible only once you look across chapters No single file in this codebase says "keep memory under X gigabytes." But look back across the chapters you've already read and a consistent pattern emerges, choice after choice, each one individually justified on its own terms and collectively adding up to a system that stays lightweight: CPU-only ONNX embeddings (Chapter 24 — BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 via fastembed , no GPU, no PyTorch runtime) instead of a larger transformer model that would need meaningfully more RAM and ideally a GPU to run at reasonable speed. A single uvicorn worker (Chapter 12's rate-limiting chapter noted this explicitly — --workers 1 ) instead of a multi-process pool that would multiply baseline memory by however many workers ran. In-memory rate-limit buckets, the outbound API queue, and the read cache (Chapters 12, 16, and the API surface chapters) instead of standing up a separate Redis instance purely to hold small, ephemeral counters. SQLite as the zero-config default (Chapter 9) rather than requiring Postgres even for a first-time evaluator just trying the tool out. Free and cheap-tier hosted LLM APIs (Chapter 24) rather than self-hosting an open-weight LLM locally, which would require the single largest chunk of RAM and compute of anything in this list by a wide margin. Client-side PDF generation (Chapter 5) instead of a headless-Chromium rendering process living inside the backend. Lazy-loaded, code-split chart and export libraries on the frontend (also Chapter 5) instead of one enormous eagerly-loaded bundle. None of these were framed, in the code or docs, as "we did this to hit a RAM budget" — each has its own local justification (privacy, cost, simplicity, avoiding a new dependency). But taken together, they describe a system whose default configuration is comfortable running on genuinely modest hardware: a small VPS with a couple of CPU cores and a few gigabytes of RAM, not a dedicated machine with a GPU and dozens of gigabytes free. The honest gap: this isn't a documented, benchmarked number yet It would overstate the case to claim BRIEFR has an official "runs in 2GB RAM on 2 cores" specification — it doesn't, and it's worth being precise about that rather than inventing a certainty the project itself doesn't claim. The project's own performance audit ( docs/audit/PHASE_06_performance.md ) says so directly, listing it as an open gap in its own words: "what's missing is guidance/limits: recommended CPU/RAM/disk envelopes." The same audit's overall score of 7/10 for performance readiness reflects real, specific findings worth knowing precisely rather than a vague "needs work": the Postgres connection pool defaults to a minimum size of 1 and maximum of 10 (modest, and consistent with a small-footprint target, but also a real concurrency ceiling nobody has load-tested against); the CVE feed defaults to OFFSET-based pagination rather than the more scalable keyset pagination that already exists but is opt-in; recharts is imported statically in chart wrappers with no bundle-size budget enforced in vite.config.js ; and roughly twenty places in the db/ layer run an await execute/fetch call inside a loop, a pattern worth watching for N+1-style query cost as data volume grows. None of these are urgent given today's usage pattern (a single operator's browser), and the audit says as much — but they are the concrete reasons "how much hardware does BRIEFR actually need" doesn't yet have a number attached to it, only a design direction. What the design direction is consistent with, stated as a target rather than a guarantee Given the choices actually made — a single worker process, CPU-only small-model inference, in-memory ephemeral state instead of a separate cache service, and a SQLite path that needs no database server at all for evaluation — the natural, honest way to state the target is: this architecture is built to be comfortable on a small VPS in the low single-digit gigabytes of RAM and one or two CPU cores, for a single operator's traffic pattern — not "requires 16GB and a GPU," and not "certified to run in 512MB" either. If you're sizing a box to run this yourself, a couple of cores and 2–4GB of RAM is the range every individual choice in this system points toward, even though — per the paragraph above — nobody has yet run the load test that would turn that direction into a documented, verified number. Chapter titled "Roadmap, reversals & open gaps" later in this book lists exactly this as an open item: publishing a real recommended CPU/RAM/disk envelope, backed by measurement rather than inference from design choices. Self-check List four separate design decisions from earlier chapters that each independently reduce BRIEFR's resource footprint, and state each one's primary stated justification (which usually isn't "save RAM" directly). Why is it inaccurate to describe BRIEFR as having an official minimum hardware requirement, even though its design choices clearly point toward a lightweight footprint? Of the five concrete performance-audit findings named in this chapter, which one would you expect to matter first as CVE corpus size grows, and why?

title: How the pieces connect — and why some deliberately don't
text: Part 0B · Chapter A3 How the pieces connect — and why some deliberately don't The single most useful mental model for holding this entire codebase in your head at once: the database is the message bus, and most "why isn't X wired to Y" questions have a real, considered answer. The one connectivity fact that explains most of the others: the database is the message bus Read across every chapter so far and one structural fact keeps recurring in different clothes: the scheduler (feeds, scoring, correlation, detection-context sync, embeddings backfill) and the request path (routers) essentially never call each other's functions directly. They communicate almost entirely by writing to, and reading from, the same Postgres/SQLite tables. A scheduled job computes a correlation snapshot and writes it to a table; a router reads that table. A scheduled job upserts a CVE's EPSS score; a router reads it. This is, functionally, the same pattern a message queue or event bus gives you in a distributed system — a durable, asynchronous handoff point between producer and consumer — except BRIEFR gets it for free from the database it already needs for everything else, with no extra infrastructure. Once you see this pattern, most of the "why does A never call B directly" questions in this codebase have the same one-line answer: because A writes to a table, and B reads that table, on its own schedule. It's worth asking the alternative directly, since "just use Postgres" can look like an oversight rather than a decision: why not a real message broker — Redis Streams, RabbitMQ, Kafka — sitting between the scheduler and the API the way a textbook distributed system would? A broker earns its cost when you need at-least-once delivery semantics across process boundaries, consumer groups scaling independently of producers, or replay from an arbitrary offset — none of which apply here, because there is exactly one producer process and one consumer process, and they're the same process (Chapter A1). Adding a broker would mean a new piece of infrastructure to deploy, monitor, and keep running on every self-hosted box, purely to re-implement a durable handoff Postgres already gives BRIEFR as a side effect of tables it needs anyway. The one thing a real broker buys that a table doesn't — a push notification the instant new data lands, instead of a poll or a fixed schedule — isn't needed either: nothing in BRIEFR promises sub-second freshness, every feed already runs on its own interval, and the API's own reads are already cheap indexed lookups regardless of exactly when the row was written. This is the same "adopt a dependency only when the simpler tool genuinely can't do the job" instinct behind the monolith decision in Chapter A1, applied one layer down. A map of what's actually connected to what Connected, one-way, through the database: feeds → the cves / kev / epss_history tables → scoring reads them on request; correlation's nightly job → per-CVE snapshot tables → routers/cves.py 's correlation endpoint reads them; the embeddings backfill job → stored vectors → semantic search reads them (Chapter 24's "must use stored vectors only" rule is this exact pattern, stated as an explicit constraint rather than left implicit); webhook-alert trigger functions (Chapter 27) are called only from scheduler jobs, never from a router, and dispatch outward to Discord/Telegram/generic HTTPS — a one-way fan-out, nothing calls back in. Connected, directly, as ordinary function calls within one request: a CVE detail request calls into scoring, matching, and template-sentence generation synchronously, because those are cheap, deterministic, in-process computations appropriate for the request path (Chapter 18's whole "explainable formula, not a request-path bottleneck" design is precisely what makes this direct call safe, where a slow correlation join was not — Chapter 20's ADR-004 incident is the cautionary tale for what happens when something that should be an async, database-mediated handoff gets called synchronously instead). Deliberately not connected, and each for a stated reason: correlation and detection engineering (Chapters 20–21) never call each other — correlation only ever hands scoring a boolean escalation flag, and detection never queries correlation state at all, because the two answer genuinely independent questions (is this CVE part of a real campaign, versus what would a detection rule for it look like) that don't need each other's internals to function correctly. The security_architecture/ module (Chapter 26) deliberately does not implement its own matching or scoring logic, reusing existing functions instead — a connectivity choice as much as a code-reuse one, since a hand-rolled second implementation would be a second thing that could silently drift from the first. Generated Sigma/SIEM rules (Chapter 21) are never automatically deployed into a live SIEM — the pipeline stops at "here's a rule for a human to review and paste in," a deliberate air gap between "BRIEFR generated this" and "this is now running in production detection," because unreviewed generated content becoming live detection logic without a human in the loop is a risk nobody chose to accept. The wallboard (Chapter 30) runs its own separate cookie-session scheme rather than reusing the main JWT auth system, and the scoped search-token bearer credential (Chapter 11) is deliberately walled off from the admin permission system entirely — two different flavors of the same instinct: a narrower credential for a narrower job, not wired into the broader system. The browser never talks to the outside world directly — everything is proxied One connectivity boundary is easy to take for granted precisely because it's so consistently enforced: the React frontend never calls NVD, OTX, GitHub, or any LLM provider directly from the browser. Every external call is proxied through the FastAPI backend, which is the only thing that ever holds an API key for any of those services. This isn't a performance optimization — it's a security boundary stated in different terms than Chapter 11's authentication chapter, but built on the same underlying principle: a credential should live in exactly as many places as it needs to, and the browser, being fully visible to whoever is sitting at it, is never one of those places for a third-party API key. Self-check Explain "the database is the message bus" in your own words, and name two subsystem pairs from earlier chapters whose connection is best described this way. title: Why AI is used sparingly — the case against a bigger role, stated once
text: Part 0B · Chapter A4 Why AI is used sparingly — the case against a bigger role, stated once Every chapter so far has made one small, local "why not more ML/LLM here" argument on its own turf. This chapter pulls all of them into a single line of reasoning, because the pattern across them is the actual answer, not any one instance of it. scoring/risk.py ai/llm_router.py ml/embeddings.py ROADMAP.md The question worth asking directly: this is 2026, AI is everywhere — why isn't BRIEFR built around it? It's a fair challenge, and worth answering directly rather than deflecting to "we use some AI." BRIEFR could plausibly have been built as an LLM-first product: a chat interface over your CVE data, an agent that decides what's a priority, a model that learns your organization's risk tolerance from feedback. None of that is what got built. Instead, across every chapter in this book, AI shows up in exactly two narrow, well-fenced roles — CPU-only local embeddings for semantic similarity (Chapter 24), and hosted-LLM calls for three specific, optional enrichment tasks (Chapter 24B) — and everywhere else, a deterministic formula, a fixed lookup table, or plain code does the job instead. That's not an oversight or a resource constraint alone; it's a position, and it's visible in four separate, independently-justified decisions that happen to all point the same direction. Four decisions, one pattern: explainability beats raw predictive power for this problem Risk Score is a fixed weighted formula, not a learned model (Chapter 18). A gradient-boosted tree trained on historical exploitation data could plausibly out-predict the six-component formula BRIEFR actually ships. It wasn't built, because a security analyst asking "why is this CVE ranked above that one" needs an answer that is the computation, not an approximation of it produced by a separate explainability layer bolted onto a black box afterward. A fixed formula is also perfectly reproducible — the same CVE and asset profile score identically today and a year from now, which matters when an analyst asks why a score changed and the honest answer needs to be a specific component delta, never "the model's weights drifted during retraining." Detection rules are generated by an LLM but never auto-deployed (Chapter 21, Chapter A3). An LLM extracts detection-rule artifacts from CVE text — genuinely useful, genuinely "AI" in the loose sense — but the pipeline stops at "here's a rule for a human to review," on purpose. Generated content becoming live detection logic in a real SIEM without a human reading it first is exactly the kind of unreviewed-automation risk this project has chosen not to accept, regardless of how good the model producing it is. Semantic search stays hybrid, never vectors-alone (Chapter 24). Embeddings are excellent at "this text means something similar" and comparatively weak at exact-token matching — a CVE ID, a specific version string, an error code pasted in verbatim. Rather than trust the model to cover that gap, BRIEFR blends vector similarity with ordinary keyword search deliberately, so the two techniques cover each other's blind spots instead of asking one imperfect technique to do a job it's structurally bad at. Every LLM feature has a deterministic fallback, without exception (Chapter 24). BRIEFR must fully function for an operator who configures zero LLM API keys — a real, supported deployment mode, not an edge case — because every LLM-touched feature is additive polish layered on a core product whose correctness never depends on it. That's the constraint that keeps the previous three decisions honest: nothing in the product is allowed to become load-bearing on a model's output, so nothing has the incentive to reach for one just because it's available. "Generic LLM chat SOC" is a named non-goal, not an oversight ROADMAP.md states this as a standing decision with a reason on record, not a gap waiting to be filled: a chat-style SOC assistant is "considered a commodity" — plenty of other tools already build a general-purpose LLM chat layer over security data, and building another one wouldn't be BRIEFR's contribution. The project's actual bet is the opposite of "put a model in front of everything": pick the handful of places where a model's output is genuinely additive (summarizing, extracting structure from messy free text) and everywhere else, do the more boring thing that can be pinned down, tested, and explained exactly. That's a scope decision as much as a technical one, and it's the same instinct — see Chapter A1's non-goals table — that also keeps BRIEFR a monolith rather than a distributed system: narrow the problem on purpose, rather than reaching for the most powerful available tool by default. What would have to change before AI's role grew None of this is a permanent ceiling — it's a statement about where the tradeoff currently lands, and it's worth being precise about what would actually move it. A learned risk-scoring model would become worth the explainability cost only once there's enough of BRIEFR's own labeled outcome data (which CVEs an operator actually acted on, and which they correctly ignored) to meaningfully outperform the fixed formula rather than just approximate it — data this project doesn't yet have because it's a young, single-operator-oriented tool, not a mature platform with years of feedback loops. Auto-deploying generated detection rules would need a much higher, independently-verified confidence bar than any current model realistically clears, plus a real rollback story if a bad rule shipped automatically. And a genuine chat interface would need to solve, honestly, the same problem every LLM-chat security product has to solve — hallucination on security-consequential answers — before it could be trusted anywhere near "should I act on this," which is precisely the question BRIEFR's fixed, auditable scoring answers today without that risk. Self-check Name the two places in BRIEFR where AI genuinely does real work, and the boundary that keeps each one from becoming load-bearing. Why would a more accurate learned risk-scoring model still be a worse fit for BRIEFR today than the fixed formula it has? "Generic LLM chat SOC" is listed as a non-goal because it's "considered a commodity" — restate that argument in your own words, and say what BRIEFR's actual bet is instead. What specific evidence would have to exist before a learned risk model became a reasonable replacement for the current formula?

title: Why Business Source License 1.1 — and the AGPL decision it reversed
text: Part 0B · Chapter A5 Why Business Source License 1.1 — and the AGPL decision it reversed The license changed twice before the public flip: proprietary → AGPL-3.0-or-later → BSL-1.1. This chapter explains the current model and is honest about the reversal, since a study guide that hides its own subject's history isn't trustworthy. LICENSE docs/planning/STRATEGY.md What's actually on record — including the reversal docs/planning/STRATEGY.md §6 records two decisions in sequence, both dated: "Decided 2026-07-10 (Track F2): AGPL-3.0-or-later," then "Superseded 2026-07-19 (Track F2-R)" in favor of the Business Source License 1.1 (BSL). Both were made before the public repository flip, which matters for exactly one reason: no external party had received code under the AGPL grant yet, so reversing it carried none of the legacy-grant complications that revoking a license already held by outside forks would create. The current, governing license is BSL-1.1 — LICENSE , CONTRIBUTING.md , and every active source file's SPDX header ( SPDX-License-Identifier: BUSL-1.1 ) all agree on this. What BSL-1.1 actually does — a paywall with a built-in expiry, not permanent copyleft BSL is a different shape of license than either AGPL or a permissive license, and it's worth being precise about the difference rather than treating "source-available" as a synonym for "open source." BRIEFR's specific terms (set in the LICENSE file's "Additional Use Grant"): anyone may read, copy, modify, and self-host the code free of charge for personal, non-commercial purposes — but use by or on behalf of a for-profit organization ("Commercial Use") requires a one-time, lifetime commercial license purchased from the Licensor. That is the paywall AGPL does not have — AGPL would let a business self-host and even modify BRIEFR commercially for free, as long as they shared modifications back over the network; BSL asks that same business to pay once, with no such carve-out. The second defining feature is the "Change Date": four years after each version's publication, that version automatically converts to the Apache License 2.0 — fully permissive, no restrictions at all. So BSL isn't a permanent restriction; it's a time-boxed head start, letting the Licensor capture commercial-use revenue on recent versions while guaranteeing that revenue window eventually closes and the code becomes as open as it gets. This is the same license family HashiCorp used for Terraform/Vault and IBM continues to use for Terraform since its BSL-authoring MariaDB origin — a well-understood, if debated, pattern for source-available commercial software that wants public code review and free non-commercial self-hosting without giving competitors a free ride to build a paid hosted clone. What this costs, honestly — and why AGPL was considered first The tradeoff is real. Some organizations and distros flatly exclude BSL-licensed dependencies from "open source" bundles (it isn't OSI-approved), which AGPL — however restrictive — clears. AGPL's specific worry (a hosted competitor built on BRIEFR's own code, contributing nothing back) is answered differently by each license: AGPL answers it by forcing that competitor to publish their modifications; BSL answers it by making that competitor pay for the right to run it commercially at all, a blunter but more directly monetizable mechanism. The Track F2 → F2-R sequence in this project's own history is itself worth understanding as a real example of a team trying the reciprocal-sharing answer first, and switching to the direct-payment answer once — reflected in STRATEGY.md 's "Adoption engineering" pillar — commercial-license revenue became the more important goal than guaranteed source-sharing by commercial forks. Self-check What does BSL's "Additional Use Grant" require of a for-profit organization that AGPL would not? Explain the "Change Date" mechanism — what happens to a given BRIEFR version four years after it's published, and why is that different from AGPL's permanence? Why could the AGPL → BSL reversal happen cleanly, with no legacy-grant problem to manage? Name one real reason an organization might refuse to depend on BSL-licensed code even though it's source-available.

title: The interface layer
text: Part I · Frontend The interface layer Covered at the level of stack decisions, as you asked — not a tour of 165 individual components. Five chapters: why React at all, the design-token system that replaced "no component library," the governance registry that keeps it that way, how state actually flows through the app, and the smaller tooling choices that round it out.

title: Why React 19, and why nothing else was seriously in the running
text: Part I · Chapter 1 Why React 19, and why nothing else was seriously in the running A plain client-rendered SPA, no meta-framework — and the reasoning for why that was never really a contest. package.json main.jsx BRIEFR's frontend is 165 .jsx files, one index.html , one JS bundle. There is no server-side rendering, no islands architecture, no meta-framework sitting on top of React — just React 19 owning the DOM end to end, wrapped by react-router-dom for client-side navigation. The whole app boots from a single entry point: import { BrowserRouter } from 'react-router-dom' import { AuthProvider } from './context/AuthContext.jsx' import { AssetProfileProvider } from './context/AssetProfileContext.jsx' ReactDOM.createRoot(document.getElementById( 'root' )).render( <React.StrictMode> <AppErrorBoundary> <BrowserRouter> <AuthProvider> <AssetProfileProvider> <ToastProvider> <App /> </ToastProvider> </AssetProfileProvider> </AuthProvider> </BrowserRouter> </AppErrorBoundary> </React.StrictMode> ) frontend/src/main.jsx — the entire provider tree the app runs inside The concept: why "just React" is itself a decision Modern frontend work almost always starts by picking a meta-framework — Next.js, Remix, SvelteKit — because most apps need at least one of: fast first paint for anonymous visitors, SEO-indexable pages, or server-rendered HTML for slow connections. Choosing "none of that, just a client-rendered SPA" is a real architectural decision, not a default, and it only makes sense when none of those three needs apply. Why this was the right call for BRIEFR specifically BRIEFR is an operator tool sitting behind a login wall (Chapter 11). There are no anonymous visitors to give a fast first paint to, and nothing here needs to rank in search results — the two biggest reasons to reach for SSR simply don't apply. What's left is the ordinary case for a plain SPA: request the login page once, authenticate, then everything after that is API calls returning JSON that React renders. Given that, the decision collapses to "which frontend library," and React won by ecosystem gravity rather than a formal bake-off: Radix UI (the accessibility primitives ADR-003 mandates) ships first-class React bindings, react-router-dom , TanStack Table, Recharts, and cmdk all assume React as the default target, and the maintainer's own familiarity mattered too, since this is a self-hosted, largely solo-maintained project. React 19 specifically, rather than pinning to 18, was chosen because Radix's primitives already certify React 19 compatibility, and the codebase carries no legacy class-component or old-Context-API code that a major-version bump would break. There's no exotic 19-only feature BRIEFR leans on (no Server Components, no use() hook doing anything load-bearing) — it's simply the current stable release of the library already chosen for other reasons, taken at face value. What you gain, and what you knowingly give up Gained: the largest available ecosystem overlap with Radix's exact primitive set; a hooks-based mental model that fits cleanly with the Context-based state approach in Chapter 4; automatic batching and improved Suspense semantics from React 19 itself; and the simplest possible deployment story — a static JS bundle served by any web server, with zero server-side runtime coupling to the FastAPI backend beyond the /api proxy. Given up, knowingly: true first paint is slower than a framework that can stream server-rendered HTML — irrelevant here because every real user is authenticated before they see meaningful content anyway. React's re-render model also needs some memoization discipline in data-dense views (the CVE list, the correlation graph); this is mitigated rather than solved, by leaning on TanStack Table's headless, virtualization-friendly model (Chapter 3) instead of hand-rolling table performance. A misconception worth heading off: "React 19 was chosen for its new compiler / Server Components" would be the wrong story to tell in an interview — BRIEFR uses neither. The version bump tracked ecosystem compatibility (Radix), not a feature BRIEFR actively exploits. Self-check If BRIEFR needed a public, unauthenticated, SEO-indexed page tomorrow (the open-core CVE snapshot mentioned in ADR-001), would the current plain-SPA architecture still be the right call for the whole app, or just wrong for that one page? What would you actually build differently? Name two libraries in BRIEFR's dependency list that would have been harder to adopt under Vue or Svelte instead of React, and explain concretely why. title: ADR-003 — semantic tokens and Radix, explicitly not Tailwind
text: Part I · Chapter 2 ADR-003 — semantic tokens and Radix, explicitly not Tailwind The UI's actual design system: how it's built, the audit that forced it into existence, and why the obvious modern default (Tailwind + shadcn) was rejected. styles/tokens.css App.css ADR-003 The concept: design tokens A design token is a named variable for a design decision — a color, a spacing value, a motion duration — referenced by name ( --severity-critical ) rather than by raw value ( #c0392b ) everywhere it's used. The payoff is that changing the definition in one place changes it everywhere, and more importantly, the name carries meaning a raw hex code can't: --severity-critical tells you what the color is for , so a reviewer can catch "you used the danger color for a neutral link" at a glance instead of having to remember what #c0392b means. Why this exists: the audit that forced it ADR-003 wasn't written speculatively — it documents the fallout of a real 2026-07-14 UX review of the running product, which found the UI "capable and deep but inconsistent and, in places, amateur/broken." The specific findings are worth reading in full because each one maps directly to a root cause in the "decision" section that follows: raw browser-default checkboxes and selects (the most visible "homemade" signal to a user); "selected/active" state rendered four different ways across the app (green feed chips, red preference radios, a red/orange nav tab, a faint sidebar highlight); the color red doing double duty for both "danger" and "just a neutral link," which is actively confusing in a security tool where red should mean something; sub-AA text contrast; bespoke, non-portaled tooltips that overflowed their containers; and one entire section of the app that had shipped essentially unstyled. The report's own diagnosis is the important part: every one of those symptoms traced back to the same root cause — un-named, duplicated color decisions made ad hoc, component by component, with no shared vocabulary to catch the drift. That diagnosis is what justifies a token system as the fix, rather than a series of one-off patches: patching the four different "selected" colors individually would leave the mechanism that produced four different colors untouched, and a fifth would appear in the next feature. /* frontend/src/styles/tokens.css — the file's own header, verbatim */ /* Authority: docs/design/design-system.md (usage rules) and docs/decisions/ADR-003-ui-design-system.md (rationale). MIGRATION RULE: new/edited code consumes the SEMANTIC names below. Legacy raw names (--red, --bg2, --text3, …) remain as compatibility aliases until components are migrated, then are removed. Do NOT add new raw hex anywhere. */ The file's own comment block doubles as a one-paragraph statement of the whole ADR. How the fix is actually built Two separate decisions do the work. First, CSS custom properties as the mechanism — not a CSS-in-JS library, not a utility framework — chosen because it's already the project's existing idiom ( App.css already had an ad-hoc token block before this ADR formalized it), it needs zero new runtime dependency, and it supports live theme-switching (dark/light mode, the tool-wide motion toggle) purely by swapping which values a variable resolves to, with no JavaScript re-render required. Second, Radix UI primitives as the behavior layer — unstyled, accessible building blocks (Checkbox, Select, Dialog, Tabs, Tooltip, DropdownMenu, Popover) that supply focus management, keyboard navigation, and correct ARIA semantics "for free," styled entirely through BRIEFR's own tokens. This is precisely aimed at the audit's findings: Radix's Checkbox replaces the raw browser-default checkbox; its Tooltip is portaled (rendered outside the normal DOM flow, escaping overflow clipping) which fixes the tooltip-overflow bug; its focus-visible handling fixes the weak focus rings. The system is organized as a three-layer hierarchy — Primitives (one Radix component per interaction pattern, styled) → Composites (things built from primitives, like a filter bar) → Features (whole page sections) — with an explicit rule against duplicate, bespoke implementations of the same pattern. Migration itself is staged and reversible: legacy raw token names ( --red , --bg2 ) are kept as aliases pointing at the new semantic tokens during the transition, so nothing visibly breaks while components are migrated one at a time, each in its own component-scoped PR with a visual-regression check. The alternatives, and why each was rejected ADR-003 records three alternatives it seriously weighed, and the rejection reasoning is more instructive than the decision itself: Full shadcn/ui + Tailwind — the modern default choice for exactly this situation, and probably the fastest path to a polished result. Rejected specifically because BRIEFR is a plain-CSS codebase today, and adopting Tailwind is a large, disruptive migration of a shared surface (every single component's className would change) for a project whose maintainer had already explicitly declined Tailwind. Note the reasoning isn't "Tailwind is bad" — it's "the migration cost and an explicit maintainer preference outweigh the velocity gain here." A styled component kit (MUI, Chakra, Mantine) — these ship both behavior and a visual language. Adopting one would have fixed the accessibility gaps quickly, but fighting the kit's own opinionated look to preserve BRIEFR's dark-terminal identity was judged not worth the cost — you'd spend as much effort un-styling MUI as you'd spend styling Radix from scratch, without the same end-state control. Hand-build every primitive, no dependency at all — zero new dependencies, maximum control, but it means re-implementing focus traps, portaling, and ARIA compliance from scratch, which is precisely the category of bug the original audit found the team getting wrong. Rejected as high accessibility risk for a self-inflicted reason (avoiding one dependency). Self-check Why is "shadcn/ui as pattern reference only" a meaningfully different decision from "use shadcn/ui the library"? Concretely, what would a PR that ran npx shadcn add literally introduce that ADR-003 forbids? The audit traced four symptoms to one root cause. Restate that root cause in one sentence, and explain why a token system fixes the cause rather than just the four symptoms individually. Why does Radix's Tooltip being "portaled" specifically fix an overflow bug that a non-portaled tooltip couldn't avoid?

title: ADR-005 — the component-library allow/deny registry
text: Part I · Chapter 3 ADR-005 — the component-library allow/deny registry Operationalizing Chapter 2's decision into an explicit list, so a future PR can't quietly reopen the question ADR-003 just closed. ADR-005 package.json ADR-003 sets direction; ADR-005 is the enforcement mechanism. Its own context section states the risk plainly: without a concrete registry, a future change is likely to add a styled component kit "because it solves a problem," quietly reintroducing exactly the inconsistency the design system exists to remove. This is a genuinely common failure mode in software governance — a good architectural decision, recorded once, slowly erodes one "just this once" exception at a time, because nobody who adds the exception was in the room for the original decision. ADR-005's answer is to make the registry itself the source of truth that every future addition must be checked against, rather than trusting institutional memory. Library Status Why Radix UI Approved — direct use Unstyled behavior layer, React 19-ready, the sanctioned primitive set Recharts Approved — direct use SVG-based, MIT license, themed entirely via --chart-* tokens cmdk Approved — direct use Powers the ⌘/Ctrl-K command palette TanStack Table Approved — headless only Table logic without imposed markup or styling; drives the shared DataGrid Floating UI Approved, prefer Radix first Positioning for custom popovers — Radix already uses it internally Chart.js Deprecated, mid-migration Superseded by Recharts (ticket E7-5); removed once every chart is ported shadcn/ui, Magic UI Pattern-reference only Copy markup/composition patterns; strip Tailwind and Framer-Motion; re-skin with BRIEFR tokens; never ship as a runtime dependency MUI, Chakra, Mantine, Bootstrap, DaisyUI, Tailwind Prohibited Ships its own theme or injects global CSS — structurally incompatible with a token-only styling contract The charting decision, as a worked example of the registry in action Chart.js and Recharts technically coexist in the repo right now, mid-migration — which sounds like exactly the kind of drift ADR-005 exists to prevent. The registry resolves the apparent contradiction with a specific rule: migration is page-atomic (every chart on a given route moves to Recharts in one PR, never split across two PRs) and chart bundles are lazy-loaded per route, so any single page loads Recharts's chunk or Chart.js's chunk, never both at once. The coexistence is real but bounded and temporary by construction — Chart.js is deleted entirely once the last chart is ported (tracked as ticket E7-5). This is worth sitting with: a registry doesn't mean "zero exceptions ever," it means every exception is named, bounded, and has an exit condition, instead of being silent and permanent. The governance gate itself Adding anything new to the approved list — or promoting something out of "conditional" — requires all of: an update to the ADR text itself with rationale, design-review sign-off against the design-system doc, a license compatibility check (the project is licensed under BSL-1.1 (Chapter A5), so dependencies must carry a permissive license — MIT, Apache-2.0, or BSD — that can be bundled without conflicting terms), a bundle-size justification against recorded budgets (the primitives layer is capped at ≤35 kB gzip incremental; Recharts' lazy chunk at ≤110 kB), and accessibility parity at least equal to the Radix baseline. This is deliberately high friction — the point of the friction is that it's cheaper to update one ADR than to discover six months later that three different component kits crept in one at a time. Self-check Both Recharts and Chart.js exist in the repo during migration. What specific mechanism — not just written policy — prevents a single page from ever loading both chunks at once? Why does the registry require a license check specifically, and why does that check matter for BRIEFR's source-available BSL-1.1 model even though BSL isn't a copyleft license the way AGPL is? A future contributor wants to add a date-picker library that isn't on any list here. Walk through, step by step, what has to happen before that's allowed.

title: State and data flow: React Context, not Redux
text: Part I · Chapter 4 State and data flow: React Context, not Redux Three providers cover the app's entire global client state. Understanding why that's enough tells you more about the app's actual shape than the code itself does. context/AuthContext.jsx context/AssetProfileContext.jsx context/InvestigationContext.jsx The concept: server state vs. client state A useful split when reasoning about any app's state: server state is data that lives in a database and is just being displayed — a list of CVEs, a risk score, a correlation graph. It's fetched per-view, and the source of truth is always the server, never the browser tab. Client state is state that only exists because the user is interacting with this particular browser session right now — who's logged in, what am I currently investigating, what's my declared asset stack. Global state-management libraries like Redux earn their complexity when an app has a lot of the second kind, shared across many distant parts of the component tree. When most of an app's state is actually the first kind, a heavyweight global store mostly ends up managing cache invalidation for data the backend already owns — solving a problem that server-state libraries (or, as here, plain re-fetching) already solve more directly. Why three Contexts turned out to be enough Looking at what's actually global here: AuthProvider holds who's logged in and their session status; AssetProfileProvider holds the analyst's declared software stack — the input that feeds the 0.35-weighted asset-match component of every risk score (Chapter 18); InvestigationContext holds in-progress investigation/drawer state. That's the entire inventory of state that's genuinely needed in more than one distant part of the tree at once. Everything else — a CVE list, a detail drawer's contents, a correlation cluster — is fetched fresh by the component that needs it and doesn't need to be "global" in any sense. Three Contexts covering three genuinely global concerns is proportionate to that shape; reaching for Redux here would be solving for a scale of cross-cutting client state the app doesn't actually have. const refreshAuthState = useCallback( async () => { try { const me = await fetchMe() setUser(me) setStatus( 'authed' ) await loadUserStack() await loadUserPreferences() return me } catch { // Access cookie may have expired while a persistent refresh cookie remains. try { const res = await fetch( '/api/auth/refresh' , { method: 'POST' , credentials: 'include' }) /* ...on success, re-fetch /me and retry */ context/AuthContext.jsx — the silent-refresh fallback baked directly into the auth state hook That snippet is worth pausing on, because it's a small piece of frontend code that only makes sense once you already understand Chapter 11's two-token auth design: the frontend never has to know explicitly "my access token just expired" — refreshAuthState just tries /api/auth/me , and if that fails, transparently attempts a silent refresh via the httpOnly refresh cookie before giving up and treating the user as logged out. The frontend's Context layer and the backend's token design were built to fit each other; you can't fully explain either one in isolation. How preferences escape the "just this browser tab" trap A common mistake in apps like this is to store user preferences in localStorage , which quietly means "your settings follow this browser, not you" — switch machines and your stack terms or display density reset to defaults. BRIEFR's AssetProfileContext avoids this by syncing to and from routers/me.py (Chapter 28) rather than localStorage : your declared stack, display density, font scale, and timezone are server-persisted per user account, so they follow you across devices and browser profiles, not just across tabs on one machine. Self-check At what point would three Context providers stop being enough? Name a concrete symptom (not a rule of thumb) that would tell you it's time to introduce a real state-management library. Why does refreshAuthState attempt a silent token refresh inside its catch block instead of just logging the user out on the first failed /me call? What would break for a user if their asset stack were stored in localStorage instead of synced through routers/me.py ?

title: Fonts, exports, and testing — the smaller decisions that round out the stack
text: Part I · Chapter 5 Fonts, exports, and testing — the smaller decisions that round out the stack Three unrelated-looking choices that share one thread: keep the runtime footprint and the operational dependencies as small as the SPA architecture already implies. @fontsource/* jspdf html2canvas write-excel-file playwright Self-hosted fonts, not a Google Fonts <link> DM Sans (body/UI), DM Serif Display (headings), and IBM Plex Mono (labels, data, monospace contexts) are bundled as @fontsource npm packages and imported directly in main.jsx , rather than the far more common approach of a <link> tag pointing at fonts.googleapis.com . The code comment in main.jsx states the reasoning directly: "no runtime requests to Google (privacy posture, offline capability, no FOUT on cold loads)." Unpacking each part — privacy posture : a self-hosted security tool shouldn't leak "someone opened this page" to a third party as a side effect of rendering text. Offline capability : BRIEFR is designed to be runnable in air-gapped or restricted-network environments, where a hard dependency on reaching Google's CDN for the app to render its own fonts correctly would be a real operational failure. No FOUT (flash of unstyled text): fonts ship in the same bundle as everything else, so there's no network round-trip during which the browser shows a fallback font and then swaps it. Client-side PDF generation, not a server-rendered report PDF reports are built entirely in the browser: html2canvas renders a DOM node to a canvas bitmap, and jspdf assembles those bitmaps into a PDF file, all without a network round trip to the backend for rendering. The alternative most backend-heavy systems reach for is a server-side headless-browser rendering service (a Chromium instance the backend drives to print a PDF) — deliberately avoided here. The tradeoff is explicit: client-side rendering costs some CPU on the user's machine and produces a screenshot-quality PDF rather than a true vector-layout one (expect subtly soft edges and awkward page breaks in a very long report, since html2canvas is literally rastering pixels, not laying out text). What it buys in return is architecturally significant: zero backend rendering infrastructure, zero headless-Chromium dependency to keep patched and running in the FastAPI process, and reports generate instantly without ever touching the request path's heavy-work constraint (danger zone 6, mentioned throughout this book) — because generating a PDF isn't "work the backend does" at all. Testing: node:test and Playwright, nothing heavier 56 unit test files run through Node's own built-in node:test module rather than Jest or Vitest — for what are mostly pure-function unit tests (scoring math, formatting helpers, validators), a full test framework's mocking/snapshot machinery isn't needed, and skipping it is one less dependency to version and configure. Browser end-to-end testing runs on Playwright, with Chromium pre-installed in this environment specifically so E2E tests don't need to download a browser on every run. A real operational trap, noted in the project's own environment guidance: running browser E2E tests against the default SQLite dev database with too few seeded CVEs (or with the background scheduler actively writing) can produce a "database is locked" error that looks like a test bug but is actually SQLite's single-writer limitation surfacing — see Chapter 9 for exactly why SQLite behaves this way and Postgres doesn't. Self-check What's the concrete tradeoff of generating PDFs by screenshotting a DOM node versus using a true PDF layout engine — what would you expect to look subtly wrong in a ten-page report? Name the three things self-hosting fonts buys BRIEFR, and connect each one back to something BRIEFR promises elsewhere (hint: self-hosted, air-gappable, security-focused). Why might "database is locked" during E2E testing be a SQLite-specific symptom that a Postgres-backed test run wouldn't reproduce?

title: Core, data & auth
text: Part II · Backend foundations Core, data & auth Everything else in the backend sits on top of these eight chapters. This is also, not coincidentally, where most of the security-relevant design decisions live — read it slowly.

title: App bootstrap and dependency injection
text: Part II · Chapter 6 App bootstrap and dependency injection What actually happens between "run uvicorn " and "the API is answering requests" — and why the shutdown path is engineered as carefully as the startup path. main.py dependencies.py The concept: application lifespan FastAPI's lifespan is an async context manager wrapped around the entire life of the process: code before the yield runs once at startup, code after it runs once at shutdown, and everything in between is "the app is up." It exists because a web app almost always needs to acquire some resources once (a database pool, a background scheduler) rather than per-request, and release them cleanly when the process stops — not leak a half-open connection pool or leave a scheduled job mid-write when the process is killed. async def lifespan(app: FastAPI): backend = "postgresql" if is_postgres() else "sqlite" logger.info( "main.py lifespan: starting backend (%s)" , backend) if settings.briefr_require_postgres and not is_postgres(): raise RuntimeError( "BRIEFR_REQUIRE_POSTGRES=1 but DATABASE_URL is not set to a postgresql:// DSN. " "Migrate via Admin -> Database, apply DATABASE_URL, and restart." ) if not is_postgres(): recovery = ensure_db_or_restore() # SQLite-only: auto-heal a corrupt file if recovery.get( "status" ) == "restored" : logger.warning( "Recovered corrupt database from backup: %s" , recovery.get( "archive" )) else : await run_postgres_migrations() # Postgres-only: Alembic upgrade to head await init_pool() await init_db() # ...operator settings bootstrap, scheduler start, Procrastinate worker start... main.py, the opening of lifespan() — abridged, real control flow Why startup is sequenced exactly this way Read the sequence as a dependency chain, not an arbitrary list. The Postgres-required check comes first because everything after it assumes the database posture is what the operator intended — failing loudly here rather than limping along on an accidental SQLite fallback in what was meant to be a production deploy. The SQLite corruption check and the Postgres migration step are mutually exclusive branches of the same idea: before anything reads or writes real data, make sure the schema on disk is the schema the code expects — for SQLite that means verifying the file isn't corrupt (and restoring from backup automatically if it is), for Postgres it means running any pending Alembic migrations to bring the schema to head (Chapter 10). Only after that is the connection pool opened, and init_pool() deliberately runs before init_db() 's idempotent DDL fixups need it. Get this order wrong — say, open the pool before migrations run — and you risk pooled connections racing a schema change mid-flight, exactly the failure mode run_postgres_migrations() 's placement in this function is designed to avoid. Why route registration order is frozen A detail easy to dismiss as bureaucratic until you understand FastAPI's route matching: it tries routes in the order they were registered and uses the first one whose path pattern matches. A literal path like /api/cves/export and a parameterized sibling like /api/cves/{cve_id} can both match a request for /api/cves/export — whichever was registered first wins. If a future change reordered router registration in main.py , /api/cves/export could silently start being swallowed by the {cve_id} handler, treating "export" as if it were a CVE ID, with no error, just wrong behavior. tests/test_router_split.py exists specifically to catch this class of regression by snapshot-testing the exact OpenAPI route list — a test that looks pedantic is actually guarding a genuinely sharp edge in how FastAPI resolves overlapping routes. Why shutdown avoids os._exit(0) dependencies.py 's trigger_graceful_restart() (used by the admin UI's "restart" button) sends a signal that lets uvicorn's normal shutdown sequence run to completion, rather than calling os._exit(0) to terminate immediately. The reason is direct: an immediate exit skips the code after the yield in lifespan() — connection pool close, scheduler stop, in-flight background task drain (Chapter 15's task_registry.py ) — none of which would run. A restart that skips cleanup isn't just untidy; it can leave a half-written scheduler job or an unflushed metrics counter, silently corrupting state that a clean restart is supposed to avoid. The dependency-injection layer: require_user and require_admin FastAPI's dependency injection lets a route declare "I need an authenticated user" as a function parameter, and the framework runs that function before the route handler, short-circuiting with an error response if it raises. dependencies.py is where BRIEFR's two most important dependencies live: require_user (any authenticated session) and require_admin (session and the admin role). The detail worth sitting with is that require_admin re-reads the user's role from the users table on every single call , rather than trusting the role claim already sitting inside the JWT the user presented. That's an extra database read on every admin-gated request — a real, measurable cost, paid deliberately. The payoff: if an admin gets demoted mid-session, the very next admin-gated request they make is rejected, without waiting for their 15-minute access token to expire on its own. This is a live illustration of a security tradeoff you'll see reasoned about explicitly in Chapter 11 too — trusting a signed token's claims is fast but stale; re-checking the database is slower but current, and BRIEFR chooses "current" specifically for the one role check where staleness is a real risk (a demoted or offboarded admin retaining elevated access for up to 15 minutes). Security callout: CSP (Content-Security-Policy) headers, added by a dedicated middleware, are reasonably strict — default-src 'self' , no unsafe-inline scripts. docs_url / redoc_url / openapi_url (FastAPI's auto-generated interactive API docs) are disabled entirely in production, which removes a free endpoint-enumeration tool from an unauthenticated attacker's toolkit. Self-check Why does require_admin hit the database on every request instead of trusting the role claim already embedded in the JWT payload? What's the exact failure mode this closes, and what does it cost to close it? Walk through, concretely, how reordering two router registrations in main.py could cause /api/cves/export to be handled by the wrong function — what would the symptom look like to a user? Name two things that would not get cleaned up if the admin restart button called os._exit(0) instead of a graceful signal.

title: Configuration and encrypted settings
text: Part II · Chapter 7 Configuration and encrypted settings Three files, three different jobs: what the process reads at boot, what an operator can change without redeploying, and how the sensitive half of that gets protected at rest. config_schema.py settings.py settings_crypto.py ADR-006 Two different kinds of configuration It's worth separating two things that look similar but aren't: process configuration — read once from environment variables or a .env file at process start, and requiring a restart to change ( settings.py 's pydantic Settings singleton: database URL, JWT secret, core rate-limit rates) — versus operator configuration — writable live through the Admin UI without a restart, persisted to the database, described by an ~80-field registry ( config_schema.py 's CONFIG_SCHEMA ) that specifies each field's type, bounds, help text, and whether changing it needs a restart to take effect. Why config_schema.py exists as a single registry Its own docstring states plainly what it replaces: three separately-maintained lists that used to live directly in routers/admin.py — WRITABLE_CONFIG_KEYS , INTEGER_KEYS , RESTART_REQUIRED_KEYS . Maintaining the same information as three parallel lists is a classic source of drift: add a new writable key and forget to also add it to RESTART_REQUIRED_KEYS , and an operator changes a setting that silently doesn't take effect until a restart they were never told to do. Collapsing three lists into one schema (one entry per key, describing everything about it at once) makes that class of bug structurally impossible rather than merely less likely — there's no second list to forget to update, because there is no second list. Environment-variable precedence, and why it's load-bearing BRIEFR resolves a config value through three layers, in a fixed order: process environment (whatever the OS/container actually set before Python started) wins over the database ( app_settings table, written by Admin UI saves) wins over the .env file . This ordering is not incidental — it's what makes container deployments predictable: an operator can set DATABASE_URL as a real environment variable in their deployment manifest and know with certainty that no Admin UI click can ever override it, because real host environment always wins. settings.py implements this precedence with a small but important piece of ordering: it snapshots which keys already exist in the process environment before calling load_dotenv() , specifically so that loading .env can't accidentally overwrite a real environment variable that happened to also appear in the file. Encrypted secrets at rest (ADR-006) Before ADR-006, an operator-saved secret — an API token, a webhook URL with an embedded credential — sat in the app_settings table as plain text. Anyone with read access to the database (a backup file, a restored snapshot, a compromised replica) could read every configured secret directly. The fix is Fernet symmetric encryption (AES-128 in CBC mode with an HMAC for integrity) applied specifically to fields whose schema entry declares type: "secret" , keyed by an optional BRIEFR_SETTINGS_KEY environment variable, SHA-256-derived into a Fernet key. The rollout design is worth studying as a model for how to ship a breaking-adjacent security improvement without actually breaking anything: it is entirely additive. An install that never sets BRIEFR_SETTINGS_KEY keeps working exactly as before — with no key configured, secrets simply aren't persisted to the database at all (they still work via .env /process env, just never touch the DB). Once a key is configured, new saves are encrypted and stored as enc:v1:<fernet-token> ; a decrypt_secret() call on an old plaintext row (no enc:v1: prefix) passes it through unchanged rather than erroring, so legacy rows keep working until the next time an operator re-saves that setting through the Admin UI, at which point it gets encrypted going forward. No forced migration, no downtime, no "upgrade and your secrets stop working" moment. Security callout — a real gap worth knowing: settings_crypto._fernet() returns None silently when no key is configured, rather than raising. Every caller must explicitly check for that None and decide what to do — a caller that forgets the check risks silently storing a secret in plaintext instead of failing loudly. If you're auditing this code, the call sites in operator_settings.py are exactly where to verify that check actually exists everywhere it needs to. Fails closed, on purpose, in production only: if BRIEFR_ENV=production and JWT_SECRET is unset, settings.py raises RuntimeError immediately — the process refuses to start rather than silently generating a throwaway secret that would invalidate every session on the next restart. In dev/test, by contrast, an unset secret is auto-generated with secrets.token_hex(32) and persisted back into .env so it survives restarts during local development. Same missing value, deliberately different behavior depending on environment. Self-check If BRIEFR_SETTINGS_KEY is generated once, used to encrypt several secrets, and then lost without a backup, what happens to those secrets — and is there any recovery path other than re-entering them? Why does environment-variable precedence matter specifically for container deployments — what would go wrong if the Admin UI's saved value could override a real deployment-manifest environment variable? Explain, in your own words, why collapsing three parallel key-lists into one schema eliminates a bug class rather than just making it less likely.

title: The database.py compatibility shim
text: Part II · Chapter 8 The database.py compatibility shim The shortest chapter in this book, and a useful lesson in why "just delete the old file" is sometimes the wrong instinct during a refactor. database.py At 57 lines, database.py contains almost no logic of its own. It defines one meaningful thing — DB_PATH , the on-disk location of the SQLite dev/test database — and then star-imports and re-exports everything from the real, current data-access modules under backend/db/ , plus a handful of underscore-prefixed "private" names that external callers happen to import directly and that a plain import * would otherwise silently drop. The backstory: the original, monolithic database.py was split apart into the current backend/db/ package during an earlier refactor phase, with every function moved verbatim into its new module. That refactor left 35-plus existing call sites across the codebase still doing from database import upsert_cves (or similar) — pointing at a module that, after the split, no longer contained that function directly. Rather than hand-editing every one of those 35+ import statements across the codebase in the same PR as a structural refactor (real risk of introducing an unrelated bug in an unrelated file, for no functional gain), the team left this shim in place: database.py still exists, still answers to every old import, and simply forwards to the real implementation now living elsewhere. The one genuinely subtle detail: DB_PATH deliberately stays a literal attribute directly on this module, rather than being re-exported from db/config.py like everything else here. The reason lives in db/connection.py , which does a lazy import database followed by database.DB_PATH specifically so that a test's monkeypatch.setattr("database.DB_PATH", ...) takes effect. monkeypatch.setattr works by reaching into a named module object and replacing an attribute on it directly — that only functions correctly if DB_PATH genuinely lives on the database module, not if it's merely re-exported through an import chain from somewhere else. Move it, and every test that overrides the database path for isolation would silently start monkeypatching a name nobody actually reads from anymore. Self-check Why can't DB_PATH simply be re-exported from db/config.py like every other name in this file — what test-isolation mechanism would break, and why? What's the actual cost of leaving a compatibility shim like this in place indefinitely, versus the cost of the mass-rewrite it avoided? Which would you have chosen, and why?

title: The data layer — BRIEFR's most important module
text: Part II · Chapter 9 The data layer — BRIEFR's most important module Dual-backend, no ORM, hand-paired SQL.
