This chapter is longer than the others on purpose — the project's own internal learning path calls this "the most important module," and after reading it you'll see why. db/connection.py db/pg_adapt.py db/config.py db/init.py db/errors.py db/*.py — 34 files Why no ORM, revisited concretely Part 0 introduced the ORM-vs-raw-SQL tradeoff in the abstract; here's what "no ORM" actually looks like in a real query module. db/app_settings.py defines its queries as paired string constants, one per database dialect, sitting side by side: _SELECT_VALUE_SQLITE = "SELECT value FROM app_settings WHERE key = ?" _SELECT_VALUE_PG = "SELECT value FROM app_settings WHERE key = $1" _UPSERT_SQLITE = """ INSERT INTO app_settings (key, value, updated_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?) ON CONFLICT(key) DO UPDATE SET value = excluded.value, ...""" _UPSERT_PG = """ INSERT INTO app_settings (key, value, updated_at) VALUES ($1, $2, $3) ON CONFLICT(key) DO UPDATE SET value = excluded.value, ...""" db/app_settings.py — the exact _SQLITE / _PG pairing CLAUDE.md's danger zone describes Notice the two dialects aren't subtly different for no reason: SQLite uses positional ? placeholders, Postgres uses numbered $1 / $2 placeholders — a real driver-level difference neither aiosqlite nor asyncpg will paper over for you. Every query module in db/ follows this same shape: write the SQLite version, write the Postgres version, and a small dispatch function ( _is_postgres_connection(db) ) picks the right one at call time. There is no automatic translation between them for new code — this is the exact meaning of the project's own rule that a new query has to be written twice, deliberately, by a human who understands both dialects' behavior for that specific query. What pg_adapt.py actually is (and, importantly, isn't) It would be easy to assume pg_adapt.py is a general SQLite-to-Postgres translation layer that saves you from writing dialect-specific SQL — that assumption would be wrong, and CLAUDE.md is explicit about it: db/dialect.py , an earlier general-purpose translator, was deleted entirely in a refactor referred to internally as "Post-B" (2026-07). Checking the current repository confirms that file no longer exists. What remains, pg_adapt.py , is scoped much more narrowly: it's internal machinery inside PostgresConnection that exists only to translate legacy SQLite-flavored SQL still being emitted by code outside the db/ package — older router and auth-layer queries written with SQLite idioms ( ? placeholders, datetime('now') ) before the Postgres-native convention was established. Its regex-based _postgres_translate_sql() rewrites those specific patterns ( datetime() / date() / julianday() calls, INSERT OR REPLACE / INSERT OR IGNORE into ON CONFLICT equivalents, placeholder renumbering) at the connection boundary, as a compatibility bridge for legacy call sites — not as a general-purpose feature new code is meant to rely on. Writing a brand-new query and hoping pg_adapt.py will make your SQLite SQL "just work" on Postgres is precisely the mistake this file's own docstring warns against. The connection abstraction: one protocol, two real implementations db/types.py defines a shared DbConnection protocol — an interface both backends implement identically from the caller's point of view, so query-module code doesn't need an if is_postgres() branch scattered through every function; the branch happens once, inside get_connection() . SqliteConnection wraps aiosqlite , opened in WAL (write-ahead logging) mode with a 30-second busy timeout and foreign keys enforced — WAL mode specifically because it lets readers and a single writer proceed concurrently rather than SQLite's default fully-serialized locking, which matters for a dev/test environment where the scheduler and an interactive request might touch the database at nearly the same moment. PostgresConnection wraps a pooled asyncpg connection, opening a transaction lazily on the first execute() call and leaving commit/rollback entirely to the caller — the connection layer doesn't guess when a logical unit of work ends, the code using it says so explicitly. Connection pooling, made concrete Part 0 defined a connection pool abstractly; here's the concrete shape. init_pool() opens a process-global asyncpg pool sized between 1 and settings.database_pool_size connections. get_connection() acquires one from the pool with a timeout — if every pooled connection is already checked out and the timeout expires, it raises a specific PoolExhaustedError , which main.py 's exception handler turns into an HTTP 503 (Service Unavailable) rather than a generic crash. This is a meaningfully better failure mode than either silently queuing forever (a request that never returns) or a raw unhandled exception (a 500 with no useful signal) — the client gets a clear, actionable "the server is overloaded, retry" response instead of either extreme. SQLite, by contrast, has no pool at all: each call opens a fresh aiosqlite connection, which is fine for the low-concurrency dev/test use case it's meant for, but is a real, deliberate limitation you should be able to name if asked "does SQLite scale here" — it doesn't, and it isn't meant to. Why the schema itself is still one database, not split (ADR-001) ADR-001 documents a genuine tension in BRIEFR's roadmap: the project has an open-core plan to publish a monthly public CVE/correlation snapshot, but a raw pg_dump of the live production database today would leak operator data alongside it — user accounts, session tokens, IOC watchlist entries, webhook destination URLs. The obvious-looking fix is a physical schema split (an intel schema containing only exportable data, an app schema containing everything operator-specific) so a dump of one schema is safe by construction. ADR-001 explicitly considers and defers that split — it would double the migration and test surface immediately, in exchange for a benefit (safe automated exports) the project doesn't need yet, since the public snapshot feature hasn't shipped. Instead, the boundary between "safe to export" and "not safe to export" is enforced today by an allowlist export script ( scripts/export_intel_snapshot.py ) that only touches tables it's been told are safe, with the physical split explicitly left as a decision to revisit in a later ADR once the open-core feature actually ships. This is worth noticing as a pattern in its own right: sometimes the architecturally "correct" fix is deliberately deferred because the feature that would justify its cost doesn't exist yet, and a narrower, additive mitigation covers the present risk well enough. Error normalization across two very different drivers SQLite and Postgres drivers raise entirely different exception hierarchies for the same logical failure (a locked database, a constraint violation). db/errors.py catches both sqlite3.* and asyncpg.* exceptions at the connection boundary and re-raises them as BRIEFR's own dialect-neutral types — DatabaseError , DatabaseLockedError — so that code outside the db/ package (routers, business logic) can catch one exception type regardless of which database is actually running underneath. This is the payoff of the whole dual-backend design done right: the abstraction boundary is drawn at exactly the right place — dialect differences are absorbed inside db/ , and everything outside it can pretend there's only one database. The trap this whole architecture exists to prevent, stated plainly: the default test suite runs against SQLite. A query can pass every test in that suite and still break in production, because SQLite silently tolerates things Postgres rejects outright (type coercion is far looser; CAST(x AS REAL) on a non-numeric string is forgiving in SQLite and an error in Postgres — you'll meet this exact example again in Chapter 22's morning-brief chapter). Any change to the data layer needs to be run against both backends before you can trust it — the project's own tooling for that is a disposable Postgres container on port 5433, specifically to avoid colliding with a developer's own local Postgres on 5432. The other 26 query modules, grouped by what they back db/ has 34 files total; six ( connection.py , pg_adapt.py , config.py , init.py , errors.py , app_settings.py ) carry the architecture lessons above. The remaining 26 are ordinary query modules, each following the same paired-constant pattern — worth knowing what each one actually backs, since "the data layer" isn't one undifferentiated thing. Core CVE/ingest data: cve.py is the biggest and most central of all of them — it holds upsert_cves , the literal function every feed in Chapter 14 eventually calls, plus the change-history diffing that powers Chapter 22's "EPSS movers" and a provenance-tagging system that protects LLM-derived product data from ever being silently blanked by an empty incoming enrichment batch. It also exports small shared helpers (chunked IN -clause building, batched change-history inserts) that cache.py , metadata.py , and correlation.py all import — making it the de facto utility module for the whole CVE domain, not just CRUD. cache.py holds the IOC/feed/exploit caches Chapters 14 and 23 both lean on; cache_retention.py is its sweep counterpart — the scheduled cleanup that expires stale rows out of every one of those caches (plus change-history, OTX mirror tables, the AI-operations audit trail, and webhook/audit logs) on their own per-table retention windows, including one genuinely subtle correctness fix worth naming: a webhook dedupe-claim row is written before delivery is attempted, so a worker that crashes between the claim and the actual send would otherwise leave a stranded claim that permanently (and wrongly) suppresses that alert forever — the sweep removes only claims old enough to be safely considered abandoned, without touching ones that are still legitimately in flight. enrichment.py is the write-side counterpart to Chapter 14's feed modules — the actual upsert functions that apply vulnrichment/CIRCL/CAPEC and similar secondary-source data onto existing CVE rows, following the same additive, never-downgrade discipline as cve.py 's own enrichment path. sync_state.py is the watermark mechanism this book has referenced in the abstract since Chapter 14 — it holds the actual NVD watermark read/write functions, including a self-healing seed from the CVE table's own max-modified date when a watermark is missing but real data already exists. metadata.py holds the full MITRE/ATLAS technique and case-study tables, including a join between two taxonomies (ATLAS case studies and ATT&CK techniques) that's deliberately done in Python rather than SQL, because the two datasets share no foreign key and only connect through common CVE IDs — doing that join in the database would mean an expensive N+1 pattern across roughly a hundred Forge coverage rows. software_catalog.py backs the stack-autocomplete feature, with a genuinely different aggregation query per backend (Postgres's ARRAY_AGG(DISTINCT ...) vs. SQLite's GROUP_CONCAT — not just placeholder syntax, a different SQL feature entirely). timeutil.py is the one place the SQLite-string-vs-Postgres-TIMESTAMPTZ divergence in timestamp handling is centralized, so every other module can import one shared function instead of re-solving the same problem. Embeddings and search (Chapter 24's actual storage layer): embeddings_pgvector.py is pure Python with no SQL at all — the shared math and rich-text-construction helpers both writer and reader modules call into, including the content-hash function that makes a model swap automatically invalidate every stored vector. embeddings_store.py is the writer, with a real per-backend branch worth knowing: Postgres casts the vector literal directly in SQL ( CAST($5 AS vector) ), while SQLite stores the raw float bytes as a BLOB — genuinely different

title: Alembic migrations — forward-only, Postgres-only
text: Part II · Chapter 10 Alembic migrations — forward-only, Postgres-only Why the two backends have entirely different migration stories, and why that asymmetry is intentional rather than an oversight. alembic/env.py alembic/versions/*.py — 33 files Alembic is a schema-migration tool: each change to the database schema is captured as a small, ordered Python file with an upgrade() function (apply the change) and a downgrade() function (undo it), chained together by a revision / down_revision pair so the tool always knows the exact linear order migrations must apply in. BRIEFR has 33 of these, from 001_initial_schema.py through 033_search_api_tokens.py , and they run automatically — not just from a developer's terminal, but from db/init.py 's run_postgres_migrations() , called during every single backend startup against a live Postgres DATABASE_URL (Chapter 6). A quick optimization keeps this from being wasteful: before running anything, Alembic compares the database's current alembic_version marker against the migration scripts' head revision, and skips the upgrade step entirely if they already match — so a normal restart with no pending migrations does one cheap comparison, not 33 no-op replays. Here's the asymmetry that matters: SQLite never touches Alembic at all. The zero-config dev/test database gets its schema from a completely separate mechanism — a large inline executescript() block in db/init.py 's init_db() , plus a long, hand-maintained list of best-effort ALTER TABLE statements wrapped in try/except, replayed in full on every process start. This is why CLAUDE.md's danger-zone warning about migrations matters so much in practice: the SQLite schema and the Postgres schema are not derived from one shared source of truth — they are two independently hand-maintained descriptions of "what the schema should look like," kept in sync by developer discipline, not by tooling. A developer who adds a Postgres migration and forgets the equivalent SQLite DDL change (or vice versa) creates a real, silent divergence between what the test suite validates and what production actually runs on. Why forward-only, and why it's not just a style preference "Never edit an applied migration, always add a new one" sounds like a stylistic convention until you trace through what editing one would actually do. Alembic's alembic_version table doesn't store a hash or diff of the schema — it stores the ID of the last migration that was run. If migration 017 has already been applied in production and you go back and edit its upgrade() function, production's schema doesn't change (that code already ran, once, in the past) but the script directory now describes a different history than what actually happened. The next deploy sees "I'm already past revision 017" and does nothing — silently leaving your edited change entirely unapplied in production, with no error, because from Alembic's point of view there's nothing new to do. The only correct way to change something migration 017 already did is a brand-new migration 034 that alters it further — history is append-only, exactly like a git log you're not allowed to rebase once it's pushed. Self-check You need a schema change today. Do you edit db/init.py 's inline SQLite DDL, add a new Alembic version file, or both — and why does SQLite never run Alembic at all? Walk through exactly what would happen in production if a developer edited an already-applied migration file instead of adding a new one. Would production error, or would it do something quieter and worse? Why does run_postgres_migrations() compare alembic_version against the script directory's head before doing any work, rather than always attempting the upgrade?

title: Authentication — sessions, tokens, and passwords
text: Part II · Chapter 11 Authentication — sessions, tokens, and passwords The full login system, replacing a legacy shared admin-key header — and the reasoning behind every one of its individually small, deliberate security choices. auth/tokens.py auth/passwords.py auth/repo.py auth/usernames.py auth_middleware.py Two tokens, not one, and why that split exists BRIEFR issues two different credentials at login, each optimized for a different property. A short-lived access token — a JWT, self-contained and stateless, checked by decoding and verifying its signature, no database lookup required — is fast to verify on every request but, once issued, cannot be individually revoked before it naturally expires. An opaque refresh token — a random string with no embedded meaning — is checked against a database table ( sessions ) on use, which makes it slower to verify but fully revocable at any moment, since revocation just means deleting or marking that one database row. The two are complementary precisely because they trade the same property in opposite directions: the access token optimizes for speed at the cost of instant revocability; the refresh token optimizes for revocability at the cost of a database round-trip. Using one alone would force a single tradeoff onto the entire system; using both lets each request pick the cheaper one (the access token) for routine reads, while keeping a slower-but-revocable mechanism (the refresh token) in reserve for the moment revocation actually matters — a stolen session, an offboarded user, a suspicious login. def create_access_token(user_id: int , username: str , role: str ) -> str : now = datetime.now(timezone.utc) payload = { "sub" : str (user_id), "username" : username, "role" : role, "iat" : now, "exp" : now + timedelta(minutes=settings.jwt_access_token_minutes), } return jwt.encode(payload, settings.jwt_secret, algorithm=ALGORITHM) def generate_refresh_token() -> str : return secrets.token_urlsafe( 32 ) def hash_refresh_token(token: str ) -> str : return hashlib.sha256(token.encode( "utf-8" )).hexdigest() auth/tokens.py, in full for the relevant functions — notice the refresh token is never stored raw, only its SHA-256 hash That last function is a small but important detail: the raw refresh token is handed to the browser once, at login, and never persisted anywhere on the server — only hash_refresh_token() 's output goes into the sessions table. If the database ever leaked (a backup file exposed, a read replica compromised), an attacker with the hash table alone cannot reconstruct the original tokens and therefore cannot replay anyone's session — the same principle as never storing a plaintext password, applied to a session credential instead. Password hashing, and the timing-attack detail most implementations miss BRIEFR hashes passwords with bcrypt directly, at 12 rounds — a deliberate choice over passlib , a popular wrapper library, because the code's own comment notes passlib is unmaintained and has broken compatibility with bcrypt versions 4.1 and above. Depending on an unmaintained abstraction layer over a well-maintained primitive is a real risk in security-sensitive code; calling bcrypt directly removes that dependency entirely. DUMMY_HASH = bcrypt.hashpw(secrets.token_bytes( 32 ), bcrypt.gensalt(rounds= 12 )).decode( "utf-8" ) def hash_password(plain: str ) -> str : return bcrypt.hashpw(plain.encode( "utf-8" ), bcrypt.gensalt(rounds= 12 )).decode( "utf-8" ) def verify_password(plain: str , hashed: str ) -> bool : try : return bcrypt.checkpw(plain.encode( "utf-8" ), hashed.encode( "utf-8" )) except ValueError: return False auth/passwords.py, in full — DUMMY_HASH is generated once at import time, from random bytes The subtle piece worth studying is DUMMY_HASH . Without it, a naive login handler might do "look up the username; if not found, return an error immediately; if found, call verify_password ." That branch has a measurable timing difference — a nonexistent username returns fast (no bcrypt call at all), while an existing username with a wrong password returns slower (a full, deliberately-slow bcrypt comparison runs). An attacker who can measure response times precisely enough can use that difference alone to enumerate which usernames exist in the system, without ever guessing a single correct password. DUMMY_HASH closes this: when a username lookup fails, the login handler still runs verify_password(plain, DUMMY_HASH) against this fixed, meaningless hash, so a nonexistent username costs the same bcrypt-comparison time as a wrong password on a real one. The two cases become indistinguishable by timing alone. Session rotation and reuse detection When a refresh token is used, auth/repo.py 's rotate_session doesn't simply issue a new one and move on — it explicitly revokes the old session row rather than deleting it outright. That distinction matters: because the hash of the old, now-revoked token is still sitting in the table (marked revoked, not gone), a second attempted use of that same old token — which shouldn't happen in normal operation, since a legitimate client only uses a refresh token once before getting a new one — is detectable as reuse rather than silently accepted or silently rejected with no signal. In the concrete attack scenario this defends against: an attacker steals a refresh token and uses it once to mint their own session. When the legitimate user's client later tries to use that same (now-already-rotated) token, the system can recognize "this exact token was already rotated once" and treat it as a signal that the token was compromised, rather than as an ordinary, unremarkable refresh. Username validation as a security control, not just data hygiene auth/usernames.py lowercases and validates usernames against a strict pattern — 3 to 32 characters, alphanumeric plus underscore/hyphen, must start and end with an alphanumeric character. The code's own comment frames this as reducing "homograph confusion" — the risk that two visually similar usernames (using look-alike Unicode characters, or subtly different capitalization) could be mistaken for each other in an audit log or a security review, which matters in exactly the way it wouldn't for a consumer app: a security operator scanning an audit trail for a specific account needs to trust that what they're reading is what's actually there. The scoped bearer-token path — a second, narrower credential Separate from the interactive-session cookie flow entirely, auth_middleware.py recognizes a second kind of credential: an Authorization: Bearer briefr_search_... token, intended for machine or service access rather than a human browser session. This token is deliberately more restricted than a full login session in two ways at once — it's checked against a small, explicit allowlist of read-only paths (semantic search, CVE detail/related/drawer GET requests only — enforced by a path regex, not by role) rather than the general permission system, and it has its own separate rate-limit bucket. The design principle here is the security concept of least privilege applied to machine credentials specifically: a service that only needs to query search results gets a credential that can only query search results, rather than reusing the same broad session mechanism a human analyst uses. The one honest tradeoff to be able to name in an interview: access tokens are stateless JWTs, which means an individual access token cannot be revoked before its 15-minute expiry, even if the corresponding session is revoked — only the refresh token is revocable via the sessions table. After a suspected token leak, an operator who revokes the session has still left up to 15 minutes of residual access on any already-issued access token. This is a deliberate, documented tradeoff (short TTL bounds the exposure window tightly), not an oversight — but it's exactly the kind of detail worth being able to state precisely rather than hand-wave past. Self-check A stolen refresh token gets used by an attacker, and moments later the legitimate user's own client tries to refresh using that same now-rotated token. Walk through rotate_session 's state change and explain exactly how BRIEFR distinguishes this from an ordinary refresh. Why does a failed username lookup during login still run a full bcrypt comparison against DUMMY_HASH instead of returning an error immediately? Why is the search-token bearer path checked against a path-regex allowlist rather than the normal role-based permission system used everywhere else? After revoking a compromised user's session, what window of residual access remains, and why can't it be closed immediately?

title: Rate limiting — inbound, and the residual risk that's accepted rather than solved
text: Part II · Chapter 12 Rate limiting — inbound, and the residual risk that's accepted rather than solved Token buckets protecting BRIEFR from abuse, with a client-identification scheme more careful than it might first appear. rate_limit.py rate_limit_store.py Chapter 16 covers the outbound half of rate limiting — pacing BRIEFR's own calls to NVD, GitHub, and OTX. This chapter covers the inbound half: protecting BRIEFR's own endpoints (login, IOC lookup, refresh, admin routes, the wallboard) from being hammered by a single client, using the token-bucket algorithm introduced in Part 0. Why buckets are process-local, and the constraint that makes that safe The buckets live entirely in the process's own memory — not a shared cache, not a database table, by default. A code comment states directly why that's safe here rather than a latent bug: the deployment runs uvicorn with --workers 1 , meaning there is exactly one process handling requests, so "the rate limit" and "this process's in-memory bucket" are the same thing. The comment goes further and flags the exact way this assumption could later break silently: if a future change added more uvicorn workers for throughput, each worker would get its own independent copy of every bucket, and the effective rate limit would be multiplied by the worker count without any code change actually intending that — five workers would mean a "10 requests per minute" limit becomes 50 per minute in practice, invisibly. rate_limit_store.py is the prepared escape hatch for exactly that future: setting BRIEFR_RATE_LIMIT_STORE=db moves bucket state into the sync_state table (SQLite or Postgres, whichever is active), shared across however many workers or replicas are running — off by default specifically to keep the zero-config dev/test path as simple as possible. def client_key(request: Request) -> str : peer = request.client.host if request.client else "" if peer not in _TRUSTED_PROXY_PEERS: # Direct connection (LAN dev, or someone bypassing nginx): the # socket address is the only trustworthy identity — forwarded # headers here would be attacker-controlled bucket keys. return peer or "unknown" # Set by the Cloudflare edge and overwritten there, so it cannot be # forged by clients coming through the tunnel. cf_ip = request.headers.get( "cf-connecting-ip" , "" ).strip() if cf_ip: return cf_ip # nginx appends $remote_addr as the rightmost X-Forwarded-For hop; the # rightmost non-loopback hop is therefore proxy-attested, while the # leftmost hops are whatever the client sent. forwarded = request.headers.get( "x-forwarded-for" , "" ) hops = [hop.strip() for hop in forwarded.split( "," ) if hop.strip()] for hop in reversed(hops): if hop not in _TRUSTED_PROXY_PEERS: return hop rate_limit.py's client_key() , real code — the exact trust boundary is worth reading twice Why forwarded headers are only trusted conditionally X-Forwarded-For and similar headers exist so a reverse proxy can tell the backend "the real client IP was X, even though I'm the one actually connecting to you" — necessary because otherwise every request would appear to come from the proxy's own address. The catch is that these are just ordinary HTTP headers, and any client can set them to anything at all when talking directly to the backend. client_key() 's logic resolves this correctly: it only trusts forwarded headers at all when the direct socket peer — the actual TCP connection, which can't be spoofed the way a header can — is a known, trusted reverse proxy (Cloudflare's edge or the local nginx). A request arriving directly, bypassing the trusted proxy entirely, gets keyed by its raw socket address only, exactly because trusting a header from an untrusted direct connection would let an attacker mint an unlimited number of fresh rate-limit buckets simply by sending a different fake X-Forwarded-For value on every request — defeating the entire point of rate limiting. The code comment is honest about a residual gap rather than pretending the mitigation is complete: a host on the same local network as the proxy, connecting to nginx directly rather than through Cloudflare, could still present a forged header that nginx would then legitimately append to. This is accepted explicitly for BRIEFR's current private-beta threat model — a security decision made visible in a comment rather than silently absorbed as an unstated assumption. Why login is rate-limited by username, not IP Every other bucket in this file is keyed by client IP, but login_username_bucket is keyed by the submitted username instead. This targets a specific attack pattern IP-based limiting can't catch: credential stuffing, where an attacker tries the same stolen username against many different passwords, spread across a large pool of source IPs (a botnet, a residential proxy service) specifically to stay under any single IP's rate limit. Keying by username instead catches this directly — no matter how many different IPs an attacker rotates through, they're all hammering the same account, and that account's bucket empties regardless of which address each attempt came from. Self-check If BRIEFR were scaled to multiple uvicorn workers without setting BRIEFR_RATE_LIMIT_STORE=db , what happens to the effective login rate limit, and why does nobody notice immediately when this happens? Walk through exactly why trusting X-Forwarded-For from a direct, untrusted connection would let an attacker defeat rate limiting entirely — what would they actually do? Why does keying the login bucket by username instead of IP specifically address credential stuffing, when every other endpoint in this file is correctly keyed by IP instead?

title: Logging and redaction — two systems, and one real gap between them
text: Part II · Chapter 13 Logging and redaction — two systems, and one real gap between them Structured JSON logs, an admin log viewer, and a documented boundary on what redaction actually covers — worth understanding precisely, not just trusting. structured_logging.py redact.py It's easy to assume a codebase has "one logging system with redaction built in," but BRIEFR actually has two separate mechanisms solving two different problems, and conflating them is the most common way to misjudge how well-protected a given piece of data actually is. structured_logging.py : the logging pipeline itself Every log line becomes one JSON object emitted to stderr — deliberately structured rather than free-text, so log aggregation tools (or a human grepping the output) can filter by field rather than parsing prose. A contextvar-based mechanism propagates a request_id / job_id / run_id through the whole call chain of a single request or job, so every log line produced while handling one request can be correlated back to it — genuinely useful when a request touches five subsystems and something in the middle fails. A fixed-size, in-process ring buffer holds the last 500 log entries specifically to back the Admin UI's live log viewer, without needing a separate log-shipping pipeline for that feature. def _should_redact_field(key: str ) -> bool : key_upper = key.upper() return key_upper in _REDACT_EXACT or any ( key_upper.endswith(suffix) for suffix in _REDACT_SUFFIXES ) structured_logging.py — this function only ever sees the keys of extra={...} kwargs, never a log message string The gap, stated exactly, not hand-waved CLAUDE.md states this directly, and reading the actual function confirms it precisely: _should_redact_field() only ever inspects the keys of whatever dictionary is passed as extra={...} to a logging call, masking the value when the key's name ends in _KEY , _TOKEN , _SECRET , or _PASSWORD (or matches a short exact-match list). It never touches the log message string itself — the human-readable text passed as the first argument to logger.info(...) . This is a real, deliberate design boundary, not an accidental gap someone forgot to close: logger.info(f"NVD sync failed with key {api_key}") interpolates the secret directly into the message text and sails straight past redaction untouched, while logger.info("NVD sync failed", extra={"api_key": api_key}) passes the exact same information through the one code path that actually gets checked. The entire safety of this system rests on every call site in the codebase following that convention correctly — there's no code-level enforcement stopping a developer from writing the first version. redact.py : a completely different surface Where structured_logging.py is about what gets written to log output, redact.py is about what gets returned from the Admin config API and stored in the audit log — a different data path serving a different purpose (an operator viewing their own saved config; an auditor reviewing what changed and when). def mask_secret_value(value: str ) -> str : text = (value or "" ).strip() if not text: return "not configured" if len (text) <= 8 : return "***" return f" {text[: 4 ]}…{text[- 4 :]} " redact.py — shows first/last 4 characters of a longer secret, enough for an operator to recognize which key is configured without exposing it Beyond this exact-field masking, redact.py also runs a heuristic — _looks_like_secret_value — over config values that don't already have a schema-declared type: "secret" , matching known API-key prefix formats ( gsk_ for Groq, sk- and sk-or-v1- for OpenAI-family and OpenRouter keys, vulncheck_ , and similar) or simply flagging any long, token-shaped string with no spaces or slashes. This is a genuinely best-effort net, not a guarantee: it will miss a short secret, an unrecognized provider's key format, or a secret embedded mid-sentence inside a longer free-text value — say, a webhook delivery error message that happens to quote back an API key as part of the upstream error text. A separate, deliberately coarser function, mask_webhook_delivery_error , exists specifically for that surface: it redacts any full URL and any string containing the words "token," "password," or "secret" (case-insensitive), or anything longer than 80 characters — trading precision for a wider net on a surface where the shape of what needs hiding is less predictable. The practical rule that falls out of both systems together: if you're extending BRIEFR and handling anything sensitive, secrets belong in extra= keyword arguments when logging (never interpolated into the message string), and in schema-typed "secret" config fields when they flow through the Admin config surface (never as free text a heuristic has to guess about). Free-text interpolation is the one unguarded path shared by both systems — and it's the path that requires no special knowledge to fall into by accident. Self-check A developer writes logger.error(f"NVD sync failed with key {os.environ['NVD_API_KEY']}") . Does BRIEFR's redaction catch this? Trace through _should_redact_field to justify your answer, then rewrite the call correctly. Why does mask_secret_value show the first and last four characters of a secret instead of fully masking it, or showing nothing at all? Give a concrete example of a secret that _looks_like_secret_value 's heuristic would miss, and explain why it would miss it.

title: Where the data actually comes from
text: Part III · Ingest & scheduling Where the data actually comes from Four chapters tracing a CVE from an upstream API to a row in BRIEFR's own database, and the scheduling machinery that runs the whole pipeline unattended, every day, without duplicating work or overwhelming any upstream service.

title: Feed sources — 29 files, four distinct shapes of the same problem
text: Part III · Chapter 14 Feed sources — 29 files, four distinct shapes of the same problem Every feed answers the same question — "how do I sync only what changed" — differently, and the differences tell you something real about each upstream's own design. feeds/nvd.py feeds/kev.py feeds/epss.py feeds/cvelistv5.py +25 more The feeds/ directory has four rough tiers: primary CVE sources (NVD, CISA KEV, FIRST EPSS, cvelistV5, vulnrichment, and cpe_catalog.py — NVD's full CPE 2.3 dictionary, checkpointed across runs since the corpus is large and never touched on the request path), exploit/PoC availability trackers (ExploitDB, Metasploit modules, Nuclei templates, PoC-GitHub), threat-intel mirrors (AlienVault OTX, ThreatFox, OSV, VulnCheck's own KEV mirror), and context feeds (MITRE ATT&CK, ATLAS, news/case studies). Rather than walk all 29 files, this chapter goes deep on four that each teach a genuinely different lesson about watermark design — the pattern from Part 0 that recurs, differently shaped, in every single one of them. NVD — pagination and hard rate limits force the shape NVD's REST API paginates at 2000 results per page and enforces a strict rate limit — 5 requests per 30 seconds without an API key, 50 with one — that a naive client would blow through in seconds on any non-trivial sync. fetch_nvd_cve_updates(watermark) branches on whether a watermark already exists: with one, it queries lastModStartDate / lastModEndDate starting from the watermark minus a 15-minute overlap window (clamped to a 120-day maximum span NVD's API itself enforces); with none — a fresh install's first-ever sync — it instead bootstraps from a pubStartDate window covering the last 14 days, since there's no watermark yet to resume from. Every page fetch passes through the shared outbound queue (Chapter 16) before the actual HTTP call, and a 429 response inside the page-fetch loop retries indefinitely rather than raising — consistent with the project's stated principle that ingestion never drops a request just because a rate limit was hit. The 15-minute overlap on every resumed sync is a small, deliberate over-fetch: it guarantees that a CVE modified in the last few seconds before the previous sync's cutoff timestamp — which might not have been fully committed to NVD's own backend at the exact moment it was queried — gets picked up again rather than silently missed by a hair. The cost is trivial (re-fetching and re-upserting a handful of already-known CVEs, which the idempotent upsert in Chapter 9's data layer makes a safe no-op); the benefit is closing a subtle race condition at the boundary of "what does 'modified since X' even mean when X is a moving target." KEV — no watermark at all, and why that's correct here CISA's KEV catalog is a small, static JSON file with no delta or "since" API of any kind — you get the whole current catalog or nothing. Given that, feeds/kev.py makes the only reasonable choice: it re-fetches and re-applies the entire catalog on every scheduled run, with no watermark concept whatsoever. Idempotency here doesn't come from a watermark at all — it comes entirely from the upsert being keyed by CVE ID downstream, so re-applying an unchanged catalog entry is simply a no-op write. The one defensive check worth noting: if CISA's endpoint ever returned a malformed or genuinely empty response, blindly applying it would look like "every KEV flag in the database should be cleared" — catastrophically wrong. A guard ( FeedFetchError("KEV catalog parsed empty") ) raises instead of silently applying an empty catalog, protecting against exactly that failure mode. EPSS — a bulk file beats one API call per CVE FIRST.org's EPSS scores update daily for the entire CVE corpus — hundreds of thousands of rows. Calling their per-CVE API once for every CVE BRIEFR tracks would be enormously wasteful; instead, feeds/epss.py prefers downloading the daily bulk CSV (gzip-compressed, published once a day) and filtering it in memory to just the CVE IDs BRIEFR actually needs, falling back to the batched per-CVE API (100 CVEs per request) only for whatever the bulk file doesn't cover — typically CVEs published so recently they postdate the last daily snapshot. A neat optimization on top of the bulk-download path: file_identity.py computes and stores a SHA-256 hash of yesterday's downloaded file; if today's download hashes identically (meaning FIRST.org hasn't actually re-published new data since the last check, which does happen), the entire decompress-and-parse cycle is skipped outright rather than redundantly reprocessing byte-identical data. cvelistV5 — a git SHA as a watermark, and why that's the cleverest one MITRE's cvelistV5 GitHub repository often has a CVE's initial JSON record hours before NVD has gotten around to analyzing and publishing it — genuinely earlier signal, worth syncing on its own timeline. The watermark design here is the most interesting of the four: instead of a timestamp, BRIEFR stores the repository's git commit SHA it last synced up to, and uses GitHub's compare API ( /compare/{base_sha}...{head_sha} ) to ask, in one cheap call, exactly which files changed between that SHA and the current HEAD. async def fetch_cvelistv5_delta(watermark_sha: str | None ) -> tuple[...]: branch = get_cvelistv5_branch() head_sha = await _fetch_head_sha(branch) if not head_sha: return [], [], watermark_sha, False # transient failure — don't advance if watermark_sha and watermark_sha == head_sha: return [], [], head_sha, True # nothing changed — a real, successful no-op base_sha = watermark_sha or await _fetch_bootstrap_base_sha(branch, ...) # ...compare base_sha..head_sha, fetch only the changed cves/**.json paths... feeds/cvelistv5.py, abridged — the fourth return value, watermark_advanced , is the whole idempotency story Why a git SHA instead of a timestamp: GitHub's compare API is exact — it returns precisely the files that changed between two commits, with no ambiguity about time zones, clock skew between BRIEFR's server and GitHub's, or what "modified since X" means when X is a wall-clock time. A SHA-based watermark is also immune to a subtle class of bug that plagues timestamp watermarks: if BRIEFR's own clock drifts even slightly, a timestamp watermark could silently skip or re-fetch records; a git SHA has no such ambiguity, because "has this exact commit already been synced" is a yes/no question with no room for interpretation. The function's explicit watermark_advanced: bool return value is the idempotency guarantee made visible in the type signature itself, not left implicit. The caller is only allowed to persist a new watermark SHA when this flag is true — meaning the fetch genuinely completed successfully, even if that success was "nothing changed." If the fetch fails partway through (a network error, a GitHub outage), the function returns False , and the caller must leave the old watermark exactly where it was. A crash or failure here doesn't corrupt anything — it just means the next scheduled run naturally re-attempts the exact same range of history, because nothing was ever marked as done. A known, accepted gap: the compare API's changed-file list is capped at roughly 300 entries by GitHub itself. If more than 300 files changed since the last sync (a large batch update upstream, or BRIEFR having been offline a long time), the sync logs a truncation warning and processes what it received — some changes could be silently missed until a subsequent run's compare call happens to catch them. This is a real, acknowledged limitation, not a closed loop, and worth being able to name precisely rather than assuming the sync is always complete. The other 24 feeds: five clusters, each solving a distinct problem Beyond the four deep-dived above, feeds/ holds five more clusters, each worth knowing at the level of "what problem does this solve and how," even where the full watermark-level detail of NVD/KEV/EPSS/cvelistV5 isn't repeated for every file. Exploit availability ( exploit_common.py , exploit_sync.py , exploitdb.py , metasploit_modules.py , nuclei_index.py , poc_github.py ): exploit_sync.sync_all_exploit_sources() orchestrates all five sequentially, each gated by its own enable flag, with a politeness sleep between them. Three sources (ExploitDB, Metasploit, Nuclei) are snapshot-style — no watermark, a full replace-by-source on every run — while PoC-in-GitHub is the one exploit source with a real watermark : it tracks the upstream repo's last-seen commit SHA and uses GitHub's compare API to fetch only newly-changed CVE files, exactly the same watermark pattern as cvelistV5, applied to a different repository. Every touched CVE gets its has_poc flag flipped additively (Chapter 9's "never downgrade" pattern) — once a CVE is known to have a public exploit, no subsequent sync ever un-marks it. ATT&CK, ATLAS, and AI-context ( mitre.py , atlas.py , ai_context.py ): mitre.py pulls the full MITRE Enterprise ATT&CK STIX bundle plus a CTID CVE-to-technique mapping and a pinned, dated CISA KEV-to-ATT&CK snapshot file — the pinned dated URL is a real, acknowledged maintenance debt (it will eventually need a manual version bump). atlas.py (MITRE's separate AI/ML adversarial-technique matrix) is genuinely more sophisticated than it looks: it follows YAML "pointer" redirect files up to 6 hops before giving up, and transparently supports two different schema versions of the same upstream dataset. ai_context.py is pure text analysis with no network calls of its own — it flags whether a CVE mentions AI/ML libraries (a hardcoded 21-term list: TensorFlow, PyTorch, LangChain, and others) and heuristically guesses at a relevant ATLAS technique via keyword-phrase matching, explicitly a guess, not an authoritative mapping. Threat-intel and vulnerability mirrors ( osv.py , otx.py , otx_continuous.py , threatfox.py , vulncheck_kev.py , extended.py ): otx.py is the main OTX pulse-fetching module Chapter 20 builds on — every call checks a quota budget first, and results are cached at two layers (an in-memory-ish generic cache, then a 6-hour DB table) before ever touching the network. otx_continuous.py is a deliberately separate, second sync path: rather than one nightly burst that risks exhausting the hourly OTX quota in one shot, it runs every 5 minutes and spends a small, bounded slice of the remaining hourly budget each time — smoothing consumption across the whole day. extended.py is a five-source grab-bag (Sploitus, GreyNoise, MalwareBazaar, URLhaus, CIRCL) with one detail worth knowing precisely: CIRCL gets a two-tier cache — a successful lookup is cached for 7 days, but a miss is separately cached for 24 hours under its own key, specifically so a rate-limited or down upstream can't be hammered with the same "does this CVE have CIRCL data" question on every sync cycle. News and case studies ( incident_sources.py , incident_news.py , case_study_feed.py , cve_record_v5.py , vulnrichment.py ): incident_news.py parses RSS/Atom feeds from five security-news sources with a defensive guard against bot-protection pages (rejecting any response that looks like an HTML challenge page rather than real feed XML). case_study_feed.py — despite its name — actually builds a combined incident-news-plus-ATLAS-case-study snapshot for the UI, with a genuinely careful cold-start design: if no snapshot exists yet on a fresh install, it schedules a background build and immediately returns an empty, explicitly-flagged "warming" result rather than blocking the request. cve_record_v5.py is shared parsing infrastructure (not a feed itself) for the CVE JSON 5.x schema both cvelistV5 and vulnrichment.py use — its merge_additive_cve_fields() function is the concrete implementation of "never downgrade, only fill gaps" this book has referenced conceptually: it only fills a missing CVSS score, only raises severity if the new value ranks higher, and only unions (never replaces) CWE/product lists. Shared plumbing ( errors.py ,

title: The scheduler and its lock layer — a danger zone, verified line by line
text: Part III · Chapter 15 The scheduler and its lock layer — a danger zone, verified line by line Why APScheduler's own overlap protection isn't enough, and the exact coupling CLAUDE.md warns you never to let drift. scheduler.py scheduler_locks.py routers/admin.py scheduler.py builds an APScheduler AsyncIOScheduler and registers roughly 28 jobs on it — one per feed sync, plus the nightly correlation engine, scheduled backups, session cleanup, and more — each identified by a stable string passed as id= to scheduler.add_job(...) . Every job's coroutine is wrapped in job_log_context(id) so its log lines carry a consistent correlation ID back to Chapter 13's structured logging, and jobs are registered with max_instances=1 , meaning APScheduler itself refuses to let a job overlap its own next scheduled run if the previous one is still executing. The gap max_instances=1 doesn't cover max_instances=1 only protects a job against colliding with its own next scheduled firing — it says nothing at all about a completely separate code path triggering the same underlying work. BRIEFR's admin UI has exactly such a path: an operator can click "sync NVD now" from routers/admin.py , invoking the same NVD sync function outside the scheduler's own timing entirely. Without additional protection, a manual "sync now" click could start running concurrently with a scheduled sync that happened to already be mid-flight — two processes racing to read the same watermark, fetch overlapping data, and write conflicting updates to the same rows at the same time. scheduler_locks.py closes exactly this gap with a second, independent layer: a plain Python dictionary mapping each job's ID string to its own asyncio.Lock . Both the scheduled job function and the manual-trigger admin endpoint check the same lock before proceeding — whichever one gets there first acquires it and the other is turned away (the admin endpoint returns HTTP 409 Conflict) rather than both running at once. # Keys must match the `id=` strings passed to scheduler.add_job() exactly. # incident_feed_refresh, backup_deadman_check, session_cleanup, # cache_retention_cleanup, watchlist_monitor_alerts, and api_key_health_check # have no entry here — they run without a lock today (each job is registered # with max_instances=1, so APScheduler itself prevents overlap; this module # only consolidates locks that already existed, it doesn't add new ones). _LOCKS: dict[ str , asyncio.Lock] = { "nvd_incremental_sync" : asyncio.Lock(), "kev_metadata_sync" : asyncio.Lock(), "epss_score_sync" : asyncio.Lock(), "nightly_correlation" : asyncio.Lock(), "cvelistv5_incremental_sync" : asyncio.Lock(), # ...16 more, one per lockable job... } scheduler_locks.py, real code and its own comment — note it documents which jobs are intentionally excluded, not just which ones are included Checking this directly against scheduler.py 's actual add_job(id=...) calls confirms the two files agree exactly — every locked job ID here matches a real registered job, with no drift as of this reading. routers/admin.py 's own _JOB_RUN_MAP (which the manual "run now" endpoint uses to find each job's function) is a superset that also lists a handful of lock-free jobs — the file's own comment explains why that's fine rather than an inconsistency: those specific jobs rely on APScheduler's max_instances=1 alone, because they don't have a manual-trigger button in the admin UI that could race them, so the second layer of protection genuinely isn't needed for them. Tracing a real request end to end Follow POST /api/refresh/nvd concretely: the request passes require_admin (Chapter 6), then checks refresh_in_progress() — which ORs together the NVD, KEV, and EPSS locks — returning 409 immediately if any is held. If clear, it spawns the sync as a background task via task_registry.spawn_background_task , which holds a strong reference to the task specifically so Python's garbage collector can't silently collect and cancel it mid-flight (a real historical bug class, referenced again in Chapter 30). The spawned function re-checks and acquires its own lock, reads the current watermark (seeding one from the maximum modified timestamp already in the cves table if none exists yet and at least 10 CVEs are already present — a sane bootstrap for a database that already has data but no recorded watermark), fetches and upserts, advances the watermark only after the upsert has actually succeeded, and in a finally block always records the job's last-run time for the admin UI and releases the lock — regardless of whether the sync succeeded or raised partway through. Self-check Why isn't APScheduler's max_instances=1 sufficient on its own, and what specific race does scheduler_locks.py close that it doesn't? If the process crashed mid-sync, right after reading the watermark but before writing the new one, what state would the database be left in — and why is that state safe to resume from? Why does task_registry.spawn_background_task need to hold a strong reference to a spawned task at all — what would silently go wrong without it?

title: The outbound queue and circuit breakers — never dropping a request on purpose
text: Part III · Chapter 16 The outbound queue and circuit breakers — never dropping a request on purpose One shared choke point every feed passes through before it ever touches the network, built around a single stated principle: wait, don't fail. resilient_client.py api_queue.py source_rate_limits.py Every outbound call any feed module makes — to NVD, GitHub, OTX, CISA, FIRST.org, any of it — is routed through resilient_client.py 's resilient_get / resilient_request , never a raw httpx call made directly by a feed module. This centralization is what makes it possible to reason about outbound reliability in one place instead of 29 separate, inconsistent implementations. CIRCUIT_FAILURE_THRESHOLD = 3 CIRCUIT_COOLDOWN_SECONDS = 60.0 def _record_failure(source: str , error: str , *, cooldown_seconds= None ) -> None : state = _state(source) state[ "consecutive_failures" ] += 1 if state[ "consecutive_failures" ] >= CIRCUIT_FAILURE_THRESHOLD: cooldown = cooldown_seconds if cooldown_seconds is not None else CIRCUIT_COOLDOWN_SECONDS state[ "circuit_open_until" ] = time.time() + cooldown def is_circuit_open(source: str ) -> bool : open_until = _circuit_open_until(source) return bool (open_until and time.time() < open_until) resilient_client.py, real code — three consecutive failures, sixty seconds of silence, then one more try The circuit-breaker state machine, made concrete Part 0 described a circuit breaker in the abstract; here it is exactly. Each source (NVD, OTX, GitHub, and so on) has its own independent health state: a count of consecutive failures, and a timestamp marking when the circuit reopens. After 3 consecutive failures, the circuit "opens" for 60 seconds — during that window, is_circuit_open() returns true immediately and calls to that source fail fast without even attempting the network request, protecting BRIEFR from wasting time and connections hammering a service that's already down. A single success resets the failure count to zero and clears the open-until timestamp entirely — the breaker doesn't require a gradual healing period, one clean response is enough to trust the source again. This asymmetry (three strikes to open, one success to close) is a deliberate choice: opening the circuit is a costly false-negative to get wrong too eagerly (you'd stop legitimate traffic to a source that was only briefly slow), so it requires a real pattern of failure; closing it back up is cheap to get wrong (worst case, one more failed request before it reopens), so a single success is enough evidence. Never dropping a request, and what that actually costs The module's own design principle, stated directly: a 429 (rate limited) response should make the caller wait and retry, not fail the entire sync outright. This is why NVD's page-fetching loop (Chapter 14) retries on 429 indefinitely rather than raising after some fixed number of attempts — a design that trades "the sync might take noticeably longer than expected on a bad day" for "the sync never simply gives up partway through and leaves data half-updated." api_queue.py implements the pacing half of this: a registry tracking, per source, how many requests are currently in flight and when the next one is allowed to start, so a caller doesn't just retry blindly but genuinely waits until pacing constraints are satisfied — visible live in the admin UI as requests move through queued → waiting → active states, rather than being an invisible internal detail. source_rate_limits.py adds one more layer of care: several distinct BRIEFR feeds — PoC-GitHub, cvelistV5, Metasploit-module sync — all ultimately hit GitHub's API under the hood, and GitHub's rate limit is per account , not per feed. If each feed paced itself independently, thinking it alone was respecting GitHub's limit, the three of them running concurrently would collectively blow straight through it. resolve_pacing_key aliases all three onto one shared pacing bucket keyed simply as github , so the constraint that actually exists (one shared quota) is modeled as one shared bucket, not three independent ones that happen to sum past the real limit. A specific, non-obvious detail: GitHub's rate-limit headers ( x-ratelimit-remaining , x-ratelimit-reset ) work differently from the generic Retry-After header most APIs use. Retry-After is a relative delay ("wait 30 seconds"); GitHub's x-ratelimit-reset is an absolute Unix epoch timestamp marking when its rolling window resets. BRIEFR's pause-duration calculation branches on which kind of header a given source actually sends — computing reset_at - time.time() for GitHub specifically, rather than naively parsing it as if it were a relative delay, which would produce a wildly wrong (usually enormous) wait time. Self-check Why does the circuit breaker require three consecutive failures to open but only one success to close? What would go wrong with the opposite asymmetry? Three different feeds all ultimately call GitHub's API. Why are they aliased onto one shared pacing bucket instead of three independent ones, and what would happen if they weren't? Explain concretely why treating GitHub's x-ratelimit-reset header as if it were a relative Retry-After delay would produce a badly wrong wait time.

title: Durable background jobs — a second job system, and why one wasn't enough
text: Part III · Chapter 17 Durable background jobs — a second job system, and why one wasn't enough Procrastinate exists specifically for the one class of job where APScheduler's "just re-run it, it's idempotent" story genuinely isn't good enough. jobs/app.py jobs/tasks.py jobs/worker.py jobs/context.py Every job discussed so far — NVD sync, KEV sync, correlation — shares a comfortable property: if the process crashes mid-run, the next scheduled run safely resumes from the last saved watermark, at worst redoing a small, harmless amount of already-completed work. That property holds because each of those jobs is a single, short-ish unit of work bounded by one watermark. It stops holding for a fundamentally different kind of job: the Tier-A stack backfill, a long-running, multi-step process (retroactively pulling every historical CVE matching a newly-declared software stack) that can span many separate ticks over an extended period. A crash halfway through that kind of job doesn't have one clean watermark to resume from in the same way — restarting from scratch would mean redoing potentially hours of already-completed work. Rather than redesign APScheduler's entire model to handle this one case, BRIEFR added a second, narrower job system: Procrastinate, a Postgres-backed durable task queue, gated behind PROCRASTINATE_ENABLED=1 and a genuine Postgres DATABASE_URL — on SQLite, or with the flag off, every Procrastinate-related call silently no-ops. This is consistent with a pattern you'll see recur throughout this book: rather than force a big migration onto the whole system to solve one narrow problem, add a small, explicitly-scoped, opt-in mechanism next to the existing one, additive rather than a replacement. jobs/tasks.py defines the actual task functions on a Procrastinate Blueprint() — a health_ping task that exists purely to prove the defer-run-succeed round trip survives a process restart (useful as a smoke test in itself), and stack_backfill_tick , which advances one increment of a backfill run and delegates the real work to services/stack_backfill_worker.py (Chapter 29). jobs/worker.py runs an in-process worker as its own asyncio task, registered with task_registry (Chapter 15's strong-reference pattern, reused here) so it participates in the same graceful-shutdown drain as everything else. jobs/context.py 's outbound_context() uses Python contextvars to let any outbound HTTP call made from inside a Procrastinate task be correctly attributed back to "which job triggered this" in the usage-metering system — necessary because the metering code (Chapter 16) has no direct call-stack link back to whichever job runner happened to invoke it. Self-check Why does BRIEFR run two separate job systems (APScheduler and Procrastinate) instead of migrating everything onto whichever one is more capable? What specific property does the Tier-A stack backfill lack that every other scheduled job in this book has, and why does that property matter after a crash? Why is Procrastinate gated to Postgres only, with no SQLite equivalent — connect this back to what you learned about SQLite's limitations in Chapter 9.

title: The product's actual brain
text: Part IV · Intelligence engines The product's actual brain Seven chapters on how a CVE becomes a number, how numbers become priorities, how CVEs get linked into campaigns, and how all of that turns into something an analyst can act on. This is the deepest and most distinctive part of the codebase — most of what makes BRIEFR BRIEFR, rather than a generic CVE list, lives here.

title: Risk and Threat scoring — six weighted components, verified against the real code
text: Part IV · Chapter 18 Risk and Threat scoring — six weighted components, verified against the real code Why a fixed, explainable formula beats a learned model here, and how the newer split-score system fixes a real flaw in the older blended one. scoring/risk.py scoring/threat.py scoring/environment.py scoring/priority.py ADR-002 # v1.1b weights — sum = 1.00 WEIGHT_ASSET = 0.35 WEIGHT_KEV = 0.25 WEIGHT_EPSS = 0.15 WEIGHT_EXPLOIT = 0.10 WEIGHT_CVSS = 0.10 WEIGHT_MOMENTUM = 0.05 scoring/risk.py — the literal constants, confirmed against the running code, matching what CLAUDE.md documents exactly Why a fixed formula, and why fixed doesn't mean simplistic Each component contributes a 0–1 sub-score, gets multiplied by its weight, and the six weighted contributions sum to a final 0–100 Risk Score. What makes this more than a toy weighted average is that every component ships a human-readable sentence explaining exactly why it scored what it did — component_sentences renders something like "Asset match: confirmed exposure on your declared nginx stack" alongside the raw number. This isn't a cosmetic nicety; it's a hard product requirement that traces directly to a broader design principle stated in this project's own UI rules: every status word, pill, or score needs a discoverable explanation. A learned model (a gradient-boosted tree, a neural net trained on historical exploitation data) could plausibly outperform a fixed formula on raw predictive accuracy, but it can't give that same per-component, audit-ready "here's exactly why" explanation without a whole separate layer of explainability tooling bolted on afterward — and even then, that tooling approximates the model's reasoning rather than stating it exactly. A fixed formula's explanation is its computation; there's no approximation gap between what happened and what gets shown. There's a second, quieter benefit: a fixed formula is trivially reproducible and regression-testable. Feed the same CVE and the same asset profile into calculate_risk_score twice, in two different environments, a year apart, and you get the exact same number — useful for an intelligence product where an analyst might reasonably ask "why did this score change between yesterday and today," and the honest answer needs to be a specific, traceable component delta, not "the model's internal weights shifted slightly during retraining." Why KEV is weighted so heavily, and why CVSS is weighted so little It's worth sitting with the relative weights rather than skimming past them. KEV membership — confirmed, real-world exploitation, per Part 0's definition — is weighted 0.25, the second-highest of all six components, just behind asset relevance itself. CVSS, by contrast, gets only 0.10, the lowest tier alongside the exploit-availability component. This ordering encodes a real judgment about signal quality: CVSS describes how bad a vulnerability could be under a worst-case exploitation scenario, but says nothing about whether anyone is actually doing that in practice — and in practice, most CVEs with a high CVSS score are never exploited at all, making CVSS a weak discriminator between "should this be your top priority today" and "should this be priority #400." KEV, meanwhile, is about as strong a signal as exists in this domain: CISA doesn't add a CVE to that catalog speculatively, only after confirming real-world exploitation. Weighting confirmed reality nearly three times higher than theoretical worst-case severity is the formula's single clearest statement of what it actually believes matters. The newer split system — Threat Score, Environment tier, Operational Priority (ADR-002) A real flaw emerges once you actually use the blended Risk Score in practice: if an analyst hasn't loaded an asset profile yet — or a CVE genuinely doesn't match anything in their stack — the 0.35-weighted asset component contributes close to zero, which drags the entire blended score down. A CVE that's critically dangerous in the abstract but irrelevant to this specific environment ends up looking indistinguishable from a CVE that's just not very dangerous at all — both show up as "low score," for two completely different reasons an analyst has no way to tell apart from the number alone. ADR-002's fix is to stop blending those two questions into one number and answer them separately instead. A Threat Score renormalizes the five non-asset weights (dividing by 0.65, since removing the 0.35 asset weight means the rest no longer sum to 1.0) into a purely asset-independent "how dangerous is this, full stop" score — and applies a hard floor: any CVE on the KEV list scores at least 80 on this scale, regardless of what the additive formula alone would produce, because confirmed real-world exploitation is treated as decisive rather than merely a strong input among several. Separately, an Environment Relevance tier — a category, not a number, one of CONFIRMED / LIKELY / POSSIBLE / WEAK / UNKNOWN / NO_MATCH — captures how strongly this CVE matches the declared stack, and is deliberately never blended back into the Threat Score. Finally, an Operational Priority band (P1 through P4) is derived from a fixed lookup table crossing the two: PRIORITY_TABLE = { "CRITICAL" : { "CONFIRMED" : "P1" , "LIKELY" : "P1" , "POSSIBLE" : "P2" , "WEAK" : "P2" , "UNKNOWN" : "P1" , "NO_MATCH" : "P3" }, "HIGH" : { "CONFIRMED" : "P1" , "LIKELY" : "P2" , "POSSIBLE" : "P2" , "WEAK" : "P2" , "UNKNOWN" : "P2" , "NO_MATCH" : "P3" }, "MED" : { "CONFIRMED" : "P2" , "LIKELY" : "P2" , "POSSIBLE" : "P3" , "WEAK" : "P3" , "UNKNOWN" : "P3" , "NO_MATCH" : "P4" }, "LOW" : { "CONFIRMED" : "P3" , "LIKELY" : "P3" , "POSSIBLE" : "P4" , "WEAK" : "P4" , "UNKNOWN" : "P4" , "NO_MATCH" : "P4" }, } scoring/priority.py, the actual lookup table — read it as a decision matrix, not a formula Notice what this table actually encodes, row by row: a CRITICAL-threat CVE with UNKNOWN environment relevance (a stack that hasn't been fully profiled yet) still lands at P1 — the system deliberately errs toward over-alerting rather than under-alerting when it genuinely doesn't know whether something applies to you, rather than silently defaulting an unknown match to "safe to ignore." Compare that to a LOW-threat CVE with NO_MATCH environment relevance, which lands at P4 regardless — a case where both dimensions agree there's nothing here worth an analyst's attention. One further mechanism sits on top of the table: corr_escalation , an optional flag that can bump a P2 or P3 band up by exactly one level (never P1, never a two-level jump) when Chapter 20's correlation engine independently finds strong evidence of an active, real-world campaign involving this CVE — a second, independent signal allowed to override the base table by a bounded, single step, not overwrite it outright. Self-check Why does BRIEFR maintain two scoring systems side by side — the older blended Risk Score and the newer split Threat/Environment/Priority — instead of simply replacing one with the other? A CRITICAL-threat CVE with UNKNOWN environment relevance lands at P1 in the priority table. Explain the reasoning behind that specific cell, not just what the table says. Why is CVSS weighted lower than exploit availability in the Risk Score, when CVSS is the more universally recognized standard? What's the maximum a correlation escalation can move a CVE's priority band, and why is that bound in place rather than letting a confirmed active campaign override the table entirely?

title: Asset and CPE matching — the mechanical layer under the 0.35 weight
text: Part IV · Chapter 19 Asset and CPE matching — the mechanical layer under the 0.35 weight Deterministic version arithmetic where the data is structured, careful fuzzy fallback where it isn't. matching/cpe.py scoring/asset_match.py Every risk score's heaviest-weighted component depends on answering one deceptively simple question: does this CVE actually affect something the analyst runs? NVD attaches structured CPE version ranges to most CVEs — machine-readable statements like "affects Apache HTTP Server 2.4.0 through 2.4.53 inclusive" — but an analyst's own declared asset stack is free text they typed themselves ("nginx", "Apache 2.4", "our web servers"), and reconciling exact structured data against messy human-entered text is the entire problem this module solves. The design deliberately keeps two concerns separate rather than reaching for one fuzzy-matching library to handle everything at once: exact version arithmetic (does 2.4.51, say, actually fall within a range with an inclusive start and exclusive end?) is handled by version_in_range() , implementing NVD's four boundary fields ( version_start_including , version_start_excluding , version_end_including , version_end_excluding ) as straightforward inclusive/exclusive comparisons — with a small but necessary wrinkle: version strings like "1.2.10" need to sort after "1.2.9," not before it alphabetically, so comparison logic treats digit-only segments numerically rather than as plain string comparison. Separately, fuzzy product-name matching handles the messy human-text side, via normalized substring and token-containment checks. Keeping these two concerns apart, in plain auditable Python rather than a general fuzzy-matching library, is a deliberate choice consistent with the whole scoring stack's "explainable over powerful" posture (Chapter 18) — you can point at exactly which comparison produced which result, for any CVE, at any time. resolve_asset_component() — the actual bridge into the Risk Score — tries the structured CPE match first, and only falls back to a nine-tier fuzzy graduation (exact CPE match, then CPE product match without version, then plain product-name match, then vendor-only match, then OS match, then AI-system match, then a description-mention match, descending in confidence) when the structured match returns exactly zero — meaning no CPE data matched at all, not merely a weak match. That distinction matters: a genuine structured "product matches, but no version specified" result already carries real signal (worth 55 out of 100 in the scoring scale), and letting a weaker fuzzy text match override that legitimate partial structured signal would actually throw away good information rather than supplement missing information — the fallback exists specifically for the case where structured data is entirely absent, not for the case where it's merely imperfect. Self-check Why does the fuzzy-matching fallback only trigger when the CPE score is exactly zero, rather than whenever it's below some threshold like 55? Explain why "1.2.10" needs custom comparison logic to correctly sort after "1.2.9" — what would a naive string comparison get wrong? What's lost, and what's gained, by keeping exact version arithmetic and fuzzy name matching as two separate code paths instead of one unified fuzzy-matching library?

title: The correlation engine — a five-phase build, and why it had to move off the request path
text:
Part IV · Chapter 20 The correlation engine — a five-phase build, and why it had to move off the request path Twenty-one files, three overlapping version-numbering schemes, one real production incident that reshaped the whole thing, and a scoring synthesis layer bolted on after the fact. This is the deepest chapter in the book — it earns it. correlation/*.py — 21 files ADR-004 What "correlation" actually means here — and what it deliberately isn't Worth being precise about scope before anything else, because the name is genuinely ambiguous across the codebase: this engine is primarily about CVE-to-CVE linkage — connecting different CVEs that share threat-intelligence evidence, chiefly OTX (AlienVault Open Threat Exchange) "pulses" and the indicators of compromise attached to them. It secondarily covers CVE-to-actor/sector attribution (via MITRE ATT&CK technique overlap and OTX's own adversary tagging) and CVE-to-vendor volume anomalies (a sudden spike in CVEs from one vendor). It is explicitly not CVE-to-detection matching (Chapter 21 owns that) and not CVE-to-asset matching (Chapter 19 owns that). Reading the file docstrings: three numbering schemes, one evolving system Almost every file in this package carries an inline "Phase N" or "CORR-PR-N" label in its docstring, and taken at face value they look inconsistent — priority.py calls itself "Correlation v3," while config.py still hardcodes CAMPAIGN_ALGORITHM_VERSION = "2.0.0-phase2" even though campaigns.py 's actual behavior (pulse-family deduplication, a later addition tagged CORR-PR-9 ) is well past what "Phase 2" meant in the original plan. The accurate story, reconstructed from a now-superseded planning document ( docs/archive/superseded/CORRELATION_V2_PLAN.md ) plus every file's own docstring: a phased plan (Phases 1 through 5) was written and largely built section-by-section — the plan's own quality-control subsections (§24.1 through §24.13) map almost one-to-one onto individual files here — and then, after the plan was formally superseded by a newer spec document, more was built on top without renumbering: a priority-scoring synthesis layer (informally "v3"), and later still, ADR-004's precompute architecture. Don't read the phase labels as a strict changelog — read them as archaeological layers, each still live in production, none of them replaced by the next. flowchart TB IN["Raw OTX pulse + IOC data"] --> N["ioc_normalize.py
defang, collapse types, flag noise IPs"] N --> H["hub_suppress.py
drop IOCs over 50-pulse cap"] H --> P["pulse_families.py
union-find dedup (CORR-PR-9)"] P --> C["campaigns.py
build one campaign per family"] C --> E["ioc_graph.py + confidence.py + freshness.py
shared-infra edges, scored"] E --> A["attribution.py + threatfox_corroboration.py
alias-aware actor match, 2nd-source corroboration"] A --> L["lifecycle.py
emerging / active / declining / stale"] L --> PR["priority.py (v3)
one 0–100 number, capped & explainable"] PR --> OUT["engine.py::get_correlation_for_cve
ADR-004 precompute-or-fallback"] F["suppressions.py + feedback.py"] -.->|analyst dismiss / confirm / reject| C M["metrics.py + status.py"] -.->|nightly self-monitoring| OUT Five archaeological phases plus the later priority layer, drawn as one pipeline — each box below is one file, in the order data actually flows through them. Phase 1 — Foundation: normalize, suppress hubs, dedupe pulses into campaigns ioc_normalize.py is the entry gate every raw OTX indicator passes through before it's usable for correlation at all: it defangs indicators (OTX data arrives as hxxps:// , 1[.]2[.]3[.]4 -style defanged text, which this module un-defangs via four regex replacements), collapses type-name drift (IPV4/IPV6→IP, HOSTNAME→DOMAIN, MD5/SHA1/SHA256→HASH), and — worth calling out as a deliberate, documented scope decision — flags a small hardcoded set of 16 well-known public DNS resolvers (Google's 8.8.8.8, Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1, Quad9, OpenDNS, and their IPv6 equivalents) as always-noise. The code comment explains why the list stops there rather than growing into a full CDN/cloud-IP denylist: maintaining a comprehensive "which IPs are too generic to mean anything" feed was judged not worth the ongoing maintenance burden, when the general popularity-based degree penalty (below) already catches broader noise structurally instead of by name. hub_suppress.py is the direct, named fix for the incident this chapter's ADR-004 section covers below: is_hub_cve() flags any CVE whose IOC pulse-count exceeds CORRELATION_HUB_CVE_PULSE_CAP (default 50), and filter_campaign_members() applies an asymmetric rule worth understanding precisely — if the CVE being queried is itself a hub, only its direct co-members survive (heavily capped); if it's not a hub, any peer that is one gets dropped from the expansion entirely. This asymmetry is what stops a single Log4Shell-scale CVE from gluing hundreds of otherwise-unrelated CVEs into one giant, meaningless "campaign" via shared low-value infrastructure. A separate function, apply_member_cap() , enforces a hard membership ceiling (default 25) by sorting CVE IDs and keeping the first N — deterministic across rebuilds, not weighted, so the same query always returns the same members. pulse_families.py (tagged CORR-PR-9 , a later addition) solves a real duplication problem: different analysts submit near-duplicate OTX pulses describing the same real-world campaign, under different names, with mostly-but-not-fully overlapping IOC sets. Two merge rules, implemented via classic union-find (disjoint-set with path compression): pulses merge if they share an identical CVE member set and identical normalized name, or if they clear a Jaccard similarity of at least 0.7 on their non-hub IOC sets (each side needing at least 3 IOCs before the comparison is considered meaningful — comparing two pulses that each have one IOC in common would be statistical noise, not a real similarity signal). Family IDs and campaign IDs are both derived deterministically as sha256(oldest_pulse_id)[:12] , anchored to the family's oldest member — so IDs stay stable across nightly rebuilds even as a family's membership grows over time.
