A bridging function, legacy_campaign_id_for_pulse() , preserves the pre-dedup per-pulse ID scheme purely so that analyst suppressions recorded before this migration still resolve correctly afterward. campaigns.py is both the nightly builder and the read path — its behavior has grown well past its own "Phase 1" docstring label. build_campaigns_from_pulses() calls rebuild_pulse_families first, then builds exactly one campaign per family (not per pulse), skips families under 2 members, computes lifecycle via the function covered below, and — notably — soft-retracts (rather than deletes) campaigns whose family vanished since the last run, preserving suppression history rather than silently losing it. The read path, get_campaigns_for_cve() , does something worth pausing on: it expands a campaign's membership with CVEs that share strong IOCs (hash/domain) with the anchor CVE even if they were never co-tagged in the same OTX pulse — a deliberate choice so that strong shared evidence isn't artificially siloed into the weaker "infrastructure" bucket (below) purely because of where OTX happened to draw pulse boundaries. Phase 2 — Evidence: shared infrastructure, confidence, freshness decay, and honest copy ioc_graph.py is, concretely, the file behind the ADR-004 incident below — its _shared_ioc_rows() function is the exact self-join ( otx_pulse_iocs against itself, joined through otx_cve_pulses ) that produced the O(n²) blowup on hub IOCs. find_shared_infrastructure_v2() is the orchestrator: batches enrichment confirmations and ThreatFox corroboration checks (rather than one query per IOC), computes per-edge confidence, aggregates multiple edges per peer CVE into one confidence tier, and sorts results by confidence first and IOC-type strength second (hash > domain > url > ip) — explicitly so a strong peer is never truncated out of the result limit in favor of one that merely sorted earlier alphabetically. confidence.py holds the per-edge scoring rules, and it's worth being precise about the exact order of operations, because the order is itself a design decision: start from a base score by IOC type (hash=high, domain/url=medium, IP=low, with IP additionally forced to low if it's a noise address per ioc_normalize.is_noise_ip ); apply confirmation adjustments from cached third-party enrichment (GreyNoise "malicious" bumps confidence up, GreyNoise "benign" pulls it down, MalwareBazaar/URLhaus hits bump it up); apply the degree penalty last freshness.py is the exact formula this book quoted earlier, and it's worth re-reading now with the full picture: base score by type (hash 0.9, domain 0.6, url 0.65, IP 0.3) × a logarithmic degree penalty (flat below a pulse-count of 3, smoothly decaying above it — a softer, graduated sibling to hub_suppress.py 's hard 50-pulse cliff) × an exponential freshness decay keyed to a per-type half-life (IP 30 days, URL 60, domain 120, hash 365 — reflecting that a file hash discovered a year ago is exactly as malicious today, while an IP from a year ago has very likely changed hands) × a corroboration factor rewarding independent confirmation with diminishing returns. One detail worth knowing: when neither an observed_at nor ingested_at timestamp is available at all, the function explicitly skips decay entirely (factor forced to 1.0, flagged freshness_fallback: true ) rather than penalizing an indicator just because its age happens to be unrecorded. confirm.py enforces a hard architectural rule worth stating plainly: it reads already-cached third-party enrichment (GreyNoise/MalwareBazaar/URLhaus, via the same ioc_cache table Chapter 23's IOC lookup writes to) and never makes a new HTTP call at correlation read-time — corroboration is only ever based on data some other subsystem already fetched for its own purposes. copy.py is small (three functions) but carries a real security property: every OTX-derived free-text string (pulse names, adversary names) that reaches an analyst's screen passes through sanitize_pulse_text() first, which HTML-escapes and truncates it — because OTX pulse names are community-submitted, user-generated text, and rendering them unsanitized would be a stored-XSS vector into BRIEFR's own UI. attribution.py handles the alias-aware conflict check already covered in this book's earlier pass, precisely: build_alias_families() indexes every alias in MITRE's mitre_groups.aliases field so that "APT28" and "Fancy Bear" resolve to the same family, and attribution_conflict() returns true — a conflict — only when there's no evidence of agreement between an OTX-attributed adversary and a MITRE-technique-matched actor, rather than requiring positive proof of disagreement. The analyst feedback loop: two genuinely different kinds of human input It's worth distinguishing two mechanisms that sound similar but record different things. suppressions.py is dismissal — an analyst saying "hide this specific finding," scoped to a campaign, a CVE pair, a pulse, or an infrastructure link. Its most intricate piece, resolve_suppressed_campaign_ids() , exists because of a real migration wrinkle: suppressions were recorded against per-pulse campaign IDs before pulse_families.py 's dedup shipped, so this function expands an old suppressed ID into whichever new, family-anchored campaign ID it now belongs to — an old dismissal keeps working correctly even after the underlying campaigns got merged. feedback.py is a separate, later addition ( CORR-PR-12 ) recording a genuinely different judgment: confirm , reject , or resolve_conflict — not "hide this," but "this correlation is/isn't actually correct," which feeds directly into the confirmation-rate and rejection-rate metrics covered below. threatfox_corroboration.py is the mechanism behind "independent corroboration" mentioned above: it cros

title: Detection engineering — a generator, deliberately not a live detector
text:
Part IV · Chapter 21 Detection engineering — a generator, deliberately not a live detector Why the rule-generation path is explicitly "no LLM," and where an LLM is allowed to help instead. detection/composer.py detection/sigma_generator.py detection/class_router.py detection/backlog.py Given a CVE (and optionally an ATT&CK technique or CWE it maps to), this subsystem assembles a "detection pack" — community Sigma and Elastic rules fetched live from GitHub, BRIEFR's own template-generated Sigma rules, ready-to-paste SIEM queries in four dialects (Elastic KQL, Splunk SPL, Microsoft Sentinel KQL, IBM QRadar AQL), and YARA rules built from file hashes OTX has observed in the wild. It's worth being precise about what this is not : nothing here executes against live logs or fires an alert. It generates and aggregates starter content for an analyst to adapt — a detection-engineering accelerator, not a detection engine in the SIEM sense. Why the generation path is explicitly, deliberately "no LLM" Community rule coverage (SigmaHQ's public repository, Elastic's detection rules) is genuinely patchy — most CVEs, especially recent or less prominent ones, simply have no published community rule yet, and waiting for one is not a real fallback plan. The obvious modern instinct is to have an LLM generate a plausible-looking rule on demand. detection/composer.py 's own docstring rejects that instinct explicitly: the template-based generation path is deterministic, keyed by ATT&CK technique ID or CWE, precisely because a generated detection rule needs to be reproducible (the same input always produces the same rule, so two analysts comparing notes are looking at the same thing) and honestly labeled — every generated rule ships with status: experimental and an explicit briefr_confidence tier (HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW), rather than an LLM's confident-sounding prose that might describe detection logic which doesn't actually work as written, with no easy way for an analyst to tell the difference between "this was carefully derived" and "this sounds plausible." LLM involvement isn't absent from the system entirely — it's deliberately isolated to a narrower, separate, scheduler-only step: extracting structured hints (HTTP paths, parameters, keywords) from CVE and exploit-writeup text, which then enriches the deterministic templates rather than replacing them. The distinction matters: an LLM is trusted to notice "this exploit writeup mentions the path /api/upload " (a narrow, checkable extraction task) but never trusted to invent the actual detection logic (the Sigma rule's condition block) from scratch. Routing a CVE to a detection class, and a documented concurrency bug fix class_router.py is the single resolution path everything else depends on: an ATT&CK technique prefix ( T1190 maps to a web_exploit class) or a normalized CWE ( CWE-89 , SQL injection, maps to sqli ) resolves to one stable "detection class" slug, which every downstream template set — Sigma generation, SIEM query generation, class-level fallback queries — keys off consistently. One implementation detail is worth knowing because it's a real, previously-shipped bug fix rather than a stylistic choice: community-rule fetching from GitHub (Sigma rules, Elastic rules) runs strictly sequentially , not in parallel via asyncio.gather as you might otherwise expect for two independent network calls. A code comment explains why directly — both lookup functions share a single asyncpg connection, and Postgres does not permit two concurrent queries on the same connection at once. Running them concurrently previously caused a documented 15-to-30-second hang (two queries silently contending for the same connection, each waiting on the other), fixed simply by making the two calls sequential instead. It's a small, concrete lesson in something Part 0 flagged in the abstract: async/await gives you concurrency, not automatic safety, and a shared resource (here, one database connection) can still serialize supposedly-parallel code in a way that produces exactly the kind of hang you'd assume async was supposed to prevent. Injecting extracted artifacts without corrupting the rule When the LLM-extracted keywords/paths from artifact extraction get merged into a generated Sigma rule, the merge only happens for rules whose condition is the flat keywords type — a simple "does the log line contain any of these strings" match. A different Sigma rule shape — say, a Windows process-tree selection/filter rule with structured field matching — has an entirely different schema, and blindly injecting extracted keyword strings into that structure would silently produce a malformed or logically wrong rule rather than a working one. The safety check here is narrow and specific on purpose: enrichment only applies where the target shape is simple enough to guarantee it can't corrupt the underlying detection logic. The DetectionContext family — one cache entity, three independent writers Four files share the word "context" in their name and are easy to assume are redundant — they aren't. context.py is purely the data model and cache accessor: it defines the DetectionContext envelope shape (CWE IDs, product, detection class, an artifacts list, plus provenance fields recording which model/provider populated it), and builds a bare version of it from nothing but static CVE metadata — no network call, no LLM. The other three files are independent jobs that populate the artifacts field of that same cached envelope, each with a different trigger and a different method: context_sync.py is the cheap, broad backfill job (disabled by default): it finds every CVE that has no context row at all yet and writes a bare, empty-artifacts envelope for it, prioritizing KEV/PoC/recency — its entire job is making sure every CVE has something to read, never adding real artifacts itself. context_nuclei_sync.py is a deterministic enrichment job (on by default), triggered specifically for CVEs just touched by the exploit-sync job (Chapter 14): it parses actual Nuclei template YAML (via nuclei_parser.py , no LLM at all) to extract real HTTP paths, parameters, and keywords, and merges new artifacts onto whatever already exists, capped at 8, deduping by content. context_llm_sync.py is the LLM-based sibling (disabled by default, needs an explicit flag and a configured provider): it targets CVEs with a public exploit that haven't had an LLM extraction attempt recently, runs inside the per-job provider-skip session from Chapter 24 (so one empty response from a provider doesn't waste the rest of a batch retrying it), and — worth flagging as a real, load-bearing difference from the Nuclei job — overwrites the artifacts field outright rather than merging. If both jobs eventually touch the same CVE, whichever ran more recently wins completely on the artifacts field, not just contributes to it. Both enrichment jobs converge on the same validation gate in artifact_extract.py : paths capped at 200 characters (max 5), params/keywords capped at 80 characters (max 10 each), HTTP method restricted to a real-verb whitelist, and an artifact that's entirely empty across all three fields is discarded outright rather than stored as a hollow shell. This shared gate is what lets a caller reading a DetectionContext never need to know or care whether Nuclei parsing or an LLM populated it — both paths are guaranteed to produce the same validated shape. flowchart LR CTX[("DetectionContext cache

The fallback tier below ATT&CK techniques: class_queries.py When a CVE maps to no ATT&CK technique at all, class_queries.py is the next tier down — ten vulnerability classes (path traversal, command injection, SQL injection, XSS, deserialization, code injection, unsafe upload, SSRF, XXE, auth bypass, memory corruption, default credentials), each with all four platform queries pre-built from one of three shared "query pack" templates (URI-based, path-based, body-based hunting terms) or, for the classes that don't reduce neatly to "look for these terms in a field" (unsafe upload needs a method-and-extension combination; memory corruption and default credentials are event-code or account-name based), fully bespoke queries instead. Per-platform SIEM query generation — four genuinely different query languages, concretely siem_queries.py is the ATT&CK-technique tier proper, covering 11 real techniques plus a generic default, and it's worth seeing the actual syntax differences rather than taking "four dialects" as an abstract claim. For the same underlying detection intent (T1190, exploiting a public-facing application), Elastic KQL reads as field:value pairs — http.response.status_code:(400 or 403 or 500 or 503) and http.request.body.bytes > 500 . Splunk SPL is space-separated implicit-AND search terms piped into aggregation stages — the same rule ends with | stats count by {{SRC_IP}}, {{URI}}, status | sort - count , using a pipe-stage syntax none of the other three platforms have. Microsoft Sentinel is Kusto — it starts from a bare table name and chains | where / | project stages, calling functions like ipv4_is_private() that don't exist in the other dialects. IBM QRadar AQL reads like SQL — SELECT ... FROM events WHERE ... LAST 24 HOURS , with QRadar's own time-window clause built into the query text itself rather than left to the platform's UI. Every generated query also ships a field-name legend, because a placeholder like {{SRC_IP}} maps to a different real column depending on which specific log source an analyst has actually configured (Splunk's {{URI}} , for instance, might really be uri_path , cs_uri_stem , or url depending on the sourcetype) — the generated query is a strong starting point, not a guaranteed drop-in. Finding rules that already exist, before generating new ones rule_sources.py is the community-rule discovery layer this chapter's class-router section already referenced for its documented concurrency fix — worth adding one more real detail: unauthenticated GitHub code search is capped at 10 requests per minute, and the module's own comment records that this limit caused a genuine 15-to-30-second hang on a CVE's very first Detect-tab view, initially misdiagnosed as a frontend bug before the root cause (an unconfigured GITHUB_TOKEN still attempting a rate-limited search) was found. The fix mirrors a pattern you've seen elsewhere for GreyNoise and OTX: if no GitHub token is configured at all, skip the search call entirely rather than let it queue. SigmaHQ is searched by CVE ID first, falling back to ATT&CK technique IDs only if that yields nothing; Elastic's rule repository, by contrast, is searched by technique ID only, since Elastic's own rules are organized around techniques rather than indexed by CVE. YARA rules from OTX-observed hashes, concretely yara_generator.py validates every candidate string against a strict format check (exactly MD5, SHA1, or SHA256 length and hex-character shape — nothing else is accepted as a "hash") and, critically, maps each hash length to the matching YARA builtin function — a 32-character hash gets hash.md5(0, filesize) == "..." , a 64-character hash gets hash.sha256(...) — rather than assuming every hash is SHA-256. Every generated rule's metadata block is explicit about its own provenance: author = "BRIEFR (generated from OTX)" and confidence = "experimental" , so a rule built this way is never mistaken for one an analyst hand-ver

title: The morning brief — read-time aggregation, and a portability lesson worth remembering
text: Part IV · Chapter 22 The morning brief — read-time aggregation, and a portability lesson worth remembering Five heterogeneous signals merged into one ranked queue, with its own deliberately separate priority heuristic. brief/service.py The morning brief assembles a single ranked "action queue" from five distinct sources: CVEs whose EPSS score jumped meaningfully in the lookback window ("EPSS movers"), newly-added CISA KEV entries, KEV remediation deadlines approaching soon, stack-matched CVEs with recent activity, and active OTX campaigns touching the operator's declared stack. Its own module docstring states the constraint plainly: "read-path only, no ingest" — this subsystem computes nothing new at all; it purely aggregates data other scheduler jobs already computed and stored, in strict compliance with the never-do-heavy-work-on-the-request-path rule you've now seen enforced (Chapter 20's correlation engine) and violated-then-fixed (also Chapter 20) elsewhere in this book. A specific implementation detail here doubles as a genuinely useful, general lesson about the dual-SQLite/Postgres architecture from Chapter 9: EPSS delta ranking (finding the CVEs whose score moved the most) is computed in Python after fetching raw change-history rows, rather than with a SQL ORDER BY on a cast numeric value — because SQLite's CAST(x AS REAL) is forgiving of non-numeric text (silently produces 0 rather than erroring), while Postgres's equivalent cast raises an error outright on a genuinely non-numeric string. A query that works fine against the SQLite test suite can fail outright in Postgres production for this exact reason — precisely the trap Chapter 9 warned you to test both ways, made concrete in a real, specific piece of code rather than left abstract. The brief computes its own _priority_score heuristic rather than reusing Chapter 18's Operational Priority system — and this is a deliberate choice, not a missed refactoring opportunity. A KEV deadline due soon starts at 100 points plus an urgency bonus that scales with how few days remain; a brand-new KEV entry starts at 90; an EPSS mover starts at 70 plus a bonus scaled to the size of its score jump; a stack match starts at 60, boosted further if it's also KEV-listed or has a rising EPSS trend. The reason a P1–P4 band alone wouldn't serve this purpose: the brief needs to interleave five genuinely different kinds of reason into one ordered list, and a coarse four-bucket priority band can't distinguish "a KEV deadline in 2 days" from "a KEV deadline in 13 days" the way a continuous urgency-scaled score naturally can — the brief's job is fine-grained ranking within a single list, which is a different problem from Chapter 18's job of assigning a stable, explainable priority tier to one CVE in isolation. Self-check Why does the morning brief compute EPSS deltas in Python instead of a SQL ORDER BY on a cast column — what specific behavioral difference between SQLite and Postgres does this avoid? Why does the brief maintain its own separate priority heuristic instead of calling scoring.priority.derive_operational_priority directly for each item? What would "heavy work on the request path" look like if the brief violated its own stated design rule — sketch a concrete example of what it deliberately does not do.

title: Threat modeling, provenance, and IOC retro-matching
text: Part IV · Chapter 23 Threat modeling, provenance, and IOC retro-matching Three small, cheap, read-only layers that share one job: being honest about what BRIEFR does and doesn't actually know right now. threat_model/scenarios.py intel/provenance.py ioc/retro_match.py Threat scenarios ( build_threat_scenarios ) generate stack-scoped, plain-English ATT&CK narratives — "an adversary may use T1190, Exploit Public-Facing Application, against systems running nginx" — paired with the actual CVE evidence backing that claim and concrete mitigation actions (patch this, deploy this hunt pack, close this coverage gap). Provenance is a meta-layer sitting over the exploit, detection, and correlation sections of a CVE's detail view, computing a per-section "as of / source / status" line — checked, pending, or source-unavailable — by checking each upstream feed's circuit-breaker health (Chapter 16) and cache timestamps. IOC retro-matching joins an analyst's saved IOC watchlist against the locally mirrored OTX and ThreatFox tables, surfacing "has anything I'm personally watching shown up in threat intel since I saved it" — retroactively, on a schedule, not the moment it happens. All three share the same underlying justification: each is a cheap, DB-local, read-only layer built entirely on data other subsystems already ingested — none makes a live external call on the request path, keeping them consistent with the heavy-work rule you've now seen enforced repeatedly. Provenance specifically exists because of a project-wide error-handling convention: every async view needs honest loading, empty, error, and data states, and exploit/detection/correlation data specifically depends on flaky third parties (OTX, GitHub, Sploitus) whose outages must be visible to an analyst as "this section is stale because a feed is down," never silently rendered as an indistinguishable, misleading "nothing found here." The retro-match query is implemented as a UNION ALL of two structurally separate joins — one against OTX's tables, one against ThreatFox's — rather than one generalized "IOC sources" table both feeds write into. This is a deliberate tradeoff: OTX carries pulse and campaign context ThreatFox doesn't have, and ThreatFox carries confidence and malware-family fields OTX doesn't structure the same way. Forcing both into one common schema would mean either dropping source-specific fields the UI genuinely wants to show, or padding a shared schema with a pile of nullable columns that are only ever populated by one source — the two-query union keeps each source's native shape intact at the small cost of writing two similar-looking queries instead of one. Self-check Why is IOC retro-match implemented as a UNION ALL of two separate joins instead of one generalized "IOC sources" table — what would be lost by unifying the schema? Construct a concrete scenario where the provenance layer's "source unavailable" state prevents an analyst from being misled, versus what they'd see without it. Why do none of these three subsystems make a live external API call, and how does that connect back to the heavy-work rule from earlier chapters?

title: ML and LLM enrichment — three genuinely different categories, and zero Anthropic dependency
text: Part IV · Chapter 24 ML and LLM enrichment — three genuinely different categories, and zero Anthropic dependency Local embeddings, hosted-API LLM calls, and plain deterministic enrichment are three separate things that get talked about as if they were one — this chapter draws the actual lines, verified directly against the code. ml/embeddings.py ml/product_extraction.py ai/llm_router.py enrichment/*.py Three categories, not one blurry "AI" bucket It's worth being disciplined about vocabulary here, because "AI" gets used loosely to mean at least three structurally different things in this codebase. True local machine learning: CPU-only sentence embeddings, computed by a small ONNX model ( BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 , via the fastembed library) running entirely on BRIEFR's own hardware, no network call involved — used to power "related CVEs" and semantic search via cosine similarity between vectors. This is env-gated off by default, and computed only during scheduled backfill jobs; the request path only ever reads vectors that were already computed and stored, with an explicit code comment stating "Related CVEs must not call this — they use stored vectors only," closing off any temptation to compute an embedding live on a request. LLM-assisted enrichment: a genuine network call to a hosted large-language-model API — extracting a structured {vendor, product, version_range} triple from free-text CVE descriptions when NVD hasn't yet analyzed a freshly-published CVE, extracting detection-rule artifacts (Chapter 21), and generating on-demand PDF executive summaries. All three are scheduler-side or explicitly on-demand, gated off by default, and every single one has a deterministic template fallback available. Plain deterministic enrichment, no ML or LLM involved at all: regex-derived MITRE technique tags and proof-of-concept flags pulled from NVD's own reference-link tags, DNS hostname format validation, and third-party IOC reputation lookups (VirusTotal, AbuseIPDB, GreyNoise) — these are just structured API calls or pattern matching, and calling them "AI" would be a real category error worth correcting if you hear it described that way. The provider chain — verified: no Anthropic client exists anywhere in this stack A direct search across ai/ , ml/ , and enrichment/ confirms there is no Anthropic or Claude API client anywhere in this codebase. ai/llm_router.py instead implements a fixed-order failover chain across free and cheap-tier providers — Groq, then Cerebras, then OpenRouter, then Gemini as the last resort — explicitly "not round-robin": one attempt per provider per call, in that exact priority order, falling through to the next only on failure or an empty response. The reasoning, visible in the code's own comments (a display-order comment states plainly that admin UI ordering matches failover priority, "Gemini is last resort"), is straightforward cost engineering: keeping a self-hosted tool's operating cost near zero by leaning on free and cheap-tier LLM providers rather than paying premium-tier API prices for enrichment tasks that are genuinely optional polish, never load-bearing functionality. Why every LLM feature has a deterministic fallback, without exception This is the detail that ties the whole chapter together: BRIEFR must fully function for an operator who configures zero LLM API keys at all — a real, expected, and fully-supported deployment mode, not an edge case. A single gate function, any_llm_provider_configured() , controls whether LLM-dependent features attempt to run at all; when it's false, PDF executive summaries fall back to a template-based _template_executive_summary instead of an LLM-generated one, product extraction and detection-artifact extraction simply don't run (CPE data and deterministic Nuclei-YAML parsing still populate the same underlying fields through non-LLM paths), and semantic search degrades to keyword-only matching, reporting that fact honestly in its response metadata rather than silently pretending to be semantic. Every one of these enrichments is additive polish layered on top of a fully-functional core product — never something the core product's correctness depends on. The actual algorithm underneath "semantic search" — cosine similarity, made concrete It's worth de-mystifying exactly what "embeddings" computes, since the term gets used as if it were magic. An embedding model turns a piece of text into a fixed-length list of numbers — a vector — positioned in a high-dimensional space such that texts with similar meaning end up as nearby vectors, even if they share few or no exact words in common. "Semantic search" then reduces to a genuinely simple piece of arithmetic: compute the embedding vector for a search query, compute (or, in BRIEFR's case, already have stored) the embedding vector for every candidate CVE description, and rank candidates by cosine similarity — the cosine of the angle between two vectors, which is 1 when they point in exactly the same direction (maximally similar in meaning) and 0 when they're orthogonal (unrelated). There's no learning or inference happening at search time at all — the model already did the hard work once, ahead of time, when it produced the stored vectors; a live search is pure vector arithmetic, which is exactly why it's cheap enough to run on the request path when a live LLM call would not be. At real scale, comparing a query vector against every single stored vector one by one (a brute-force linear scan) becomes too slow to do on every request once the CVE corpus is large. This is what pgvector's ANN (Approximate Nearest Neighbor) index solves — a data structure that finds vectors very close to the true nearest matches, in a fraction of the time a brute-force scan would take, trading a small, usually irrelevant amount of ranking precision for a large, very relevant speed gain. BRIEFR's hybrid search then blends this vector-similarity ranking with ordinary keyword search rather than relying on vectors alone — deliberately, because embeddings are excellent at "this text means something similar" and comparatively weak at exact-token matching (a CVE ID, a specific product version string, an exact error code an analyst pastes in verbatim) — the two techniques cover each other's blind spots. Why BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 specifically — and why not a bigger, "better" model Embedding models span an enormous size range — from tens of millions of parameters up to models comparable in size to a full LLM. BRIEFR's choice sits deliberately at the small end for reasons that connect directly to Chapter 25's resource-consciousness thread: bge-small-en-v1.5 is a compact model (roughly on the order of tens of millions of parameters, not billions) specifically chosen so it runs acceptably fast on ordinary CPU hardware via ONNX through fastembed — no GPU, no PyTorch runtime dependency, no meaningful extra RAM budget beyond loading one small model file. A larger, more capable embedding model would very likely produce marginally better semantic rankings, but at a real cost this project has explicitly declined to pay: slower CPU inference (mattering directly for how long a bulk backfill job takes, since Chapter 24 established this only ever runs in the scheduler, never on the request path), a meaningfully larger memory footprint just to hold the model in memory, and — for anyone considering a hosted embedding API instead of a local model — a recurring per-call cost and a dependency on sending CVE and asset-stack text to a third party, which cuts directly against BRIEFR's self-hosted, privacy-conscious posture (the same instinct behind self-hosting fonts in Chapter 5, stated again at the ML layer). A small, local, CPU-only model is the one choice that satisfies "works fully offline," "costs nothing per query," and "keeps analyst data on the box" simultaneously — three properties a larger or hosted model would each individually break. The real restrictions this choice imposes — worth naming precisely, not glossing over A small local model is not a free lunch, and the honest restrictions are worth stating explicitly rather than only praising the upside. Fixed dimensionality: every vector this model produces has the same fixed length, set once by the model architecture — switching to a different embedding model later isn't a drop-in config change, because old and new vectors would live in incompatible spaces, meaning a model change requires re-embedding the entire historical corpus from scratch, not a quiet migration. English-biased: the model name says it plainly ( -en- ) — this is trained predominantly on English text, so semantic quality for non-English CVE descriptions or analyst queries would be meaningfully weaker, a real limitation for any future internationalization of the product. No fine-tuning on BRIEFR's own domain data: the model is used exactly as published, off the shelf, with no additional training on CVE-specific or security-specific text — it brings general-purpose semantic understanding, not a specialized notion of, say, which CVEs security professionals consider "similar" in a way a general text model wouldn't naturally capture. CPU-bound throughput: embedding a large historical backlog of CVEs is measurably slower on CPU than it would be on a GPU, which is precisely why the backfill is scheduler-only, resumable, and explicitly never something the request path can trigger inline — a direct, load-bearing consequence of the CPU-only choice, not an unrelated design decision. Self-check Explain cosine similarity in your own words, and say precisely why a search request needs to compute only one new embedding (the query's), not embed every CVE again. Why does an ANN index trade a small amount of ranking accuracy for a large speed gain, and why is that trade acceptable for this specific use case? Name three properties a larger or hosted embedding model would break for BRIEFR that bge-small-en-v1.5 preserves — connect each one back to a specific project value (cost, privacy, offline capability). If BRIEFR wanted to switch embedding models in the future, why couldn't it simply swap the model name in a config file and move on? An operator configures zero LLM API keys. Walk through, category by category, exactly what breaks — and justify why the honest answer is "nothing user-visible." Why is the LLM provider chain a fixed-priority failover rather than round-robin load balancing across providers? Give a concrete example of enrichment that sounds like "AI" but is actually plain deterministic code, and explain what specifically makes it deterministic rather than learned. Why does the code comment insist "related CVEs must not call [the embedding model] — they use stored vectors only"? What would break the heavy-work rule if that constraint were violated?

title: Inside the LLM failover chain — pacing, quota, audit trail, and the one request-path exception
text: Part IV · Chapter 24B Inside the LLM failover chain — pacing, quota, audit trail, and the one request-path exception Eleven more files behind llm_router.py 's four-provider chain: how BRIEFR keeps every free-tier provider from ever seeing more traffic than it publishes, and how every attempt gets a permanent, queryable record. ai/llm_pacing.py ai/quota.py ai/model_catalog.py ai/operations_recorder.py ai/summary.py Proactive pacing vs. reactive quota tracking — two different mechanisms, easy to conflate Worth separating two things that sound like the same job. llm_pacing.py is proactive : before ever making a call, it computes the minimum safe interval between requests to a given provider from that provider's published RPM (requests/minute) and TPM (tokens/minute) limits, takes whichever bound is more restrictive, and applies a safety-margin "headroom" percentage on top (85% by default — treating a stated 30-RPM plan as if it were really 25.5 RPM, so normal jitter and estimation error can't accidentally exceed the real limit). quota.py is reactive : it's a plain in-process dictionary that simply records whatever rate-limit headers a provider actually sends back after a real call (remaining requests, remaining tokens, reset timestamps), purely as an observability cache for the admin UI — it computes nothing and enforces nothing itself, it's just a cache of ground truth the provider handed BRIEFR after the fact. The real, published free-tier numbers behind the pacing math are worth knowing because they explain the failover order: Groq's own limits (30 RPM / 8,000 TPM, held in groq_config.py ) are the most generous, which is why it's tried first; Cerebras's free-trial limits (5 RPM / 30,000 TPM) are the tightest of the four on requests-per-minute, explaining why it sits mid-chain rather than first despite otherwise being a fast, capable provider; OpenRouter's free tier (20 RPM / 40,000 TPM) sits third with the only 1-second pacing floor of the four (the others default to 0.5s); Gemini Flash-Lite's free tier (15 RPM / 250,000 TPM) is deliberately last — not because its limits are worst, but per the code's own ordering comment, because it's explicitly reserved as the last resort. Each provider's quota-warning threshold is a flat, hardcoded "5 requests remaining" trigger for the admin UI's low-quota banner — not configurable, a deliberately simple tripwire rather than a tunable alert system. Two small guard files sit in front of every one of these calls. llm_payload.py checks that a prompt actually has substantive content before any HTTP work happens at all — an empty or near-empty message never leaves the process, closing off the cheapest possible way to waste a scarce free-tier quota. llm_session.py scopes a per-batch-job memory of which providers have already returned an empty (not erroring, just content-less) response during the current job, so a Groq that goes quietly unresponsive partway through a 50-CVE batch doesn't get retried on every remaining CVE in that same run — it's skipped locally for the rest of the job while still counting toward the shared circuit breaker globally. The actual wire-format clients are split in two: openai_chat.py is the one shared client for the three providers (Groq, Cerebras, OpenRouter) that all speak the OpenAI-compatible chat-completions format, while gemini_client.py exists separately because Google's generateContent API has a genuinely different request shape (a contents / parts structure and a top-level systemInstruction , rather than a flat messages array) and its own header-based auth convention rather than a bearer token. operations_admin.py is the read-only payload builder for the admin "AI Operations" page — assembling per-provider health, quota, and configuration state into the JSON the frontend renders, with no database queries of its own beyond what's handed to it already aggregated. One source of truth for which model runs which task, in what order model_catalog.py is the single place that answers "which provider, which model, in what order, for this specific task" — its own docstring calls it the system's SSOT. There are exactly three LLM-backed tasks in the whole system (product extraction, PDF summaries, detection-context extraction), and the file's insertion order for provider env-var keys is the documented failover order the admin UI displays. One task-specific branch point is worth knowing: PDF summaries use a larger Groq model (120b parameters) as their first hop, while the other two tasks use a smaller one (20b) — a summary is generated rarely, on explicit user request, so the extra cost/latency of a bigger model is worth paying; product and detection extraction run in scheduler batches across potentially hundreds of CVEs, where a smaller, faster model matters more. A small operational scar is preserved directly in a code comment: OpenRouter's free Gemini Flash-Lite model ID was removed from OpenRouter's own catalog at one point, forcing a fallback default model swap — evidence that even a carefully engineered free-tier stack is still exposed to upstream catalog churn outside BRIEFR's control. Every LLM attempt gets a permanent audit row — success, failure, or empty alike operations_recorder.py writes one row to the ai_operations table for every completion attempt, not just successes — including a classified error reason ( empty , circuit_open , timeout , auth , rate_limit , model_not_found , or unknown , derived by pattern-matching the raw exception text) and, critically, fallback_from_provider / fallback_from_model fields — so a single logical operation that failed over from Groq to Cerebras to Gemini before finally succeeding leaves a reconstructable trail of the entire chain it walked, not just the final outcome. This recorder deliberately swallows its own exceptions (wrapped in a bare try/except with a warning log) — a design point worth connecting back to Chapter 16's outbound-metering discipline: the audit trail must never be capable of breaking the actual LLM call it's recording. The one LLM call that does run on the request path — and why it's allowed to ai/summary.py 's PDF executive-summary generator is explicitly triggered by an analyst clicking "export," not by any scheduler job — making it the one clearly-marked exception to this book's heavy-work-never-on-the-request-path rule. It's allowed precisely because every safeguard elsewhere in this chapter still applies: the function always computes the deterministic template result first — cheap, instant, no I/O — and only attempts the LLM path on top of that if a provider is configured and there's real data to summarize; the LLM call itself uses a 50-second timeout distinctly longer than the ~30-second floor used for scheduler-side calls, since a human is actively waiting rather than a batch job that can simply retry later; and the function's own docstring states it "never raises" — a malformed LLM response, an empty completion, or a total provider failure all fall back to the pre-computed template result rather than surfacing an error to the user exporting their PDF. The template composer itself is worth knowing as more than a placeholder: it's a real four-sentence rule engine (severity, then a conditional exploit/EPSS/actor clause, then a business-risk statement naming affected products, then a recommended action branching on whether a patch exists, the CVE is KEV-listed, or IOCs are present) — genuinely serviceable prose, not just "no data available." Self-check Explain the difference between what llm_pacing.py computes and what quota.py records — why does BRIEFR need both instead of just one? Why does an 85% headroom percentage matter — what would eventually happen to a provider's real rate limit if BRIEFR paced itself at exactly 100% of the published number? Why does PDF summary generation use a bigger Groq model than product extraction or detection-context extraction, given both ultimately go through the same failover chain? Why must operations_recorder.py swallow its own exceptions rather than let a logging failure propagate? PDF summary generation is the one LLM call allowed on the request path. Name the three specific safeguards that make this an exception rather than a violation of the heavy-work rule.

title: Everything above, exposed over HTTP — and kept running
text: Part V · API surface & operations Everything above, exposed over HTTP — and kept running Seven chapters: the 23 router files that turn every engine in Part IV into an endpoint, the tool's own self-documented security posture, outbound webhook safety, and the operational plumbing — backups, migrations, diagnostics — that a self-hosted instance actually needs to survive being run by someone other than its authors.

title: Routers — 23 files, and the provenance that explains their shape
text: Part V · Chapter 25 Routers — 23 files, and the provenance that explains their shape Why one file still holds four logically separate sub-routers, and what that tells you about respecting a refactor's history. routers/cves.py routers/admin.py routers/auth.py +20 more The 23 router files group naturally by feature area. CVE core ( cves.py — itself containing four distinct sub-routers: changes, list, detail, intel — plus atlas.py , correlation.py , and a small shared _validators.py holding the one require_cve_id helper every one of those sub-routers imports rather than re-validating CVE ID shape independently) covers listing, filtering, exporting, and the full per-CVE detail view: sentences, EPSS history, related CVEs, the "drawer" bundle, risk, momentum, detection, correlation — most of it read-heavy, with on-demand enrichment calls fanned out concurrently via asyncio.gather so a detail view stays responsive even while quietly checking several external sources at once. Admin ( admin.py , 2,667 lines — the single largest file in the entire backend) is the full operator control plane: system health, scheduler introspection and manual triggers (Chapter 15), backup management, a deliberately read-only, allowlisted database explorer (deny-by-default — there is no arbitrary-SQL box anywhere in this UI, on purpose), and the entire runtime configuration surface from Chapter 7. Auth ( auth.py , me.py , notifications_me.py ) covers the whole login lifecycle plus per-user preferences and the notification inbox. Detection engineering ( forge.py , detection_backlog.py , proof.py , threat_model.py ) exposes the MITRE coverage map, hunt-pack generation, rule testing, and scenario narratives from Part IV. The remainder — IOC/search, wallboard/brief/health, refresh/watchlist — round out the surface. The detail worth understanding, not just noting in passing: cves.py still contains four sub-routers rather than being split cleanly into four files, and the code carries explicit "moved verbatim from main.py " provenance comments explaining why. Before an earlier router-split refactor, these four concerns were interleaved with ATLAS and IOC routes in one large monolithic main.py , and — recall Chapter 6's lesson about frozen route registration order — reordering or restructuring those routes risks the exact same silent-route-shadowing bug that snapshot test exists to catch. The refactor prioritized "move code into logical modules without changing observable behavior" over "achieve the cleanest possible file boundaries" — a reasonable trade when the alternative risk is a subtle, hard-to-detect routing regression in a security-relevant surface. The ten routers behind "the remainder," named precisely config.py is small but worth knowing exactly: its one endpoint returns the Risk Score weight constants purely for frontend display, reading from the same single source of truth ( scoring/risk.py ) Chapter 18 covers — the actual score is always computed server-side, this route can never itself change a score, only describe one. stack_catalog.py is the real implementation behind the "My Stack" autocomplete and Tier-A backfill feature: it prefers Procrastinate (Chapter 17) for the backfill dispatch, catching an "already enqueued" condition gracefully, and falls back to an in-process background task if Procrastinate isn't available — a concrete instance of the dual-dispatch pattern this book has described in the abstract. wallboard.py implements exactly the cookie-exchange design Chapter 30 describes: one endpoint trades the raw WALLBOARD_TOKEN for a signed session cookie, a second endpoint reads the kiosk payload gated on that cookie — the raw token itself is never handed to a browser tab that stays open. brief.py is a single, notably auth-free endpoint (the morning brief has no session requirement) delegating straight to Chapter 22's service module. health.py backs /api/health and the true liveness probe, both read through the 45-second cache from Chapter 31. meta.py is a small grab-bag: build-version info, a timezone-aware clock, IOC usage counters, and the PDF/investigation summary endpoints that call into Chapter 24B's ai/summary.py . ioc.py is the router surface for Chapter 23's IOC lookup and per-user IOC watchlist. search.py is the one-endpoint surface for Chapter 24's hybrid semantic search. refresh.py is entirely admin-gated — every manual "sync now" trigger from Chapter 15 lives here, each one auditing itself before spawning, and the full daily-ingest route returns 409 if a sync is already in flight while, notably, the MITRE-refresh route does not, since it can't collide with the same lock. watchlist.py is the CVE pin/snooze feature — worth flagging directly as one of the few genuinely single-user (not per-account) tables left in the schema, a fact the router's own docstring acknowledges as a known scope gap rather than an oversight. Self-check How do you add a second admin account to a running BRIEFR instance? Why is that path deliberately not exposed over HTTP at all? Why does cves.py still contain four logically separate sub-routers instead of being split into four files — connect this back to Chapter 6's route-ordering lesson. Why is the admin database explorer read-only and allowlisted rather than a general SQL query box, given that it's already gated behind require_admin ? Why does refresh.py 's full-ingest route return 409 when a sync is already running, while its MITRE-refresh route doesn't need that same guard? watchlist.py 's CVE pin/snooze feature is still single-user, unlike ioc.py 's IOC watchlist. What would have to change in the schema to make it per-user, and why hasn't that happened yet?

title: security_architecture/ — the tool documenting its own posture
text: Part V · Chapter 26 security_architecture/ — the tool documenting its own posture Not exploit tracking, not a diagramming feature — BRIEFR turning its own threat model into a living, evidence-gated artifact instead of a document that goes stale the moment it's written. security_architecture/*.py — 12 files The name is genuinely ambiguous on first encounter, so it's worth stating plainly what this module actually is, confirmed by reading the code rather than guessing from the directory name: BRIEFR introspectively documenting its own architecture, trust boundaries, security controls, and threat model — mounted at /api/security-architecture/* , gated behind session auth for analyst-and-above roles. The underlying data is a structured YAML corpus split cleanly into two categories with very different trust levels: generated facts (components, the API inventory, scheduler job list, database table list, BRIEFR's own detected tech-stack terms — all regenerated automatically by scripts/generate_security_corpus.py directly from the codebase) and curated judgment (trust boundaries, security controls, abuse-case scenarios, documented security decisions, known risks, and their review history — each curated record requires an explicit review_date and supporting evidence , not just an assertion). The design principle stated directly in the module's own code is the single most important thing to understand about it: "no new matching/scoring code." Every view in this feature deliberately reuses logic that already exists and already ships in the real product — the stack-match clause from routers/cves.py , the coverage-map builder from routers/forge.py , the threat-scenario generator from Chapter 23 — rather than computing its own independent version of anything. This is a genuinely clever piece of engineering discipline: it guarantees, by construction, that the security-architecture view can never silently drift out of sync with what the product actually does, because it has no separate code path capable of drifting in the first place. A less careful implementation might reimplement "does this CVE match our stack" a second time for this feature specifically — and the two implementations could quietly diverge the moment one of them gets updated and the other doesn't. A staleness mechanism keeps the curated half honest over time: any curated record whose review_date is more than 90 days old renders as explicitly STALE in the UI and is excluded from the feature's aggregate ratio calculations (like "percentage of controls actively verified"). Without this, a security review written once could sit unchanged for years, silently presenting a snapshot of a system that has since changed underneath it as if it were still current — the 90-day cutoff forces the curated content to be periodically re-attested or visibly marked as no longer trustworthy, rather than aging silently into a false sense of assurance. Beyond the merge logic, a few sub-modules are worth naming individually. Three files split the "four lenses" work cleanly by responsibility: frameworks/scope.py runs the one live, CWE-scoped CVE query every lens is a projection of, honestly reporting when a requested scope (like "my stack") can't be satisfied rather than silently falling back to the whole corpus; frameworks/reference.py is pure static reference data — CWE names, the OWASP Top 10 2021 list, a documented-as-heuristic STRIDE mapping, and a CWE-to-CAPEC lookup — with no logic beyond dictionary lookups; frameworks/aggregate.py buckets the scoped rows from scope.py into per-category counts using reference.py 's mappings, counting each CVE once per category even if it carries multiple CWEs, with an honest "unmapped" bucket for CVEs that don't cleanly fit any known category in that framework, rather than silently dropping unclassifiable CVEs from the count and quietly overstating coverage. graphs.py computes an "attack surface" figure purely at read time, as a count of endpoint inventory crossed with linked controls — explicitly a count, not an invented score, consistent with the whole feature's evidence-first ethos. All of this is exposed through exactly one router, security_architecture/routers/security_architecture.py , mounted at /api/security-architecture and gated by the same session-auth middleware as every other analyst-facing route — there is no separate, weaker auth path for this feature just because it's introspective. Worth heading off directly: this is not the tool being paranoid about its own supply chain, and it's not a marketing feature dressed up as security theater. Every number it shows traces to either a piece of committed YAML with a review date and cited evidence, or a live query against real product data — never an invented or estimated score. If you're evaluating whether to trust a given figure in this feature, the honest question to ask is "is this generated from code, or curated by a human with a review date" — and the UI is built to make that distinction visible rather than blur it. What "drift detection" precisely means, verified against the code "Drift detection" is a claim easy to leave vague, so it's worth being exact about what corpus_drift.py actually compares. It imports the generator script ( scripts/generate_security_corpus.py ) directly, runs it into a fresh temporary directory, and does a parsed-value equality comparison — not a byte-for-byte text diff — between each committed generated YAML file and its freshly-regenerated counterpart. Concretely, this is a check of "does re-running the static-analysis generator right now produce the same answer as what's committed to git," not a check against a live runtime snapshot or a historical baseline. If a router was added and the generator wasn't re-run afterward, this is exactly what would flag it: the corpus's api_inventory.yaml would no longer match what generating it fresh right now would produce, and check_corpus_drift() reports precisely which files disagree plus the exact command ( python scripts/generate_security_corpus.py ) to fix it. corpus_loader.py is the read side of the same corpus, worth knowing has a real integrity check built in beyond just parsing YAML: _validate_record() requires every curated record's related_ids field to resolve to an ID that actually exists somewhere else in the corpus — a dangling cross-reference (a control that claims to relate to a risk ID that was since deleted or renamed) raises a hard validation error rather than silently rendering a broken link. Loading is cached and invalidated by the maximum modification time across every corpus file, so an edit to any one YAML file correctly busts the cache for the whole merged corpus, not just that file. merge.py 's "merge" is entirely read-time glue, never new logic — worth naming its actual pieces precisely: resolve_control_active() checks a control's real runtime env-var flag to report whether it's actually enabled right now (a control with no flag defined is treated as structurally always-on); self_stack_terms() reads BRIEFR's own dependency list (from its own requirements.txt / package.json , captured by the generator) and self_cve_exposure_summary() runs that list back through the same stack-match logic every operator's own asset stack uses — literally BRIEFR checking whether any of its own dependencies are KEV-listed or critical, using no code path other than the one every operator already relies on. security_audit_log_events() filters the real audit log down to a fixed prefix allowlist ( auth. , backup. , database. , config.apply , system.restart , and a few others) — a further instance of the "read real data through an allowlist, never invent a number" discipline running through this entire module. Self-check Explain precisely how "no new matching/scoring code" prevents this feature from silently drifting out of sync with the actual product — what would a less disciplined implementation have done differently, and what risk would that introduce? Why does a curated security-control record become STALE after 90 days rather than remaining valid indefinitely once written? Why do the CWE/OWASP/STRIDE/CAPEC lenses each maintain an explicit "unmapped" bucket instead of silently excluding CVEs that don't fit? "Drift detection" compares generator-output-now against generator-output-committed. What kind of real-world drift would this not catch — say, a manual hand-edit to the committed YAML that happens to still match what the generator currently produces? Why does corpus_loader.py treat a dangling related_ids reference as a hard error rather than silently dropping the broken link? self_cve_exposure_summary() checks BRIEFR's own dependencies against KEV using the exact same code path an operator's asset-stack check uses. What would be lost if this feature had instead written its own, separate self-check logic?

title: Webhooks and SSRF — a textbook mitigation, applied because the input is genuinely attacker-influenceable
text: Part V · Chapter 27 Webhooks and SSRF — a textbook mitigation, applied because the input is genuinely attacker-influenceable Resolve, validate, then connect to the pinned IP while still presenting the right hostname for TLS — read the real code, because the reasoning in the comments is better than any paraphrase. webhooks/engine.py webhooks/alerts.py webhooks/ssrf.py BRIEFR can push notifications to Discord, Telegram, or a generic HTTPS endpoint when specific conditions fire — a KEV entry lands on the operator's stack, a watched CVE's EPSS score jumps, a watchlisted IOC shows up in threat intel, a scheduled backup silently stops running (a "dead man's switch" alert). webhooks/alerts.py holds the actual trigger logic — process_watchlist_kev_alerts , process_kev_stack_alerts , check_backup_deadman , and similar functions — every one of them called exclusively from scheduler jobs, never from the request path, matching the pattern you've now seen enforced throughout this book. webhooks/destinations.py merges destinations configured via environment variables with ones an operator has added through the Admin UI, and engine.py 's dispatch_event fans a single alert out to every configured destination, with an atomic dedupe-claim mechanism (referenced internally as IDEM-001 ) that prevents the same alert firing twice if two concurrent triggers happen to race each other, retrying by clearing the claim on delivery failure. Why this specific feature needed real SSRF hardening Recall Part 0's definition of SSRF: a server tricked into making a request on the attacker's behalf, often reaching internal-only services the attacker couldn't otherwise touch directly. Webhook destination URLs are exactly this shape of risk in BRIEFR, because they're operator- or user-supplied input that the server then dutifully fetches — a malicious or compromised operator account (or a webhook URL copied from an untrusted source) could point a "destination" at an internal-only admin panel, a cloud metadata endpoint, or any other service the server can reach but an external attacker normally couldn't. BLOCKED_NETWORKS = ( ipaddress.ip_network( "10.0.0.0/8" ), ipaddress.ip_network( "172.16.0.0/12" ), ipaddress.ip_network( "192.168.0.0/16" ), ipaddress.ip_network( "100.64.0.0/10" ), # CGNAT ipaddress.ip_network( "127.0.0.0/8" ), ipaddress.ip_network( "169.254.0.0/16" ), # link-local ipaddress.ip_network( "0.0.0.0/8" ), ipaddress.ip_network( "::1/128" ), ipaddress.ip_network( "fc00::/7" ), # unique local (IPv6 private) ) FORBIDDEN_OUTBOUND_HEADERS = frozenset({ "authorization" , "x-briefr-admin-key" , "x-api-key" , "x-virustotal-api-key" , "x-nvd-api-key" , "x-github-token" , ... }) webhooks/ssrf.py — the blocklist covers RFC1918 private space, loopback, link-local, CGNAT, and IPv6 equivalents The real request flow, worth tracing exactly because the details are what make this mitigation actually correct rather than superficially plausible: safe_webhook_request() first parses the destination URL and resolves its hostname via DNS, then runs every resolved IP through validate_resolved_ips() , rejecting any address that falls in the blocked-networks list above before a single byte is sent anywhere. Only then does it connect — critically, to the pinned, already-validated IP address literal , not to the hostname again. This detail is the one most naive SSRF mitigations get wrong: if you validate the hostname's DNS resolution once and then reconnect using the hostname a second time, an attacker who controls the DNS record (or exploits a very tight timing window between validation and connection) can have it resolve to a safe address for your check and a dangerous internal address for the actual connection — a class of bug called DNS rebinding. Connecting to the exact IP you already validated, rather than re-resolving the hostname, closes that gap by construction. That creates a second problem the code has to solve immediately: if you connect to a bare IP address literal, standard TLS certificate validation checks the certificate against that IP — which fails for essentially every real-world webhook destination, since Discord, Slack, and similar services sit behind CDNs whose certificates are issued for the hostname, not for whichever of their many backend IPs happens to answer a given connection. The code's own comment explains the fix precisely: it sets sni_hostname to the original hostname, so the TLS handshake presents and validates against the correct hostname via SNI (Server Name Indication) while the actual TCP connection still goes to the pre-validated, pinned IP — getting both properties at once, correct certificate validation and SSRF safety, that would otherwise seem to be in tension. The same code carves out two narrow, correct exceptions: it skips setting SNI when the destination URL is itself a bare IP literal (RFC 6066 forbids IP literals in SNI, and there's no hostname to validate against in that case anyway), and it IDNA/punycode-encodes non-ASCII hostnames before use, because Python's ssl module raises a UnicodeEncodeError during the handshake otherwise. One more layer, easy to overlook: sanitize_outbound_headers() strips a hardcoded list of BRIEFR-internal authentication and API-key headers before any outbound webhook request is sent — Authorization , the internal admin-key header, and every configured third-party API key header. This closes a completely different risk than SSRF itself: even a validated, safe destination shouldn't ever receive BRIEFR's own internal credentials as a side effect of some header being carried along accidentally from an internal context. A naming correction worth making explicitly: it would be reasonable to assume webhooks/sender.py holds the low-level HTTP transport logic this chapter just walked through — it doesn't. Read directly, it's a thin, six-name facade re-exporting dispatch_event / send_alert / send_test_message from engine.py and two small "is this destination configured" convenience checks. The actual SSRF-hardened transport lives entirely in engine.py and ssrf.py — sender.py exists purely to give other modules a small, stable import surface without needing to reach into engine.py directly. Self-check Why does the code connect to the resolved IP literal instead of re-resolving the hostname a second time immediately before connecting? Name the specific attack this prevents. Why does connecting to a bare IP address break standard TLS certificate validation, and how does setting sni_hostname to the original hostname fix it without reintroducing the SSRF risk the IP-pinning was meant to prevent? Under what two specific conditions does the code skip setting sni_hostname at all, and why is each one correct rather than an oversight? What risk does stripping outbound authorization/API-key headers close, and how is it different from the SSRF risk the rest of this chapter addresses? What does webhooks/sender.py actually contain, and why might its name mislead you about where the real transport logic lives?

title: User-facing settings: notifications, onboarding, preferences
text: Part V · Chapter 28 User-facing settings: notifications, onboarding, preferences Three small modules, each answering a slightly different question about what a specific user has configured. notifications/emit.py onboarding/checklist.py preferences/*.py notifications/emit.py is the in-app inbox writer — distinct from Chapter 27's outbound webhooks, this is purely internal: watchlist hits, detection-backlog gaps, background job errors, and unhealthy API keys all land here as dismissable, deduplicated notifications a user sees inside the app itself, scoped to either the analyst or operator cohort depending on relevance, and deduplicated by a stable key so a repeatedly-failing job doesn't spam the same notification into existence a hundred times over. onboarding/checklist.py computes a first-hour operator checklist entirely live, from real database and environment state — has CVE ingest actually started producing data, are stack terms configured, are backups enabled and recent, is feed health good, are there any production-posture warnings (Chapter 7's production_posture_warnings() ) — with no persistence beyond a simple dismiss timestamp; there's no separate "onboarding progress" table to keep in sync with reality, because the checklist simply re-derives its own state from the same live facts every time it's viewed. preferences/{repo,validate,display_validate}.py is the server-persisted counterpart to Chapter 4's frontend Context discussion — an analyst's declared stack terms and asset profile, plus display preferences (font scale, density, timezone, reduced motion), stored per user rather than per browser. The validators here are worth noting specifically because they use strict allowlists of exact permitted values, rather than loose type-checking (accepting "any number" for font scale, for instance). This is a deliberate defensive posture: type-checking alone would happily accept a technically-valid-but-nonsensical value — a font scale of 500, a density setting that doesn't correspond to any actual CSS class the frontend knows how to render — that could produce a genuinely broken UI for that user with no clear error message pointing at the cause. An enumerated allowlist rejects anything outside the specific, known-good set of values the frontend was actually built to handle. Concretely, preferences/display_validate.py enumerates the exact permitted sets — font scales from extra-small to extra-large, density modes (compact/comfortable/spacious), a fixed set of allowed poll intervals (15/30/60/120 seconds), and per-role typography sizes clamped to a 9–20px range — and its sanitize_display_prefs() raises rather than silently clamping an out-of-range value, so a bad write fails loudly at the API boundary instead of quietly storing something the frontend was never built to render. preferences/validate.py is the separate validator for the "My Stack" feature's actual input — it normalizes comma-separated stack terms and enforces a 4096-character cap, and its sanitize_profile() whitelists the shape of a declared asset profile (operating systems, applications, AI systems, plus an environment sub-object for internet-facing/industry/criticality) — but defaults missing fields rather than rejecting the whole submission, a deliberately more forgiving posture than the display-preferences validator, appropriate because a partially-filled stack profile is still useful, whereas a partially-valid display preference risks actually breaking the UI. Self-check Why does the display-preferences validator use an allowlist of exact permitted values instead of simply checking that a submitted value is the right data type? Why doesn't onboarding/checklist.py need a separate "onboarding progress" database table to track completion state? What's the practical difference between an in-app notification ( notifications/emit.py ) and an outbound webhook (Chapter 27) — when would a system use one instead of the other for the same underlying event? Why does preferences/validate.py 's stack-profile validator default missing fields rather than rejecting an incomplete submission, while display_validate.py raises on anything invalid instead of defaulting it?

title: Proof, services, and templates — three more names worth clarifying precisely
text: Part V · Chapter 29 Proof, services, and templates — three more names worth clarifying precisely "Proof" here means rule-testing, not exploit tracking. Getting that wrong would genuinely misdirect a security review of this codebase. proof/bench.py services/semantic_search.py services/stack_backfill_worker.py templates/intelligence.py Worth stating directly, because the directory name genuinely invites the wrong guess: proof/ is a rule-proof bench , not exploit proof-of-concept tracking or storage of any kind. POST /api/proof/run takes pasted log lines alongside either a Sigma rule (Chapter 21) or explicit match patterns, extracts the actual match/keyword conditions from the Sigma detection block, and reports which log lines hit and which missed — a lightweight way for an analyst to sanity-check a detection rule against real or sample log data without needing a live SIEM connection to test against. Confirmed directly by reading the code: there is no exploit code and no proof-of-concept database anywhere in this module. It's purely a rule-testing sandbox, and the name refers to "proving" a detection rule works, not to offensive tooling. services/semantic_search.py orchestrates the hybrid keyword-plus-vector search introduced in Chapter 24, gracefully degrading to keyword-only matching whenever embeddings are disabled or unavailable — and, notably, always reporting which method actually served a given request ( meta.method in the response) rather than silently returning keyword-only results labeled as if they were semantic. services/stack_backfill_worker.py is the actual work behind Chapter 17's Procrastinate-driven Tier-A backfill: paginated NVD keyword fetching, upserting, and EPSS/KEV enrichment application, resumable via checkpoints — and it deliberately never calls OTX, exploit-availability feeds, or the correlation engine, deferring all of that to the ordinary background jobs that already cover it, rather than duplicating that work inside the backfill path itself. templates/intelligence.py is template-based English-sentence generation — deliberately no LLM involved — for the CVE detail drawer: severity_sentence , epss_sentence , kev_sentence , patch_sentence , exploit_sentence , plus classification of reference URLs into recognizable exploit-source categories (Metasploit, Exploit-DB, GitHub, PacketStorm). This is the actual mechanism behind something you might otherwise assume required an LLM call: CVE summaries in the detail view read as fluent, natural prose without any request-path AI call at all — every sentence is assembled from a fixed template filled in with real data, an approach consistent with the whole product's "explainable, deterministic where it can be" posture running all the way through to the sentence level. enrichment/ — the plain, deterministic tier this book has referenced but not yet named Chapter 24 already described this tier conceptually as "no ML, no LLM" — here are the actual three files. enrichment/cve.py is rule-based display-field derivation: it regex-extracts MITRE technique IDs from NVD's own reference-link tags, heuristically flags whether a CVE has a public PoC by matching reference-tag text and known exploit-hosting domains, and builds a plain-English summary preferring CISA KEV's short description, then OSV's, and only falling back to an auto-truncated first sentence of the raw NVD description if neither richer source exists — with a companion function that can tell whether a stored summary is genuinely enriched or just that auto-truncated fallback, by re-deriving it and comparing. enrichment/domain_validation.py is a single, careful function backing IOC lookup input validation: it IDNA/punycode-encodes for proper international domain support, validates real DNS label structure, and explicitly rejects a bare IP address as not being a "domain" — this is the exact function Chapter 23's IOC lookup calls to return a clean 422 rather than silently mishandling a malformed input. enrichment/ioc.py is the actual multi-source orchestrator behind IOC lookup: it deliberately sets retries to zero on every quota-billed API call (VirusTotal, AbuseIPDB — both hard-capped daily quotas where an automatic retry would waste a scarce budget on a request that's already failed), and layers VirusTotal plus a type-appropriate second source (AbuseIPDB for IPs, MalwareBazaar for hashes, URLhaus for domains) with GreyNoise and OTX as further optional enrichment on top. Self-check Why does semantic_search.py report its own fallback method in the response instead of silently returning keyword-only results labeled as semantic? Why does the stack backfill worker deliberately avoid calling OTX or the correlation engine directly, deferring to the ordinary scheduled jobs instead? What would you have assumed proof/ did from its directory name alone, and why does that assumption matter for someone auditing this codebase's security posture? Why does enrichment/ioc.py set retries to zero specifically for VirusTotal and AbuseIPDB calls, when Chapter 16's outbound queue elsewhere in this book insists on retrying rather than dropping requests? Why does enrichment/domain_validation.py explicitly reject a bare IP address as an invalid "domain," rather than accepting it as a trivial special case?

title: Ops and observability — keeping a self-hosted instance alive without its authors watching over it
text: Part V · Chapter 30 Ops and observability — keeping a self-hosted instance alive without its authors watching over it Backup, a genuinely separate data-migration path, redacted diagnostics, and a kiosk dashboard with its own auth scheme. backup/manager.py migration/sqlite_to_postgres.py diagnostics/support_pack.py monitoring/api_key_health.py wallboard/service.py Backup is dual-backend, matching Chapter 9's split: SQLite uses its own online backup API ( sqlite3.Connection.backup() ) plus a PRAGMA integrity_check both before and after, with automatic restore-from-backup on startup if the live file is found corrupt (this is the exact recovery path Chapter 6's lifespan() invokes). Postgres instead shells out to pg_dump --format=custom and restores with pg_restore --clean --if-exists . Both backends produce tar bundles with optional X25519 encryption — and the encryption key is required, by an explicit enforced check, to live outside the backup directory itself, for a reason that should be obvious once stated: an encrypted backup whose decryption key sits right next to it in the same backup archive or directory provides no real protection at all if that directory is ever copied, leaked, or compromised as a whole. Migration ( migration/sqlite_to_postgres.py ) is a completely separate concept from Alembic, despite touching some of the same territory — Alembic (Chapter 10) only ever handles schema DDL, forward-only, automatically, on every startup. This module is a one-shot, admin-triggered data copy: an operator moving from the zero-config SQLite dev setup to a real Postgres production deployment runs this once, and it first runs alembic upgrade head against the new Postgres target to get the schema right, then copies actual rows table by table in dependency order (respecting foreign-key relationships so a child row is never inserted before its parent exists), persisting progress into sync_state so that a crash mid-migration is correctly reported to the operator as "interrupted, needs attention" rather than silently appearing to have succeeded, or worse, silently appearing as if it simply hadn't started. Diagnostics ( support_pack.py ) assembles a single redacted JSON bundle — health status, database integrity, feed health, correlation status, production-posture warnings, and recent log entries — for an operator to hand to someone helping them debug an issue, explicitly redacting database connection URLs and never including secrets of any kind, consistent with Chapter 13's redaction discipline. Monitoring ( api_key_health.py ) actively pings every external API key BRIEFR has configured (NVD, Groq, Gemini, GitHub, OTX, GreyNoise, AbuseIPDB, and others) with a cheap, low-cost probe request, persists the result, and emits an operator notification (Chapter 28) the moment one goes unhealthy — with a genuinely thoughtful dedup detail: it normalizes digit runs inside error messages before comparing them for deduplication purposes, so an error message whose only difference from the last one is an embedded timestamp or a changing port number doesn't defeat deduplication and spam the operator with what looks like a new, distinct failure every single time it's checked. Wallboard ( wallboard/service.py , session.py ) is a read-only kiosk-mode dashboard — the kind of thing you'd put on a wall-mounted monitor in a SOC — cached for roughly 45 seconds since kiosk displays typically poll every 60 to 120 seconds and don't need fresher data than that. It runs its own entirely separate signed httpOnly cookie session scheme rather than reusing the main JWT auth system from Chapter 11, specifically so the raw, shareable WALLBOARD_TOKEN secret is never actually stored client-side in any form a browser could expose — a deliberate isolation between "credential a human logs in with" and "credential a kiosk display authenticates with," even though both ultimately grant read access to similar data.
