The rest of the backup toolchain, and two smaller ops files backup/postgres_util.py holds every Postgres-specific helper manager.py calls into rather than implementing directly: locating the real pg_dump / pg_restore binaries (checking both the system PATH and Debian's versioned /usr/lib/postgresql/N/bin/ path), running them as subprocesses with --no-owner --no-acl (so a restore doesn't fight over Postgres role ownership on a different box), tolerating pg_restore 's exit code 1 as "warnings only" rather than a hard failure, verifying a dump file's integrity by checking its magic-byte header before trusting it, and redacting the connection URL's embedded credentials before it's ever written to a log line. backup/__main__.py is the CLI surface an operator actually runs by hand or from a cron job ( python -m backup run|list|restore|verify|ensure|keygen ) — pure argument dispatch onto the functions above and in manager.py , each subcommand returning a shell-appropriate exit code so it composes correctly in scripts. monitoring/notifications.py is the aggregation layer sitting one level above the API-key health checker: it merges recent audit-log rows, job-error entries, and unhealthy-key alerts into a single, time-ordered operator notification feed — reusing Chapter 13's audit-log redaction rather than re-implementing it. metrics/request_counter.py is genuinely trivial, confirmed directly rather than assumed: a thread-locked integer counter with an atomic read-and-reset, existing purely to answer "how many requests came in since the last resource sample" for the resource-monitoring collector this chapter's Chapter 31 companion covers. Self-check Why must a backup's encryption key live outside the backup directory itself — what specific failure scenario does this prevent? Why is migration/sqlite_to_postgres.py a separate module from Alembic, when it still invokes Alembic internally as its very first step? Why does the API key health monitor normalize digit runs inside error messages before deduplicating them? Why does the wallboard use its own separate cookie session scheme instead of the main JWT auth system covered in Chapter 11? Why does backup/postgres_util.py tolerate pg_restore exiting with code 1 rather than treating any non-zero exit as a hard failure? Why does monitoring/notifications.py reuse Chapter 13's audit-log redaction rather than building its own masking for the merged feed?

title: Scripts and top-level admin guardrails
text: Part V · Chapter 31 Scripts and top-level admin guardrails The last chapter of Part V — smaller pieces, but each with a specific, deliberate reason for existing exactly as it does. scripts/create_user.py destructive_actions.py task_registry.py tracking.py scripts/create_user.py is the only way to provision or reset a login account in BRIEFR — deliberately never exposed over HTTP, referenced explicitly by auth.py 's own comments as a security boundary rather than an accidental limitation: account creation requires shell access to the box the instance runs on, closing off any possibility of a network-reachable account-creation or password-reset endpoint being abused. scripts/backfill_poc.py and scripts/sync_env.py are smaller maintenance utilities — a one-shot backfill of proof-of-concept availability flags for legacy rows, and a tool that regenerates .env from .env.example while carefully preserving existing values and comment structure. All three scripts re-exec into the app's own virtual environment if run under system Python that lacks the right dependencies ( aiosqlite specifically) — a small systemd-deployment convenience that avoids a confusing "module not found" error for an operator who ran the script with the wrong interpreter. DESTRUCTIVE_ACTIONS: tuple[DestructiveAction, ...] = ( DestructiveAction( "storage.purge.ioc_cache" , "clear" , "Deletes all rows from ioc_cache. Next lookups will re-query external APIs." ), DestructiveAction( "storage.purge.feed_cache" , "clear" , "Deletes all rows from feed_cache. Next incident feed load will be slower." ), DestructiveAction( "storage.purge.epss_history_old" , "prune" , "Deletes epss_history rows older than 90 days." ), # ...one entry per destructive action, each with its own required confirm word... ) destructive_actions.py, real code — one dataclass instance per confirm-gated action The module's own docstring explains exactly what it generalizes: before this file existed, confirm-gated destructive actions lived only as a hardcoded map inside routers/admin.py , specific to storage purges alone. Every other destructive admin action (scheduler pause/resume, a full restart, the Postgres data migration from Chapter 30, deleting a webhook destination) either had no confirmation step at all, or had one hand-coded separately, differently, in whatever router happened to implement it. Generalizing this into one dataclass-based registry means the frontend can render a correct, appropriately-worded confirmation dialog generically for any destructive action, by simply calling GET /api/admin/destructive-actions — rather than the frontend needing to hardcode a matching confirm string per page, which would inevitably drift out of sync the next time someone changed the required confirm word on the backend without remembering to update the frontend's copy of it. task_registry.py exists because of a genuinely subtle Python detail worth knowing in its own right: asyncio 's event loop only holds a weak reference to a task you spawn with asyncio.create_task() and don't otherwise keep a reference to — meaning Python's garbage collector is technically free to collect that task object (silently cancelling it mid-execution) the moment nothing else refers to it, even while it's still actively running. A fire-and-forget background operation (an ingest sync, a snapshot build) spawned this way could simply vanish partway through, with no exception, no log message, nothing — a bug class documented internally as REST-002/REST-012. task_registry.py 's fix is to hold a strong reference to every such spawned task in a registry the module itself owns, specifically so shutdown can wait (with a bounded timeout, not indefinitely) for in-flight tasks to finish cleanly, instead of either killing them mid-write or leaving them to be silently garbage-collected at an unpredictable moment. Finally, tracking.py is worth a one-line correction to a natural first assumption: despite the generic name, this is external API quota tracking — daily, weekly, monthly, and hourly usage counters per external service (NVD, VirusTotal, AbuseIPDB, GreyNoise, OTX, and the LLM providers from Chapter 24) — not user analytics or telemetry of any kind. Its has_quota() check gates outbound calls before they're made, letting BRIEFR proactively avoid exceeding a provider's quota rather than discovering the violation only after a request fails. The last five files: metering's two halves, queue-status labeling, the read cache, and resource sampling Top-level api_metering.py and db/api_metering.py (Chapter 9) share a name but split a single job in two: the top-level file is the write-path hook , called from resilient_client.py after literally every outbound HTTP attempt anywhere in the system, pulling actor/job/request context from contextvars and handing off to the db/ module's actual SQL — wrapped in a bare try/except specifically so a metering failure can never take down the outbound call it's trying to measure. api_queue_operations.py is not a queue implementation at all — it's pure labeling and redaction for the API-queue status UI Chapter 16 describes: it translates internal operation keys into analyst-facing strings ("Fetching vulnerability intelligence" rather than cve_lookup ), and sanitizes any context ID before it's ever displayed — a CVE ID or IP address passes through cleanly, but a webhook URL gets its path tail stripped so a Discord/Slack webhook secret embedded in a URL never surfaces in the admin UI. read_cache.py is exactly as small as it sounds, confirmed directly: an in-process dictionary plus a monotonic clock, a 45-second default TTL, no Redis, no persistence — this is the literal mechanism behind /api/health 's caching from Chapter 25. resource_collector.py is the scheduler-side sampler feeding the admin Resources dashboard (Chapter 30's resource_metrics.py table): it walks BRIEFR's own process tree (and Postgres's, when applicable) via psutil , computes CPU percentage from raw time deltas rather than trusting a blocking library call, and pulls the request count from metrics/request_counter.py on every sample specifically so the counter can be reset immediately after each reading. storage_metrics.py is the complementary table-level view: per-table disk usage (a genuinely different query per backend — Postgres's own size functions vs. SQLite's dbstat virtual table) and a rough daily-growth estimate derived from comparing successive backup archive sizes over time, honestly reporting "insufficient history" rather than guessing when fewer than two backups exist to compare. Self-check Why is account creation deliberately never exposed over HTTP, even behind admin authentication? What specific attack surface does that close off entirely? Explain, precisely, why a fire-and-forget asyncio.create_task() call can be silently garbage-collected mid-execution, and how holding a strong reference in a registry prevents that. destructive_actions.py and operator_settings.py (Chapter 7) are both sometimes described as "admin guardrails." Do they actually share any code, or only a theme? Why does that distinction matter? Why does top-level api_metering.py wrap its entire body in a bare try/except, when most of this book's other outbound-call code paths are careful to raise on genuine failures? Why does api_queue_operations.py specifically strip the path tail from a webhook URL before displaying it in the admin queue-status view? Why does storage_metrics.py explicitly report "insufficient history" rather than producing a growth estimate from just one backup archive?

title: Deployment, CI, and testing
text: Part V-B · Operations in production Deployment, CI, and testing Everything in this book so far describes what runs. This short part covers what makes it keep running unattended, and what stops a broken change from reaching that production box in the first place — a category this book hadn't covered on its own terms yet.

title: Deployment and infrastructure — the real systemd unit and nginx config, read closely
text: Part V-B · Chapter 32 Deployment and infrastructure — the real systemd unit and nginx config, read closely Every hardening flag in these two files is a specific, named decision — not boilerplate copied from a tutorial. deploy/briefr-backend.service deploy/nginx-briefr.conf deploy/setup.sh The systemd unit — hardening flags that are each a real decision Reading deploy/briefr-backend.service directly rewards close attention, because nearly every line is a security or reliability decision with its own comment explaining why, not a default left in place. ExecStart runs uvicorn main:app --workers 1 — and the file's own comment states plainly why this specific number is load-bearing rather than a starting point to tune upward: Chapter 12's rate-limit token buckets are in-memory per worker process; raising the worker count without also switching to the shared database-backed rate-limit store ( BRIEFR_RATE_LIMIT_STORE=db ) would silently multiply every configured limit by the worker count, exactly the failure mode that chapter described in the abstract, now confirmed as a real, named risk in the deployment config itself. TimeoutStopSec=15 exists for a similarly specific reason: the same comment notes that when the database pool is exhausted (Chapter 9's PoolExhaustedError ), in-flight requests hang on pool acquisition and a graceful uvicorn shutdown would otherwise block for systemd's ~90-second default — capped at 15 seconds so a restart doesn't stall that long. The security hardening block is worth reading as a checklist of what a compromised BRIEFR process would not be able to do: NoNewPrivileges=yes blocks privilege escalation via setuid binaries; ProtectSystem=strict makes the entire filesystem read-only to the process except explicitly listed paths; ReadWritePaths is a short, deliberate allowlist (the backend directory, the backup directory, and the embeddings model cache, the last one marked optional with a leading - so its absence doesn't block startup); ReadOnlyPaths covers the Python virtual environment itself, so even a fully compromised application process can't modify its own interpreter or installed packages on disk. This is the same "least privilege, allowlist everything" instinct you've now seen in the DB explorer (Chapter 9), the SSRF blocklist (Chapter 27), and the search-token scoping (Chapter 11) — applied one more time, at the operating-system level. nginx — TLS termination, security headers, and a caching split that matters deploy/nginx-briefr.conf sits in front of uvicorn and does three jobs. First, unconditional HTTP→HTTPS redirect plus certbot-managed TLS. Second, a layered set of security headers in addition to the ones FastAPI's own middleware already sets (Chapter 6) — defense in depth rather than relying on the application layer alone, including server_tokens off to stop nginx from advertising its own version in response headers. Third, and worth understanding precisely because getting it wrong breaks deploys in a confusing way: a deliberate caching split between two kinds of static asset. Hashed Vite build output under /assets/ gets Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable — safe to cache essentially forever, because Vite's build process changes the filename itself whenever the content changes, so a stale cache simply can't serve wrong content. index.html — the SPA shell — gets the opposite treatment, explicitly never cached, because it's the one file that references the current build's hashed asset filenames; caching it would mean a browser could keep loading old references to asset files a fresh deploy already deleted, breaking the app in a way that only clears on a hard refresh. Self-check Why is --workers 1 a load-bearing constraint rather than a conservative default, and what exact change would you need to make elsewhere before safely raising it? Walk through what ProtectSystem=strict plus the specific ReadWritePaths allowlist would prevent, concretely, if an attacker achieved code execution inside the BRIEFR process. Why must index.html never be cached while everything under /assets/ is cached for a full year — what would a stale index.html actually cause a returning user to experience?

title: CI/CD and testing — the pipeline that's been running in the background of this very book
text: Part V-B · Chapter 33 CI/CD and testing — the pipeline that's been running in the background of this very book Two workflow files, four backend-test jobs, 207 backend test files, 56 frontend test files — and the two jobs that are red on every run, by policy, not by accident. .github/workflows/backend-tests.yml .github/workflows/gitleaks.yml backend/tests/ If you've been watching this document's own pull request, you've already seen this chapter's subject matter fire, repeatedly, as live CI events. backend-tests.yml ("Backend tests") defines four jobs: test (the default suite against SQLite — the zero-config path, matching Chapter 9's dev/test story exactly), test-postgres (the same suite, run again against a real Postgres instance — the concrete enforcement mechanism behind Chapter 9's warning that a query can pass the SQLite suite and still break in production), dependency-audit , and playwright-smoke (a thin browser smoke test using the same Playwright/Chromium setup Chapter 5 covers). A second, separate workflow, gitleaks.yml ("Secret scan"), runs an independent secret-scanning pass over every commit. Two of these five jobs — dependency-audit and gitleaks — are documented project-wide as known-red on every run, a deliberate, explicit decision (not silently broken CI) that keeps them visible without treating them as merge blockers until someone specifically prioritizes fixing their underlying findings. The test suite itself is substantial enough to be a real subject in its own right: 207 backend test files exercise everything from admin config to Alembic revision integrity to AI quota tracking, and 56 frontend test files run through Node's built-in node:test (Chapter 5). The test-postgres job is the single most direct piece of evidence in this entire repository for why Chapter 9 spends as long as it does on the SQLite/Postgres split: it exists purely because relying on the default suite alone was judged insufficient to trust a data-layer change, and running the identical test files against a fundamentally different database engine is the actual mechanism that catches the class of bug (looser SQLite type coercion, different aggregate-function syntax) this book has named specifically in Chapters 9 and 22. Self-check Why does a project deliberately keep two CI jobs ( dependency-audit , gitleaks ) permanently red rather than either fixing them immediately or removing them from CI entirely? What specific class of bug does test-postgres catch that the default test job structurally cannot, no matter how thorough the SQLite-side test suite is? If you were reviewing this exact PR's CI output and saw dependency-audit and gitleaks fail alongside a genuinely new failure in test-postgres , how would you tell which one actually needs your attention?

title: Security posture, in full
text: Part VI · Closing Security posture, in full You've now met every security-relevant decision in this book once, embedded in the chapter where it belonged. This closing chapter pulls them together into one connected argument, organized by the kind of risk each one addresses, so you can hold the whole posture in your head at once rather than as 25 scattered facts.

title: Identity and session security
text: Security posture · 1 Identity and session security BRIEFR's authentication design (Chapter 11) rests on a genuinely coherent set of choices rather than a checklist of unrelated best practices bolted together. The two-token split — a stateless, fast, short-lived JWT paired with a database-backed, slower, fully-revocable refresh token — exists because "fast to check" and "instantly revocable" are in real tension, and rather than pick one property and accept the other's absence everywhere, BRIEFR picks the cheap option for routine requests and keeps the expensive-but-safe option in reserve for exactly the moment revocation matters. Bcrypt with a dummy-hash comparison closes a timing side-channel that a more naive login implementation would leave wide open; refresh-token hashing at rest means a database leak alone can't be replayed as a live session; rotation-with-reuse-detection means a stolen and replayed refresh token leaves a fingerprint rather than vanishing into ordinary-looking traffic. And require_admin 's live database re-check of role on every request is the one place BRIEFR deliberately pays a real performance cost — an extra query per admin request — specifically because staleness in that one check is the highest-value target for a real attacker (a demoted or offboarded admin retaining elevated access). The one tradeoff worth being able to state without hedging, because it's a genuine limitation rather than a mistake: an issued access token cannot be revoked before its 15-minute expiry, full stop, no matter what happens to the session it came from. A well-run incident response for a suspected token leak still has to account for that window.

title: Network trust boundaries
text: Security posture · 2 Network trust boundaries Two subsystems in this book deal directly with "can input from outside be trusted to shape a network request," and both get it right in ways worth naming specifically rather than vaguely. Chapter 27's webhook SSRF hardening does the full correct sequence — resolve, validate against a real blocklist, then connect to the pinned, already-validated IP while still presenting the correct hostname via SNI for TLS — closing the DNS-rebinding gap a naive "just check the hostname" mitigation would leave open. Chapter 12's rate-limiting client-key resolution applies the same underlying discipline to a different problem: forwarded headers ( X-Forwarded-For , CF-Connecting-IP ) are only ever trusted when the actual TCP peer is a known, trusted proxy — never trusted from a direct, untrusted connection, because trusting them unconditionally would let anyone mint unlimited fresh rate-limit buckets simply by lying in a header. Both mechanisms share the same underlying principle, worth generalizing beyond just these two examples: never trust something an adversary can influence without independently verifying it through a channel they can't equally influence. A hostname can be manipulated via DNS; a header can be set to anything by whoever sends the request. A resolved-and-validated IP, and a raw TCP socket's actual peer address, can't be forged the same way — which is exactly why both mechanisms anchor their trust decision there instead.

title: Secrets, at rest and in logs
text: Security posture · 3 Secrets, at rest and in logs Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 together describe how BRIEFR protects sensitive values in two different states — stored, and logged — and the honest thing to notice is that neither protection is total, and both say so about themselves rather than overclaiming. Fernet encryption for operator secrets (Chapter 7) is genuinely additive and non-breaking, but its safety is entirely contingent on BRIEFR_SETTINGS_KEY actually being backed up somewhere separate from the database itself — lose that key and the encrypted secrets are, by the very definition of encryption working correctly, unrecoverable. Log redaction (Chapter 13) only ever inspects the keys of structured extra= fields, never a message string's interpolated content — a documented, deliberate boundary rather than an oversight, which places real weight on every developer's discipline never to write a secret directly into an f-string passed to a logger. The unifying lesson, stated as plainly as possible: BRIEFR's security here comes from structure — a schema-typed secret field, a keyword argument passed correctly — not from a blanket scanner that catches mistakes regardless of how they're made. That's a real, deliberate design choice (a general-purpose secret-scanning system would be slower and noisier), and it means the actual security of any given piece of sensitive data depends on whether the code touching it followed the structural convention correctly. Auditing this codebase for a secret-handling issue means checking call sites against the convention, not just trusting that "redaction exists" as a blanket assurance.

title: Availability, and the request-path discipline underneath all of it
text: Security posture · 4 Availability, and the request-path discipline underneath all of it It would be easy to read Chapters 15, 16, and 20 as three unrelated stories — scheduler locking, outbound circuit breakers, and a correlation-engine performance incident — but they're really the same underlying architectural rule, enforced in three different places: heavy or unbounded work never runs on the request path. Chapter 20's ADR-004 is the clearest illustration of what happens when that rule gets violated even briefly — a 61-second query that silently broke an entire unrelated UI element (Operational Priority) simply because it shared a code path with the actual slow computation. Every subsystem built after that incident — precomputed correlation snapshots, the outbound queue's never-drop-a-request design, the scheduler's dual-lock protection against manual/scheduled collisions — is, in effect, institutional memory from that one production failure, generalized into a standing constraint the rest of the codebase now respects by default rather than by accident. Rate limiting (Chapter 12) closes a more conventional availability gap — protecting BRIEFR's own endpoints from a client, human or automated, that simply sends too many requests — with an honestly-stated residual gap (the LAN-adjacent header-forging scenario) rather than a false claim of completeness.

title: Self-assessment as a first-class feature
text: Security posture · 5 Self-assessment as a first-class feature Chapter 26's security_architecture/ module deserves a place in this closing chapter specifically because it's an unusually mature thing for a project of this size to have built at all: a structured, evidence-gated, self-updating record of the system's own trust boundaries and controls, engineered so it cannot silently drift from what the code actually does, and that ages out of validity automatically rather than silently going stale. Most projects treat "our threat model" as a document written once and never revisited; BRIEFR treats it as a living artifact with the same freshness discipline as anything else that matters — a design instinct worth noticing on its own, independent of any of the specific findings it happens to surface.

title: Roadmap, reversals, and open gaps
text: Part VI · Closing Roadmap, reversals, and open gaps Everything so far described what BRIEFR is today. This chapter covers the other three tenses: what it deliberately will never be, what it used to be before a decision reversed it, and what nobody has gotten to yet — pulled from the project's own roadmap, backlog, and change history, not speculation.

title: Explicit non-goals — what this will never try to be
text: Roadmap · 1 Explicit non-goals — what this will never try to be A short, deliberately-scoped list, stated once in ROADMAP.md and treated as binding until explicitly revisited. Five non-goals are recorded as standing decisions, each with a stated reason rather than left as an assumption: Non-goal Reason on record Commercial SIEM replacement BRIEFR is an intel / detection-content / investigation pane, not a log-ingestion platform Log firehose ingestion in core app Handled by an optional Jupiter (ClickStack) sidecar if wanted, kept out of core Multi-tenant SaaS in V1.x Single operator today; schema seams left for future multi-user support, not built now Forking HyperDX / rebuilding Kibana Use stock ClickStack for a telemetry UI instead of maintaining a bespoke fork Generic LLM chat SOC Considered a commodity; BRIEFR uses LLMs sparingly, only for summaries and detection-card enrichment Read together, these five decisions are what keep Chapter A1's monolith architecture viable — each one rules out exactly the kind of workload (massive log ingestion, many independent tenants, a general-purpose chat interface) that would eventually force the system toward the distributed architecture it currently, deliberately, doesn't have. Self-check Pick one non-goal and explain, concretely, what would break in BRIEFR's current monolith architecture if that boundary were crossed. Why does the project prefer adopting an existing tool (ClickStack) for optional telemetry rather than building the equivalent feature natively?

title: What was tried, shipped, and later reversed
text: Roadmap · 2 What was tried, shipped, and later reversed Real decisions this codebase made and then deliberately undid — the most honest way to understand a system is to see what it tried and walked back, not just what it currently does. The legacy admin-key header, replaced by real accounts (Spec A0, decided 2026-07-05). Before Chapter 11's login system existed, BRIEFR authenticated administrative access with a single shared secret header ( X-BRIEFR-Admin-Key ) — effectively one shared password for anyone who needed admin access, with no per-user identity, no audit trail of which admin did something, and no way to revoke one person's access without rotating the key for everyone. It was removed in favor of the full account system this book covers in Chapter 11 — individual users, roles checked live against the database, sessions that can be revoked per-account. This is worth reading as the clearest single example in this codebase of "we shipped the simple version first, learned its limits, and replaced it" rather than getting the design right on the first attempt. Anthropic/Claude, removed from the LLM failover chain. Track K's own record states plainly: "No paid APIs — no Anthropic (removed from the chain for now)." Chapter 24 already established that BRIEFR's current LLM chain (Groq → Cerebras → OpenRouter → Gemini) contains no Anthropic client anywhere in the code — this entry confirms that's a reversal, not an oversight: a premium-tier provider was in the chain at some point and was deliberately taken back out, consistent with the project's stated goal of keeping a self-hosted tool's operating cost near zero. "For now" signals this is a scoping decision tied to the free-tier cost strategy, not a permanent technical exclusion. db/dialect.py , a general SQL translation layer, deleted entirely (Post-B, 2026-07). Chapter 9 already covers what replaced it — paired _SQLITE / _PG query constants written by hand — but it's worth naming this explicitly as a reversal rather than just a current-state fact: a general-purpose translator that tried to make one SQL string work on both databases automatically was tried, and abandoned in favor of deliberately writing both dialects out by hand. The lesson embedded in that reversal: an automatic translation layer that almost works is more dangerous in a data layer than an explicit, slightly more verbose approach that always works. Chart.js, mid-reversal right now. Chapter 3's library registry already covers this as a live migration rather than a completed one: Chart.js is explicitly deprecated in favor of Recharts, ported chart-by-chart, page-atomic, with both libraries coexisting temporarily and Chart.js scheduled for full removal once the last chart moves. Worth including here specifically because it's a reversal you can watch happen in real time across pull requests, rather than one you only see after the fact in a changelog. Self-check What specific capability did the legacy admin-key header lack that the current per-user system provides — name the exact gap, not just "it was less secure." Why might a project deliberately exclude a premium-tier LLM provider from its failover chain even if that provider would produce marginally better output? What made a general-purpose SQL dialect translator riskier than writing both dialects by hand — tie your answer back to Chapter 9's data-layer discussion.

title: What's next, what's parked, and what hasn't been considered yet
text: Roadmap · 3 What's next, what's parked, and what hasn't been considered yet Pulled directly from the open backlog and the performance audit's own findings — the honest "not yet" list, not a guess at future features. Explicitly parked, by the maintainer's own signal (not forgotten, just deprioritized): a STIX/Sigma bulk export feature planned for an earlier release phase; a full, production-grade docker-compose.yml covering the entire stack (today's compose file covers Postgres alone, per Chapter 9); and the remainder of one performance-hardening track beyond what's already shipped. These are recorded as deliberately paused, not abandoned — a distinction worth preserving when discussing them, since "parked" and "rejected" mean different things in this project's own vocabulary. Explicitly out of scope for the resource-benchmarking program, by decision rather than oversight: synthetic load simulation, Prometheus/Grafana metrics export, per-endpoint latency histograms, and alerting on resource thresholds. What did ship in that same program is real and already covered in Chapter 30's territory: a resource-metrics table with a psutil -based collector job and retention policy, plus an admin-facing Resources page showing CPU/memory trends over 1/3/7/30-day windows. The gap between what shipped and what's out of scope is precise: BRIEFR can show an operator their own instance's resource trend, but does not (yet, by decision) simulate load, export to external monitoring stacks, or alert automatically when something crosses a threshold. Genuinely not yet considered, per the performance audit's own words: a documented, recommended CPU/RAM/disk sizing envelope — the exact gap Chapter A2 discussed in detail, restated here as a concrete backlog item rather than an abstract observation. Alongside it, the same audit flags the connection-pool sizing defaults, the OFFSET-pagination default, and the unbounded frontend vendor chunk as measured-but-unaddressed findings — real, specific, and modest in scale today, but the first places load would show up if usage grew meaningfully beyond a single operator. Near-term "next," in the project's own words from its most recent working sessions: admin-facing retrieval health monitoring and operator-tunable knobs for the semantic search system (Chapter 24), following directly on from the embeddings work covered in this book. This is the kind of "next" that's genuinely close — already scoped, waiting on the current program to close out — rather than a distant aspiration. Self-check What's the practical difference, in this project's own usage, between something "parked" and something "rejected as a non-goal" (Chapter Roadmap·1)? Give one example of each. Why would a team deliberately ship resource-trend visibility (the Resources admin page) while explicitly declining to build alerting on top of the same data? Connect one item from this chapter's "not yet considered" list back to a specific design decision from an earlier chapter that makes it a natural next step rather than an arbitrary one.

title: Glossary
text: Reference Glossary Watermark A saved checkpoint (timestamp, ID, or commit SHA) marking how far an incremental sync has progressed, so a resumed run knows exactly where to continue from. Idempotent An operation whose repeated application has the same effect as applying it once — the property that makes crash-and-retry safe. Circuit breaker After N consecutive failures calling a dependency, stop trying entirely for a cooldown period, rather than continuing to fail slowly and repeatedly. Token bucket A rate-limiting algorithm where a bucket refills with tokens at a fixed rate and each request consumes one, smoothing bursts while still permitting occasional spikes. SSRF Server-Side Request Forgery — tricking a server into making a request on an attacker's behalf, often reaching internal-only services. CVSS Common Vulnerability Scoring System — a static 0–10 technical severity score for a vulnerability. EPSS Exploit Prediction Scoring System — a live 0–1 probability of real-world exploitation in the next 30 days. KEV CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog — confirmed, not predicted, real-world exploitation. CPE Common Platform Enumeration — NVD's structured naming scheme for exactly which software/versions a CVE affects. MITRE ATT&CK A knowledge base of real-world adversary tactics and techniques, each with a stable ID like T1190 . Sigma rule A vendor-neutral YAML detection-logic format, translatable into any SIEM's native query language. Hub IOC / hub suppression An indicator (often an IP) shared across so many unrelated threat-intel pulses that it carries no real distinguishing signal — excluded from BRIEFR's correlation expansion above a configured threshold. Operational Priority BRIEFR's P1–P4 band, derived from a fixed Threat Score × Environment Relevance lookup table, with an optional one-band bump from correlation escalation. Connection pool A set of already-open database connections handed out to requests as needed, avoiding the cost of opening a fresh connection per request. Dependency injection FastAPI's mechanism for declaring "this route needs X" as a function parameter, run automatically before the route handler.
